div.head: ATHLETIC RECORDS.
div.p: ATHLETIC RECORDS.
Cross Country Running.

In local circles recently there has been discussion I concerning athletics, their national value, prospects, and particularly the part Warrington will play in the eflort to overcome the lethargy by which Britishers have lost prestige in allowing National supremacy to slip from them. It will be remembered that in the 8,000 metres cross country race,at the 1912 Olympiad, the United Kingdom cut a moderate figure, whereas Sweden specialised and won. Britishers were chagrined with the knowledge that a better team, including Vose and Holbrook, had been left at home, and that the team which our athletic legislators did take was poorly managed, for financial reasons—nice excuse from the "richest nation in the world. NEXT OLYMPIAD. The Crown Prince cf Sweden proved himself a national asset at the Stockholm games and according to report his Government have made a substantial grant towards finding and preparing Swedish athletes for the Berlin celebration in 1916, in connection with which Germany is alive to all the moves on the board and with the Kaiser at the head of affairs, the Teutons evidently mean business. The "almighty dollar " people were very conspicuuus at the last three Olympiads and for the next a " million " has been subscribed to " sweep the decks," but whatever else we have done, our distance runners have proved superior to the Americans who now claim to have the greatest coaches in the world. Our Gallic friends will spare no effort to send up, in Berlin, the tricolour, and the first six in the recent international were :—France : Bonliu I, Keyser 3, Lavaux 5 9 points; England : Glover 2, Lee 4, Vose 6 - 12 points and an olympic count is three aside Baldwin, Wallach, Scott, Sanderson and Kerr all -finished before the next French representative, Arbide (Algerian), who was 75 seconds behind Vose, but the youth Arbide should improve more than the others.

div.head: NATIONAL WANT.
div.p: A NATIONAL WANT.

The United Kingdom requires plenty of young and enthusiastic raw material, also public spirited effort to develop it by advice and encourage it by apprecia- tion and with financial support when necessary. The highest authorities agree that athletics, chiefly cross- country running, require clean living and clean thinkit g and represent the keystone to the welfare of ths nation's young maohood.

div.head: 10-MILES FLAT RECORDS.
div.p: 10-MILES FLAT RECORDS.

The fastest professional time : On September 28th, 188 c, W. Cummings did smins. 6 3-s,3ecs. against W. G. George in a match run at Lillie Bridge. This stood until September 16th, 1899, when H. Watkins did 51mins. 5 1-Sat ca. in one hours' race against time, at Rochdale. W. Steele did the American professional record of 52 10 1-5 at New York on May 19th, 1883. The fastest amateur time for Canada is 53min. 598ec5. On the Continent the record is held by J. Bonin (France) with 51 32 3-ssecs. George V. Bonhag did the American amateur record of 52 34 4-5 at Celtic Park, New York, on November 6th, 1909, but in a one hour run for rEcord at West of Scotland Harriers sports held at Ibrox Park, Glasgow, on November sth, 1904, Alfred Shrubb accomplished 50min. 40 3 secs. and this still stands not only as the British Amateur best but as a world's record. This is a propositicn for 11-,uin, Glover, &c. Owing to meaFuremnt difficulties with grass tracks the many otherwise well accredited per- formances do not appear on the official records, but in the Northern Counties Championship which is to be held under the auspices of the local athletic club, on the Warrington Football ground next Saturday, arrangements are to be made for the measurement to be certified and, with Glover in good trim, he should put down a performance worthy of the best traditions of British athletes and rumour says be will be made to run to do it. ERNEST GLOVER.

At the first attempt Ernest Glover won the A.A.A. 10 miles fiat championship, time 51 56 4-5 and the Yorkshireman's friends were not surprised, if other people were. Glover who is very enthusiastic about his running, and has the advice and help of one of the best cc aches in the country, is better known as a cross country runner. He won the " Yorkshire " in 1911, 1912 and 1913. In the Northern a third in 1910 was expected to be followed by a win in 1911, but Chris Vose triumphed on the Haydock Park Racecourse. Glover won at Lofthouse Park in 1912, and again at Stockton this year be was first home in 53nrin. 42sec. (the fastest Northern) with Chris Vose second doing 51mios. In the " National " Glover has always been prominent, and the title was his at Wolverhampton recently. In the " International " Glover's performances have been good and in this season's race he was second to Bonin, the man with the best cross country reputation.

div.head: BOWLING GREEN.
div.p: THE BOWLING GREEN.
Four Municipal Greens now Open.
TO-DAY'S COMPETITIONS

Away, King Football, away ! Your lease has expired and will not be renewed for a few months! What! we shall be lost without you? May be we shall miss you, but, never fear, we have our attractions even when you are gone. The dirty, muddy, foggy days go—or we hope they will—with you. The more rapidly they disappear, the better, for we want none of them. With the advent of the brighter days it is to the bowling green we chiefly turn. Au reroir.

Now that the fo tball season is over, local trundlers are greatly interesting themselves in their favourite pastime and during the past week the various greens have been exceedingly well patronised. The thunder- storm of Tuesday played havoc, but if the fine weather of the past few days continues the various swards will be in tip-top condition.

div.head: MORE MUNICIPAL GREENS.
div.p: MORE MUNICIPAL GREENS.

Warrington has now four municipal greens. The one in Victoria Park proved to be a huge success, and the Corporation, after much delay, has provided others, an additional one in Victoria Park, Manchester- road, and one in Liverpool-road recreation ground. Another is in course of construction on the site of Grace's Pottery, Winwick-road, but this will not be opened this season.
On account of the Northern Union Cup Final the various competitions in the town were postponed last Saturday, but they will be resumed to-day.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. Peter Peacock Challenge Cup. This competition commences to-day on the Bank Quay Green, which is reported to be in excellent condition. The games for to-day were published last week. The following is a list of the games for next Saturday, May 10th : 2.0 Whitecross C. v Latchford E. 2.45 Howley D. v St. Johns A. 3.30 Bewsey D. v Orford D. 9.15 Whitecross D. v Whitecross a 5.0 Wbitecross N. v Fairfield G. 5.45 Whitecross R. v Bewsey A. 6.30 Howley K. v Orford A. 7.15 St. Johns E. v St. Johns B, 8.0 St. Johns C. v Howley E. Referee, W. Unsworth ; assistant, J. Bailey and W Vose, gate-keeper.

div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING ASSOCIATION.

The first round championship in connection with the above association should have commenced last Saturday but the games were postponed, as follows : Liberal Club v Senior Coneervative, May 3 end 10. King and Queen v Fearnhead, May 10 and 17. Penketh Tannery v Oros&lds No 2,Nlay 10 and 17. Whitecross v Junior Conservatives May 17th. Rylands v Bulls Head, home and away May 17. Cemetery v Crostlelds No 1 home and away May 17. For to-day's match with the Conservatives, the Liberal Club will take an exceptionally good team to Sankey-street and their chances are very rosy. The chosen contingent is :—T. O'Brien (captain), F. Walker, A. Gleave, Joe Gleave, M. Tobin, C. Jordan, W. Patrick, J. Firth, J. W. Rigby, F. Dale, A. Lawton and ft Fogg, W. J. Smith, J. Gibson, W. Taylor and J. Broadbent, senior, (reserves.) LANCASHIRE COUNTY BOWLING ASSOCIATION.

A start in this competition will he made to-day. The Warrington teams who have entered this season are Bull's Head, Junior Conservative, Cemetery, Rylands' and Whitecross. There are about 50 teams in the competition and the games played on the knock- out principle will be decided on neutral greens.

div.head: DRAW FOR THE CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP.
div.p: DRAW FOR THE CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP.

The annual business of tbe Lancashire County Bowling Association, presided over by Mr. J. G. Coombs, was held on Thursday evening at the Albion Hotel, Manchester. There was a good attendance of delegates and the chief business was the draw for the first round of the club championship, which will be decided to-morrow.

To the selection committee, in place of Mr. H. Dawtion, Mr. C. W. Smith was elected. An applica- tion was received from the Walker and Hocutray's Association to hold the annual charity handicap and this was granted. The decision of the individual merit committee to again divide this year's individual merit championship into four sections—Manchester, Liverpool, Southport, and Blackpool was adopted—players being allowed to play in any section. Entries for this event close on Wednesday, June 11th.
The drav for the club championship shows that the Warrington teams fixtures ere : Calderston Park v. Whitecross Works. Whitecross Works received a walk-over.

Warrington Cemetery v. Griffin (Lower Broughton), at Lord Nelson, Urmston. Pendleton Belmont v. Warrington Bull's Head, at Leigh Railway. Peel Green v. Rylands Workmen's, at Irlams-o'-th'- Height. Urmston Victoria v.Warrington Junior Conservatives at Cadishead.
"THUMB BIAS."
HIGH PRICES FOR TAPESTRY.

A set of four panels of Burgundian tapestry represent- ing the history of Isabella the Catholic sold for £14,700 at Christie's. They formed part of the Lionel Phillips collection, which to date has realised nearly £lOO,OOO. A panel of Brussels tapestry sold for £504. A Persian rug Oft. by 4ft. 9in. fetched £367, and a five-leaf screen. of Chinese lacquer £3Ol.

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: THE FOOTBALL CLUB.
WARRINGTON'S RECORD FOR 1912-13.
By " Ovalist."

Cup-tie glories alone saved Warrington from having to report a dismal season in 1912-13,and much will be forgiven them for reaching the final of the Cup Com- petition for the fifth time, even though success was denied the W arrington lads. The similarity between this season and the last is remarkable. Twelve months ago an uncommon run in the cup-ties saved the situa- tion but more strikpg -still is the parallel between Warrington's League records for the two seasons. They are practically identical, as witness.

Last season was the worst on record, and the one I just concluded is no better. In fact, a close examina- tion of the figures given above shows the Club in even more sombre colcurs. The attack is dwindling away to nothing. Six years ago the scorers accumulated 554 ' points in 34 League games; last season the total had oropped to 23S for 3f games, and this season it has fallen to 21-1. Luckily the defence is still holding out, —another tribute to, at any rate, the resoluteness of Warrington football. The Wirepullers are still lacking the same big LACK. Pace and combination seemed to vanish with Fish, Isherwood and Co. Allied to the great defence, which has been strongly in evidence in all big matches for the last two seasons, they would not only have raised Warrington to a commanding position among the League clubs, but they would have brought the Cup to Wilderspool. Last Saturday's final with Huddersfield eloquently confirms my views. War- rington were forced to fill the roll of spoilers because all the pace and cleverness were on the other side. And it was the two latter qua.ities which eventually settled the issue against the Wirepuller'. But 1 need not harp continually on the same string. The Warrington Committee are as well aware of the club's shortcomings in a playing sense as I am, and, they are entitled to some credit for having tried man- fully to remedy the defect, even if they have not actually succeeded. I say without hesitation that records notwithstanding, the club is stronger in a play- ing sense than it was a year ago.

div.head: HOPE OF THE TEAM.
div.p: THE HOPE OF THE TEAM.

There are more young players in the side, the shirkers have been weeded out, and it on:y needs the discovery of one or two hacks of outstanding ability to make a senior thirteen capable of grest things in the League as well as in the Cup competition. The average age of the players to-day is probably lower than ever it was— which is a good sign. G. Thomas, Brooks and Renwick are the only ones in the veteran class, and even they have been among Warrington's best this season. Among the acquisitions are Ben Jolley, the youthful full back who is not only upholding an honoured name, but is fast ni.sking a big reputation for himself, Warrington are fortunate in their custodian. Then there is Tranter, who from being a fine forward has developed into a centre .of absolute reliability. At half, young Nicholas is proving to be the best Welsh capture,. for years past and he is the " baby" of the team. Forward, we have six men who are second to none, but in this department the reserves are inade- quate. On the "A" team there are distinctly promising players like P. Clare, A. Brown, Douglas, Bardsley, Davies and Blundell. There has been no lack of experimenting during the season, as the extended trials of such men as Rushton and Williams of Halifax amply prove. Every investment cannot be expected to turn up trumps! Warrington can face the future with considerably more optimism than for some time past. They have already got a promising new half back in Ruddick, of Coventry, who made his initial appearance this week, and all anxieties in regard to this department—long a source of weakness—may be considered at an end. The one great need is a speeding-up of the three-quarter line. Our four "threes "to-day are better detenders than attackers, and the acquisition of both speedier wings and centres can alone raise the Club to the eminence it occupied half-a-dozen years ago. Dickenson has already dropped out—but his benefit has to comel-r Brooks is getting older, and was never an ideal wing, while Renwick is obviously slowing down. When Warrington have got another scoring three-quarter line, Huddersfield will not be the only great team in the land! "Hone lives eternal," and thrives nowhere better than in the breast of the football enthusiast. And in Warrington the breed is a tough one! RECORD OF THE SEASON.

div.head: RYLANDS' RECORD SEASON.
div.p: RYLANDS' RECORD SEASON.
LEAGUE CHAMPIONS AND FINALISTS FOR THE MANCHESTER SHIELD.

Sportsmen of Warrington have every reason to be exceedingly proud of the achievements of the Rylands Recreation Rugby Football Club during the past season for not only have they won the premier position in the Manchester Rugby League, but they are also finalist for the Manchester and District Shield which is the trophy in a knock-out competition for the teams in the first and second division of the Manchester and District Rugby League. Last season, the team justified for admission from the second to the first division of the league and to top that in the first season is a remarkable and noteworthy achievement. Their record was as follows :

Cadishead occupy the second position, being seven points behind the leaders. The teams who defeated the wireworkers were Prestwich C. I. away by five points to three and Ashton-under-Lyne away by eight points to four. In the Lancashire Junior Cup competition the local team were defeated in the third round by Pemberton Rovers by six points to three, Pemberton Rovers ultimately winning the final tie against Leigh Rangers. In the Northern Union qualifying rounds they were beaten at Leigh by Leigh Shamrocks on a wretched ground, by three points to nil. The wireworkers will retain the Manchester and District Shield, which they won last year, until they meet Weaste in the final to be played on the first Saturday in September, the clubs not having been able to get an extension of the season. In this competition Rylands have had a very easy time. They should have met Flixton and Barton in the first and second rounds but both teams failed to appear. They defeated Cadishead on April 19th by 19 points to nil. Nearly every player has taken part in the scoring and the League points were: 343 f3r ; 46 against; Lancashire Junior Cup, 48 points for and 15 points against; Northern Union Qualifying rounds, 45 points for and 5 points against. Prayers for China.

The request of the Chinese Republican Government to the Christian churches throughout China for the holding of services of prayer on Sunday for the success of the new National Assembly, and the new Govern- ment received an almost world-wide response. In this country both the Established and the Free Churches received the suggestion with great cordiality, and in cathedrals, churches, and chapels throughout the land special prayers for the future welfare of China were offered up. There was a very great demand for the forms of prayer issued by the S.P.G. and the C.M.S.,and at the request of the Sunday School Union over 10,000 affiliated Sunday schools, containing 2,244,6C8 teachers and scholars also observed tne day as one of intercession ior, Chine.
The special form of prayer was used in the Warring- ton churches. It took the form of a Litany asking for Divine guidance for the new Government, and especially in its choice of a President.

A Plea for Protestantilnity. Rev. H. Ogden, of the Got borne-street Baptist Church preached last week upon the subject "Anglicans and Baptists agree in India: A plea for Protestant Unity." The division of the Church, said the preacher, had been the serious cause of weakness in the Christian army. The Chancellor of the Exchequer in the presence of a dean or two and under the presidency of a Bishop, had declared that there was no combination in these islands that could withstand the policy of a united Church. There was no social scheme which they could not com- plete, there was no evil but would be overcome; there was no statesman would dare to contradict the combined will of all the Christian Churches of England. But when had we seen a united Church? When dad all the churches emphasise the matters in which they agreed and minimise the minor matters in which they disagreed? An evangelical basis would never harmonize with a sacerdotal one,and Protestantism would never be allied with Romanism, but as we saw from India,there was no reason why Protestant and Anglican and Baptist should not agree. From the pages of "The Herald," the Baptist missionary monthly for March 1913, there was the story of a remarkable service in which a Bishop of the Anglican Church took part. On the 29th of last December which day was the 112th anniversary of the baptism of Krishna Pal, two students were baptised. Bishop Azariah the Hindu Bishop of Dornahial baptized the two students by immersion, and he was helped all through the service by Mr. Gee of the Oxford mission. At the chapel there was a service of special prayer, conducted by Mr. Carter, of the Y.M.C.A. The Bishop of Madras "hoped to live to see Mr. Jones, a prominent Congregationalist, celebrate tbe Holy Communion in the Cathedral of Madras. In the face of Brahrninism and Mahomme- denim, all the Protestant forces of India were corn pelled to unite. There was the equal need for unity at home. Only a mere handful of people understood our differences, only a mere handful cared. All men rever- ence the Christ and his message to men and were he churches as one to show to men the seamless robe, instead of quarrelling about the fringe, we could hope to see the day when Christ and the Churches would be one.

The Church and Sunday School. Canon Stevenson Suggests a Syllabus. Representatives from each or the six dioceses in the Province of York met in conference at Manchester, on Tuesday to discuses the work of the Sunday schools. The Bishop of Liverpool presided at the morning session, and gave an address on the growth of the Sunday school movement and the great work it accom- plished among the young. They had at the present time about 7,000,000 Sunday school scholars and 700,000 Sunday school teachers. His Loroship said he was quite sure that if Lord Haldane had 700,000 men at his disposal in the Territorial force he would sleep more calmly than he did now.(Laughter.) "It we had an army of 700,000 men ready to defend our shores we should have no fear of invasion, and the bogey of conscription would he gone for ever." The Bishop added that be had never found among the poor any widespread opposition to religion. He, however, believed that in the day schools there was not the same pertotat touch as there used to be between the day teacher and the day scholar. There was the danger of religion being taught rather as a matter of the head then of the heart. The great danger of the picture houses,another speaker declared, was that things were brought to the know- ledge of young people that ought not to he set before them until a later age.

div.head: S-YLLABDS WANTED.
div.p: A S-YLLABDS WANTED.

The question of a syllabus for Sunday sohools was introduced by Canon Morley Stevenson, of Warrington. He said that in the past there had not been a sufficient planning ahead of the child's course of instruction. The syllabus should be so drawn up as to enable a child to understand that he belonged to the Church of England, and to enter fully into the worship of the Church. In the north it was a tremendous advantage that the Sun- day school life was very much longer than in the South of England. He had seen it stated that 70 per cent, of those who passed through the Church of England Sunday schools did not become members of their churchesif this statement were true, it was a most startling and serious thing. He thought a syllabus, such as he had suggested, was calculated to bind the scholars to the Church as intelligent and loyal members. The Bishop of Liverpool said that the syllabus should be systematic, comprehensive, and graded. He was surprised to hear that the teachers still worsed at their own sweet will. The syllabus ought to cover the whole course of the child's Sunday school life, and it should not be cast iron, but elastic. " 'flank God," the Bishop added, " the day of preaobing teachers is past. We want teaching teachers to-day." (Applause.) - -

Sunday School Anniversary Services were held at this church on Sunday when, notwithstanding the very unfavourable weather, there were large congregations. The pastor, the Rev. T. r. James preached morning and evening. In the course of a sermon On" Wisdom at the Cradle" he refeired to the visit of the Magi to the Infant Christ. Here, he said, was to be discovered a symbolic representation of the truth, vital in its nature, that wisdom displayed itself by gathering round the child. Whatever hopes might stir in the minds of men as to the future, whatever ideals they might conceive as to the possibilities for their own nation or for the race, whatever aspirations might hsve tired their spirits or awakened their courage, it was well that the emphasis should be laid at the right point. And that point was the child. We were beginning to understand tbat better than we did. The note of all our domestic legislation for the last century—Factory Acts, Educa- tion Acts and Temperance reforms—was that of con- sideration for the child, and realization of the infinite value of child life. That was not a mere matter of sentiment, though it, was good as that; it was also a matter of reason, the ordered judgment as to what was our absolute necessity if the future was to have any guarantee of stability. fhe right way to build a race was to begin at the beginning. If we wanted the better future, if we had visions of purer laws, fairer cities, nobler races, ideal commonwealths, kingdoms of God on earth, then we had better get the emphasis on the only possible place. Wisdom gathered round the cradle. And all this reached into regions where legis- lation could achieve something, but where there was much that it could not accomplish. It reached to the permanent influence of tho home life of our nation. 110 MES THAT ARE NOT HOMES.

He was more and more convinced that we needed re-emphasis of the common responsibilities of the home; that we needed to recover a sense of its sanctity and eternal importance. It war, iu the midst of our vaunted civilization,an appalling truth that there were thousands of children to whom religious ideas ought never to be taught in the form of the Fatherhood of God. Their idea of what the word father meant was of such a nature that to identify God with it would be to rob religion of its beauty. The sweetest word of Jesus was His declaration "God is a Father," but the presentation of it in innumerable instances became either impossible or monstrous. There were children in our own town whose greatest misfortune was that they had to live at home. We might say that those were extrme cases; they %ere at least so many as to constitute a standing menace to the future.
THE WAR OF THE FCTURE.

Referring to the importance of the Church's dealing with child life, the preacher said tbey were at present largely engaged in overtaking work that ought never to have belonged to them. The vast mass of the population now outside the churches was once inside their Sunday schools. Must every generation re-create this problem ? Finally the preacher emphasised the fact that the qualities of the child were the essentials of the religious life, and in this connection he laid stress upon sincerity and forgiveness. In an appeal on behalf of missionary enterprise, he said that, youth gloried in a war. Not long ago a Church dignitary publicly lamented our desire for peace, because nations that ceased to make war, lost their vitality. Everyone descended upon him with scathing criticism. Yet at the bottom he was on a great truth, for there was

TRADE UNION GROWTH. STRIKES AND INCREASED MEMBERSHIP.

It appears from a Blue Book issued on Saturday that during the ten years up to 1911 the number of members of trade unions increased by nearly 800,000, equal to one half the membership of 1902. The number of members of the 680 unions making returns in 1911 was 2,378,957. If deductions are taken into account, the increase in membership would amount to about half a million. It is believed that only about one half of all the trade unions in existence are registered but it has been estimated that the mombership of registered unions represents about 80 per cent. of the total membwship of trade unions in the -United Kingdom. The majority of the unions showing heavy increases in membership are connected with the transport trades and general labour. These increases may be attributed, to the transport workers' strike.

Calceolaria, chelidoLifolia, C. pinnata and C. mexicana are the most commonly known, each being useful for this purpose.—" The Garden." Planting Old Walls with Flowers.—For growing plants in the joints, an excellent way is to attach " pcckets " for soil to the front of the wall. Two spike nails are driven into a j lint, and on those a flat stone is cemented. Stones are cemented round the edges of these to form pockets, three or four inches deep, leav- ing a hole or two for the egress of the water. A little drainage is put in the bottom of the pocket and the remainder filled up to about half an inch with th.: usual soil for plants of the class. The flowers are then planted and kept well watered. Many of the Saxifrages, Sednms, Erinus alpinus, Saponari ocymoides, Primula marginate, Arenaries, Achilleas, Cerastfutns, and such like plants are excellent for this wall. The great need is watering in dry weather.— Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review.

div.head: FAILIIIG AT FORTY.
div.p: FAILIIIG AT FORTY.
The Woman at Mildle-age finds Strength in Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

When a woman reaches the age of forty she regards the next few years before her with some anxiety and misgiving, for, wi,h most of the weaker sex, the approach of middle-age brings a serious disturbance of health. At this period of life a state of excessive weakness is usual, with violent headaches and severe pains in back and loins, fits of melancholy and faintiog attacks develop, and the sufferer becomes agitated and irritable over trifles. To build up her health and maintain her strength with new good blood is the surest way to tide over this time of trial, and thousands of women at this crisis have gratefully acknowledged that in Dr. Williams' Pink Pills they have found btreng th , comfort and new health. One of the many grateful patients is Mrs. E. Periy, of 26, Henry-street, Crewe.

"Friends said that I MRS. PERRY. wanted tonics. I tried many of these, but Indigestion followed, with pains and aches in all my limbs. Then I had dreadful headaches, and a backache as though my spine was being dragged apart. Hot flushes swept ovcsr me from head to foot ; my feet and ankles swelled, and my body seemed more than my legs cPuld support. div.head: SIR H. HIBBERT ON EDUCATION EXPENSE.
div.p: SIR H. HIBBERT ON EDUCATION EXPENSE.

Opening a new county school at Tyldesley, which has been built at a cost of nearly £7,000 to accommodate 500 scholars, Sir Henry Hibbert M.P., chairman of the Lancashire Educaticn Committee, said, on Saturday, there could be no doubt that curses loud and deep had been uttered at the miscalled extravagance of the Lancashire County Council in compelling localities, as was said to build schools at an extravagant cost. But the County Council were not masters in their own house. The ratepayers stood, as it were, between the devil and the deep sea, one being the Board of Educa- tion, the other the Lancashire County Council. The Board compelled the County Council to spend money on pain of withdrawing the grant or issuing a mandamus, and the result had been en extensive building pro- gramme in Lancashire, which meant an expense on capital acaount for the next six years, at any rate, of something like .£55,000 per annum. The interest and the sinking fund on that would add to the rate of Lancashire £20,000 per annum.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN. Expert Notes from all Points of View.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN. Expert Notes from all Points of View.
BLAMED THE PM

John Brown,of Peterborough, charged with begging explained that when he was offered an odd day's work pig came along and ate his overcoat, his insurance card, and an ounce of tobacco. Brown was let off with a nominal penalty. IMPROVED CONDITIONS.

The improved conditions, last week, (says the " Times " Agricultural corresppndent) gave a welcome opp )rtunity for pushing on with the sowing of barley, oats, and small seeds, the planting of potatoes, and the prepara- tion of the land for mangels. The accumulation of field work that awaited the change in the weather was greater than could be overtaken within a week, but by making full u9e of every working hour the arrears have been appreciably reduced (in the more pressing classes of work. In their haste to get all the cereals in before the end of the month farmers have had to curtail the amount of surface cultivation, and a good deal of the oats and barley has been drilled in a rather rough seed bed. The typical April showers in the beginning of the week were as valuable in soften- ing the land as in stimulating vegetation. Field work is still backward, but -the outlook is decidedly more hopeful, and if the present week is favourable the sowing of corn will be finished and a beginning made with the planting of mange's. Pastures and meadows have made a fine response to the more inviting conditions, and there are good prospects for both grass and hay. The clovers and mixed seeds have every appearance of giving a bounti- ful yield, the thickness of the plant, as well as the exuberance of growth, justify great expectations of the rotation hay. The indifference of cattle and sheep to the supplementary allowances of roots and hay is a sign that they are able to gather a fair amount of herbage on the pastures. No bulky food is so palatable at this time of year as the young grass, and the animals make the change readily from a partial to a wholly grass diet. A ration of cake and meal never comes amiss, and where supplementary feeding is desirable either to hasten fattening or to increase the flow of milk a small allowance of concentrated stuffs can be given at any time.

div.head: THREATENED DAIRY FARMER.
div.p: THE THREATENED DAIRY FARMER.

In the opinion of those well qualified to judge, there are dangerous rocks ahead for British dairy farmers. It is even being said that thousands of those who have found milk-selling the sheet-anchor of their farming business will be driven to abandon it by the combined effects of the Tuberculosis Order and the Milk Bill, which will shortly become an Act. These measures have been looming on the horizon for years, and the long-threatened storm seems now about to break. It is a very serious matter, and no good can come of shutting our eyes to the difficulties before us. •The worst of the position for the old-fashioned, easy• going milk producer is that be has practically no defence, for even the powerful organisations which exist for the safeguarding of the intercsts of farmers have no word to say in favour of the old methods of handling milk, and ignoring any longer the danger to the public health which are supposed to lurk in the pail. Even the leaders in the projected reforms are known to be apprehensive of serious dislocation of trade by a possibly great shortage during the time of transition, and a consequent rise in the price of milk to the consumers. They believe, however, that the blessing of a pure supply is worth the risk of temporary trouble, and so the country will have to face the crisis as best it may. Most of the large dairy farmers will doubtless fall into line with the new requirements, and so weather the storm, but it may well be feared that large numbers of the small producers will be squeezed out. We may regret this , indeed, but can only bow to the inevitable.—" Old 'Breeder " in " Farm and Home.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Roses.—A good mulching of decayed manure should be given to the roses. As the new growths begin to push out, a watchful eye should be kept for that pest known as the rose maggot; syringing or spraying will not eradicate it, there is nothing safer than going over each shoot carefully, and where the leaf is seen to be curled up, or not opening quite flat, give it a squeeze between the thumb and forefinger. If blooms are wanted for show purposes some of the buds and shoots will have to be rubbed off.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

Hardy Annual Calceolarias.—Among the many hardy annuals, few are more deserving of a place in our gardens than the annual calceolarias. Seeds of these sown now in beds or borders containing Aquilegias, Sweet Williams, or similar early-flowering plants will make such beds look bright at the latter part of the summer when the permanent occupants are over. They are easily grown. Seeds may be scattered among the early-flowering plants and raked in the Soil, which should be fairly rich. A good watering occasionally during the dry weather is all that will be found necessary.

div.head: KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.
div.p: KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.
Warrington Widow's Claim for Compensation.

At Lelgh County Court on Friday last, Mary 'Toward of 22, Queen-street, Warrington, applied for an award under the Workmen's Compensation Act against Messrs. Roberts and Sons, of Leigh, earthenware dealers, in respect of the death of her husband, William Howare.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of the applicant and explained to the Court that the deceased had been in the employ of tho firm for seven years as a traveller and salesman for them at different markets—in Leigh, Warrington and Earles- town. Every Wednesday after he bad completed his day's round with Mr. Thomas Roberts, one of the partners, he invariably went with him to Leigh either by the 9.30 or the 6.33 train, to get out the orders received, and he would not return home until the following Friday noon. On th 3 2nd of October last, Mr. Thomas Roberts called for the deceased whilst having his breakfast, and asked him to be quick as he had a lot of work to do that day, and they must got back to Leigh by the 4 30 train if possible. Mrs. Howard, having two children ill, vsited Mr. Roberts if he could excuse him going back with him that night to Leigh, as she was afraid to be alone with her two sick children. Mr. Roberts repliel "If he does not gJ back with me to-night, he never need come near us again." Later in the day Mr. Thomas Roberts and the deceased were met on their way to Bulk Quay station together, the deceased carrying the respondents' brown beg con- taining samples, and a basket. On the arrival of the 6 30 train at West Leigh, the deceased picked up the bag and basket and got out of the train before it stopped, with the result that he got between the plat- form and the carriage b,ard and was killed. An inquest was held, and verdict of " Accieeatal death" return7d.

The respondents gave to Mrs. Howard several small presents until she consulted her solicitor, who wrote the usual notice of claim to the respondents, whose insurance company's representative attended and denied nat the deceased was a servant of Messrs. Roberts, and said they wonld not pay anything under the Act. Owing to the kindness of two Warrington ladies a request fel arbitration was then filed, when to their surprise it was not denied that the deceased was a servant, but it was contended that the accident did not arise out of and in come of his employment—a defence which cou'd not be understood, as on the body of the deceased a return half market ticket dated the 2nd of October was foun I.
Evidence was then called corroborating the opening
atement.

Mr. Adam Greenbalgb, solicitor of Bolton, who represented the Insurance Company, said that the deceased was only a casual worker and not a servant, and that it was at his own suggestion that he went to West Leigh the night when he was killed to be ready for work the nest morning. He was therefore, in accordance with certain cases quoted, not working for the firm at the time of his death and such death did not arise out oj and in the course of his employment. After some dircassion between His Honour Judge Stanger, K.C., and the solicitor, his Honour suggested a settlement, and thereupon an award was made for £lOO and costs on scale B. the amount to be apportioned between the widow and her two young children at the next Court.

div.head: ST. HELENS HOSPITAL
div.p: ST. HELENS HOSPITAL
STATE INSURANCE lIAS NO ADVERSE EFFECT.
Colonel W. W. Pilkington presided at the yearly meeting of the St. Helens Hospital on Tuesday at the Town Hall.

Sir David Gamble (chairman of the Hospital Com- mittee) said he was glad to see that the collections at the churches were higher this year, as they had been a dwindling figure for some years. The committee had spent rather a large amount on repairs, and, unfor- tunately, they would have to do a great deal more as the hospital buildings had fallen into a rather bad state and were costing a good sum. They had sent no patients to Southport Convalescent Hospital during the year simply beciuse they could not get them in. The penny-a-week subscriptions were rather less than the previous year owing to the coal strike. Mr. T. Killey said it was thought that when the State Insurance came into operAtioa their funds might suffer, but he was glad to ray that there had been no diminution, and the hospital was going forward success- fully in its work. The idea of increasing the benefits given to the penny-a-week subscribers was being con- sidered, and that would mean that the subscriptions should be fully maintained during the coming year.

div.head: ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION.
div.p: ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION.
Dr. Manson and the Case fo? Vivisection.
' CROSS-EXAMINATION " OF NATURE,
At the annual meeting of the Warrington Field Club, held in th 3 Museum Lecture Room on Saturday night, Mr. A. J. Jolley presiding, Dr. Manson contributed P paper on animal experimentation.

div.head: AN Tl-VIVISEC nomsTs' CONTENTION.
div.p: AN Tl-VIVISEC nomsTs' CONTENTION.

Dr. MANSON explained that vivisection comprised only a very small 'art of animal experimentation, and that out of 1(0,000 experiments on animals only about 5,000 were really of the nature of cutting experiments; and these were experiments designed to further the knowledge of the science of physiology. The anti- viviseca)n movement was based on a right and proper sentiment which had a practical result in the passirg of the Vivisection Act to regularise experiments and prevent cruelty, but now this movement had become perverted chicfly owing to the indiscreet zeal induced by the rivalry of the seven or eight anti-vivisection societies that now exist.

It was said by the anti-vivisectionists that animal experiments are useless, but if this be, then it-is only a logical extension to say that all experiments are useless and that the experimental method of advancing know- ledge is a failure. This is a practical impugnment of the Baconian or inductive philosophy upon which all modern science is based, it is possible that the anti- vivisectionists may seek a philosophical basis for their attitude in the new intuitive philosophy. The experimental method is the interrogation or cross- examination of nature. Observation and classification together comprise nature's evidence in chief but in order to get an exact answer, the question has to be put to nature in the shape of an experiment, in problems of life the moss-examination of nature must proceed along the lines of animal experiments and in these there arises the question of the infliction of pain. Before the discovery and the application of anaesthetics this question involvet: a grave moral issue which was felt by many illustrious scientists, among them the great Sir Charles Bell, who discovered the constitution of the nervous system, a discovery equal in importance to tha discovery of thecirculation of the blood by Harvey To day an Act of Parliament provides that anaesthetics must be used in every cutting operation other than the lancing of a vein so that pain is now lessened to a minimum, although not quite abolished. Ninty-five per cent. of the experiments are inoculations to test milk for tuberculosis or water for evidence of sewage pollution, or for the testing and standardisation of drugs. The inoculation itself is practically painless and if disease developes in the animal, it is killed as soon as the main result of the experiment is attained. The experimenters are licensed by the Home Office and tleir laboratories registered. Inspectors are appointed to see that the provisions of the Act are carried out. WHAT EXPERIMENTS IHAVE ACCOMPLISHED. It is by such experiments that almost all the exact and enduring knowledge of physcology, pathology and bacteriology has been attained. In physiology Harvey established his theory of the circulation of the blood, and Bell the constitution of the nervous system by experiments on animals. In more modern times such experiments have established the localisation of the functions of the brain and the importance of the duct- less glands in the structure of living beings. In pathology, Hunter not only experimented on animals, but inoculated himself with a dread disease in order to understand it better. Other workers in this branch of science, such as Virchou, have made permanent additions to our knowledge by means of animal experi- ments. Bacteriology is quite a recent science based almost wholly on animal experimentation. It was established by Pasteur, Koch and Lister and it is %holly due to the latter that the surgical procedures of to-day are relatively safe, to what they were 20 or 30 years ago. Bacteriology has solved the causes of many di.eases hitherto obscure and mysterious, and by indi- cating the cause of tuberculosis, diphtheria, cholera, 1( ck jaw, t3phoid fever, plague, malaria, glanders and others, it has pointed out the way to their prevention and in some cases to their cure.

div.head: BAFFLES RESEARCH.
div.p: BAFFLES RESEARCH.

One great scourge—cancer—has hitherto baffled research, and a tremendous responsibility rests with those who would hinder in any way measures designed to discover its cause, prevention and cure. The Research Defence Society exists to defend the experimental method on living animals, but it is no way antagonistic to such control and precautions as are necessary to prevent needless pain. Its members believe that, if the experimental method be cramped or abolished, the hope ‘Nhich science holds out to suffering humanity will be datkened if not completely eclipsed. A vigorous discussion followed, in which the CHAIR- MAN, the Mayor (Dr. Joseph) and others took part.

TIIE MAYOR AND REPEATED EXPERIMENTS VIVISECTION AND CANCER. The MA von said he was not present as president of the local Anti-Vivisection Scciety, but had attended at the invitation of the secretary of the club. Time did not allow of a reply to all the points raised by Dr. Munson, but he would direct attention to certain aspects of the case. One fact which Dr. Manson had not mentioned was that vivisection was practised from the days of Ilyppocrates to those of llarvey—about 1500 years—by representatives of medicine, without a single discovery having been made. Dr. manson had con- tended that Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood through operations on snakes, but he (the Mayor) was under the impression that he discovered it through the web of a frog's foot, as it could be observed with the naked eye, with the aid of a lens, and lenses were in use at that time. Dr. Manson had stated that it vim Nlalpighi who elaborated Harvey's discovery in that way, but if that were so, it was still strenger argument in favour of anti-vivisection, as the circula- tion of the blood, which was the first actual important discovery with regard to life, was elucidated without any blooodshed. He (the Mayor) was not a total abolitionist—because he did not believe in the principle of " Can any good thing come out of Nazareth "—but, even assuming that physiological discoveries had been made through vivisection, he contended that, in the name of common humanity and commonsense, they bad a right to expect that experiments should not be repeated ad infinitum. The fact that some medical schools were less prone to repetition than others showed that it was not absolutely necessary to the curriculum. As to the licensing of certain places for vivisection, no doubt when experiments were made under those conditions the animals would be properly anwsthetised, but in his own private laboratory a man might not be so careful, and ho believed there were many instances of abuse. The inoculation of animals with poisonous germs was just as cruel as vivisection and, moreover, the effect of drugs and the dosages required were quite different in some animals as compared with others. Morphia caused pain, instead of relieving it, in some animals. With regard to cancer, the MAYOR said his conten• tion was that it was mainly a disease of the human subject ; it was much more common in human beings than in eny of the lower animals. One of the causes— if not the main one—he assumed to be worry and metal disturbance which could only occur, as a rule, in the human being. That being so, it would be useless to experiment upon animals with regard ta a disease, of which the causes were practically absent and which was of very rare occurrence in their case.

div.p: EMPIRE'S DISGRACE.

Mr. Ellis Griffith, M.P., Under Home Secretary, said at a dinner in Cambridge, on Saturday night, that no no one could go through the towns or villages or country districts without being impressed by the con- ditions under which the paople of this country were living. Their homes were a disgrace to a great Empire like (-airs, and it was for the Liberal party to take the matter in hand. Whether it was half a million houses or a million that were required, they would find in time that they had to he provided. In a certain cotton mill in Lancashire there 'worked a man of abnormal appetite, and his workmates used. to refer to a, ppm], ef food he brought for breakfast and diuiter- as "tiir weekly wesh." One dinner-hour the hungry man,. after polishing off a heap of food stuff, turned to in mate and said he didn't feel satisfied; summat else to "stick in his ribs." "Send to th' corner shop for a. div.head: VERY TOLITEI.
div.p: VERY TOLITEI.

There is a differencelaetweext practical hirirrotrr land practical joking; which fact cannot be better illustrated than by a. story conceriringope of the most notable pioneers of LancasTrirs irt,- dustry, to wit, William Grant, Isko, with hie brother Daniel furnished the mead for the Cheeryble Brothers immortalised by Dickens. The Brothers Grant, who, wit-diillieir father for- sook Scotland and cattle-dealing to devote them- selves to commerce at Bury, ultimately became) princes among manufacturers and merchants, but the foundation of their prosperity was laidl by the most strenuous and painstaking efforts,. Beginning as shopkeepers, they did not wait for customers to come to them, but waylaid passers- by -with invitations to enter and purchase. These importunities, though earnest, were al- ways characterised by an impeccable politeness- This is illustrated by the fact that a certain,in- dividual laid a 'wager that if he bought only a: •pennyworth of anything from the Grants he would be thanked for it, no matter how muck trouble he had given over a purchase. Proceed- ing to the shop, he asked to be shown numerous; pieces of linen, cloth, print, and other fabrics- Alter having many pieces unrolled and dis- played, the customer at length carefully selected some linen cloth and asked the obliging shop- man to measure him—a pennyworth, quick! William Grant took the customer's penny, laid: it on the cloth, cut a circular piece exactly the size of the coin, and handed it to the purchaser, saying, "Thank you, sir !" Thus the customer won his wager, but from the practical standpoint it must be acknowledged that the canny shop- keeper had by no means the worst of the joke, • or of the bargain.

div.head: "BILL- 0-70 E'S."
div.p: "BILL- 0-70 E'S."
To a stranger there is much humour, albeit 11 'quite Tinconscious, in the practices almesk
EINMI
OMMIIe

irniversai in the Lancashire factory- district, af conferring upon every individual what to an unaccustomed ear sounds like an 4iltlandish nickname, though it is in. reality nothing of the kind. Throughout the manufacturing dis- trict of Lancashire surnames are practically dis- carded, the Christian name alone being used, together with a cognomen in which pedigree, or place of locality, or both, are linked. hi a certain village, for example, it would have been useless to inquire for Mrs.- by her proper name, but anybody, even the villages idiot, would instantly direct you to "Susy o' Jem's o' l'airoff's at the Top-o'-th'-Rake!" Sons and daughters often have the names of their father or mother applied to them, along with their own; thus, "George o' Jack's," "Abram o' Bob's," and so on. One instance is on record of a father being distinguished by a. reference to his son. Jobber Pilling, the son, being the most prominent member of the household, the elder representative of the family came to be generally known merely as "Jobber Pilling's feyther." The nicknaming propensity is not confined to the human factors in the industrial organisation, but extends sometimes to the machinery. There is a storr of a stranger from the South who, having asked. a Lancashire lad what was his occupation, was staggered to learn that the youth helped to "tent a devil at He!- shore!" In explanation, it should be stated that the process of tearing applied to some raw materials in manufacturing is called "devilling,", whilst the word "tent" means "attend."

div.head: MASTER OR MAN?
div.p: MASTER OR MAN?

"Cp. Mills" is a term. popularly designat- ing the many cotton factories which are worked on the joint-stock principle, and a good propor- tion of the mill-hands hold shares, though often this proprietary interest is on the smallest pos- sible scale. The manager of a " Co-op. mill" one day encountered one of the hands "larking " about the premises instead of attending to his work, and administered a sharp verbal admoni- tion, together with a semblance of a kick to better enforce the rebuke. The culprit, whilst rubbing the aggrieved portion of his anatomy, turned to the manager a menacing countenance and thus expostulated: "Seep thi foot to thi'sel and mind what thar't doing; dos't know 'at aw'm one of thi msaistersr He held a five- pound ,share in the concern!

div.head: W ASTEIP POWER.
div.p: W ASTEIP POWER.

Cotton operatives, as the whole history of t'.3 industry exemplifies, are generally strongly averse to the introduction of labour-saving machinery, but conditions sometimes occur which dissipate this prejudice. A mill-hand of Oldham—or "Dwcraam chap" as he would describe himself—got into trouble in a town in the same 'county, but situate a few .miles distant from Oldham, and, AS the consequance of a mis- demeanour was committed to prison and put on the treadmill. Ile worked it for a sufficient time to cause his back and legs to ache with the unaccustomed exertion, and then. exclaimed: "By gum! if this devil were at Owdltam they'd a. had it turned by power afore now!" A COCKSIIRB WITNESS,

A passion for cock-fighting was the bane of a certain factory, as so all-absorbing did the sport prove to a large proportion of the hands that when they weren't actuaJ3y engaged in super- intending matches betweert their bantams, they were discussing the details of a recent en- counter, or arranging preliminaries for a pro- jected bout. Some of the men breught their birds with them to the factory in baskets, ven- tilated boxes, and other Lieceptacles. One of the mill-owners having become aware of the preva- lence of. this baneful practice, and conceiving that it .was detrimental to the business, had a grave interview with his foreman, and charged him absolutely to prohlbit the men bringing cocks to the factory under paimi of instant dis- missal. The foreman, anxious to display his real. in his employer's interest, lost no time about making the announcement. which he did that day, and In the presence of the employer. He stopped the work of the roont whilst, in a Silence that could be felt, he proolaimed with the most getermined words and gestures the firm's rigorous determination to put an end to the practice. his harangue, however, was in- terrupted at an impressive period by a "Cock-a-doodledoo!" coming from no one knew where. The foreman proceeded with his ora- tion, but again " Cock-a-doodle-doo!" resounded through the roemk This untimely interruption was repeated so frequently that the graVity of the men coitld no longer resist the ludicrousness of the situation, and their merriment, begin- ning with a titter, culminated in a roar, as the employer. having apparently located the place whence the clarion notes proceeded, went to the foreman's desk, and, opening it, revealed the presence there of a very flue eitautieleer!
The Examiner, Saturday, May 3, 1913

div.head: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR.
div.p: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR.
Warrington Wesleyans' Great Effort for
the Orford Church Scheme.
PICTURESQUE HOMELAND SCENES.

So many of the modern scenic bazaars attempt to transport the visitor to the romantic sutroundings of Oriental lands, that it is a refreshing novelty to find one that depicts the beauties of our own country. Even in these days, when the march of industrialism has done so much to pollute the air and disfigure the fair face of Nature, there are many favoured districts on which the hand of the Vandal has not yet fallen and which have a charm peculiarly their own. The old English bazaar, which the Wesleyans of the Waning- ton ci:cuit held in the Parr Hall this week, took us back to the days before the advent of the railway train —to say nothing of the motor car—and the growth of great manufacturing towns, when England had more claim to be called" Merrie England." By most effective scenic devices, a typical village of the olden times was represented. There was a background of hills, with a winding river, flowing through meadows and vales, while a further artistic touch was given by the old windmill, with sails, and a creeper- covered bridge. A picturesque homestead, with dove- cote, beehives, and kindred objects of interest, filled in the picture. The stalls were arranged in the form of quaint old English houses, with their curi usly shaped windows, some lattice and some over-banging, with foliage and flowers clinging- to the walls and roofs. Then there was the model of an old inn, such as Scott or Dickens would have loved to write about, with banging sign and all the outward tokens of comfort and reposefulness which greeted the travellers by stage coaches in the days of yore. The whole scheme was a triumph of artistic taste and decorative ingenuity—in fact the Parr Hall has never presented a more pleasing spectacle. KEEPING PACE WITH THE TIMES.
The purpose for which the bazaar waa held spoke eloquently of the desire of Wesleyan Methodists to keep pace -with the demands of the titr.e3. It was hoped to

his early days there was no Central railw.y, barracks or Council school, and only a solitary farm house and a few cottages here and there. Now thousands of houses had been built. There was still the historic Orford Hall, which used to be the beauty spot of the neighbour- hold, and he well remembered the time when it was surrounded with pools of water and artistic bridges, well-kept lawns and splendid trees, and one of the finest avenues he had ever seen led from the hall to the main road. Those had passed away but the changed conditions demanded special effort. Great manufactories, of all kinds, had appeared and with such material prosperity all round them, they ought to be prepared to give generous support to enterprises for the furtherance of spiritual work. He hoped the bazaar would realise more than £l,OOO asked for and expected, so that in due time they could begin the building. (Applause.) THE METHODIST FAMILY.

Mrs. PARKER, in referring to family associations with Arlethcdism, said that whenever she came to a big Methodist gathering in Warrington, her mind always went back to previous occasions when they had these with them who bad since passed away. No-one would have taken a .greater intere.st in the inauguration of the Norris-street scheme than her beloved father wito,laJ he been spared, would have en.darsel all that Mr. Bennett had said and wocld have been cue of their best helpers that day. She felt. it was chiefly bec thin of the bolour. her family Ind held in SVarrieg'ol Methodism, that she had been invited to open the bazaar. There was nothing in life which made such an appeal to them as the idea of the family. It was E 0 full of variety of experience and iich iliterest; its prest.--,rvatien and development seemed to bring out all that was best end truest. In her opinion, the family idea in We3leyan Methodism was the most delightful i at of their church system. Just as the solicitous pa-oat was for ever correcting and watching Over the growing family, giving r tis.e here and rebuke there, so the superintecd3et of the Wesleyan Circuit, with his worthy colleagues and the various officers of the church, st.emed to be continually watching the great

object, and that must have a unifying effect. There was no doubt about it that unity was strength, and he hoped success would attend their united enterprise. He also hoped that the good work at Orford would go for- ward to a successful conclusion. (Applause.) Mr. F. A. HARRIS proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. Ransoms, and said they welcomed the latter as one of the representative manufacturers of the town and as a gentleman who took a leadivg part in the industrial life of Warrington. They also welcomed him as a memLer of the kindred sister body, the Society of Friends, and they also welccmed him on his own account. Their thanks were also due to Mr. Withinshaw to whom the circuit owed a great deal. (Applause.) Mr. R. H. MELDRUM seconded and said they were all pulling together to make a new beginning. Their thanks were due to Mr. Harris, for if it had not been for him,they would not have had a bazaar worth calling one. (Hear, hear.) The vote was heartily carried.

div.head: LADIES' DAY.
div.p: THE LADIES' DAY.
Thursday was Eet apart as ladies' day, the opening ceremony being entirely in ihe hands uf the lady workers for the bazaar. Miss Bessie Dutton presided and the bazar was opened by Mrs Dodds.

div.head: RELIGIr.s.N IN THE SCHOOL.
div.p: RELIGIr.s.N IN THE SCHOOL.

Mic:s DUTTON pointed out that the proceedings were in contrast to the usual order of things, as ladies were generally tabooed at meetings nowadays. (Laughter.) c ommending the Norria-street scheme, Miss Dutton said she was glad to hear the new building was to be called a school-cbapel. They could not !lONE+ all that the Sunday school movement had el.)ne for England. Sometilne3 people said " Look how many scholars lapse," or " What a neighbourhood to plant a s:hool in!" But what would the neighbourhood have ba(n if the school had not, been there—probably twice as black al it was at present, (Applause.) If they did not see the result in any given region of the good work dune by the Suneay school teechers, they were

raise at least £l,OOO for the erection of a new church in the rapidly-growing Orford district. In December 1908, a plot of land was secured at the corner of Norris-street and O'Leiry-street, facing Hallfields- road, by Dr. Bennett, Mr. J. G. Withinshaw, tnd the late Mr. E. J. Guest, and this has now been trans- ferred to a body of trustees under the Connexional model deeds. The site consists of about 2,000 square yards, and is sufficient to contain church, schools, lecture rooms' &e., but at present it is proposed to erect a school only for which plans have been pro- visionally approved.

div.head: IN PRAISE OF THE WORKERS.
div.p: IN PRAISE OF THE WORKERS.

The bazaar project has received the enthusiastic support of all the Churches in the circuit and fully 250 workers have been engagad in its preparation. The stalls,heavily laden with all manner of useful and fancy gr ode, were sufficient proof of the value of their labours.

Special praise is due to the following officers and committes who have directed the organization of the undertaking in a most efficient manner : I President, Rev. W. A. Beckett; hon. treasurers, Mr. J. G. Withinshaw and Mr. R. H. Yeldrum ; hon. secretaries, Mr. F. A. Harris, the Rev. H. Williamson and Mr. T. B. Weaver. Executive Committee: The Revs. W. A. Beckett, E. Morgan, H. Williamson, and H. Middlewood, Messrs. Frank A. Harris,Dr. Ferguson, J. G. Withinshaw, R. H. Meldrum and T. B. Weaver. Bold-street : Mr. F. Penketh : Miss Davies, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. Withinshaw and Mrs. Ambler. Sankey Bridges: Mrs. Gorst and Mrs. Cawley. Latchford: Mrs. Wheatley, MI s. W. Walker and Mrs. Ford. Lyinro : Mrs. B. S. div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: THE OPENING CEREMONY.

The large attendance at the opening ceremony 'on Tuesday afternoon argued well for the success of the bazaar. Mr. William Bennett, one of the veterans of the Warrington Circuit, presided and the bazaar was opened by Mrs. C. E. Parker.

div.head: RECOLLECTIONS OF OLD WARRINGTON.
div.p: RECOLLECTIONS OF OLD WARRINGTON.

The CHAIRMAN referred to his official connection with the circuit, extending over the past fifty years and pointed out that he had been the trustee for a number of chapels for the greater part of his life. He had seen the erection of every chapel in the circuit, except two or three in Cheshire. He could recall the building of the chapels at Bold-street, Bewsey-road, Penketh, Sankey Bridges, Padgate, Latchford, Stockton Heath, Lymm and Moore and of the schools at Silver- streat. The Methodists of Warrington had been very active in the Past, but there was something still to be done. They were now called upon to extend their borders in the direction of Orford where a place of worship was much needed. There was no Wesleyan Church nearer than Padgate or Bewsey-road, so that a splendid opening was presented. (Hear, hear). An admirable site had been secured and he was glad to say it was bought and paid for. It now remained for them to raise funds in order that building operations might be commenced. They did not expect to be able to com- plete the whole scheme at once, but it wonld be a good beginning if they could build a mission room, school or lecture hall, with vestries and eventually follow it up with a church would be worthy of the neighbourhood and a blessing to the inhabi- tants. (Applause). He well remembered the time when the population of Warrington was only a little over 30,000; new it was considerably over 70,900. The question arose: Were they,as Wesleyan Methodists, keeping pace with the spiritual needs of the people? When he thought of the changes which had taken place in the Orford district during his life-time, he believed there was a great scope for Christian activities. In

div.head: PROMISING OPENING DAY.
div.p: A PROMISING OPENING DAY.

'circuit family and administering adominition and encouregement. She did not know which was the oldest branch of the family —Lvmm or Penketh—as they ran it'pretty close,but he believed Stockton Heath was the Laby, or was it Ellecmere-street ? The great family event that they all looked forward to with the most interest SI a the prospect of a new arrival and that was the point which tho Warrington Circuit had reached. As soon as the last place was fairly on its legs, their minds were casting about for a suitable spot for a new addition. Their attention was at present centred on Norris-street, where there was the prospect of the speedy and healthy advent of another church in the near future. During the last few months every branch of the family had been working hard, with self-sacrifioe and eagor interest, so that the new clmor might hsv3 a grod start in life. She hoped a suffloiently large sum would be raised by that bazaar to give Norris-street a right dowri, good "send-off." (Applause.) Mr. Bennett had alluded to the nece,sit y for a Nonconformist place of worship in the locality,and she was sure they all trusted and prayed that the new church would be a centre of guat blessedness and usefulness. As soon as the scheme was an accomplished fact, she thought the circuit would be pretty complete. She hoped the work at the bazaar would produce the happiest sense of unity among the various places that formed the circuit, and that the greatect success would attend their efforts. (Applause.) A lovely bouquet was then presented to hfrs. Parker Ly Miss Lilian Parkinson and Mr. Bennett received a Lu tton hole at the hands of Master William Hickman.

The Rev. W. A. BECKETT, in proposing a vote of thanks to Ma. Parker and Mr. Bennett, said that Mr. Bennett provided a striking instance of " the old man eloquent," The new mission was not-being erected for any mere purpose of Methodist aggrandisement, but to meet the moral and spiritual needs of a growing district. They were grateful for the splendid help which had been given to the Warrington circuit in the past by the Bennett and Garnett familbs. (Applause), Mr. G. WEAVER seconded. He said that throughout his 31 sears' association with the Warrington circuit, Mr. William Bennett had been one of its most loyal and devoted helpers. No bazaar had been held in con- nection with Bold-street Church, without receiving magnificent assistance from him. (Applause.) To Mr. end Mrs. Parker they were indebted for ranch service at the last bazaar in connection with the circuit. _ _
The vote was heartily passed, and the business of the bazaar was entered upon.

div.head: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
Mr. Withinshaw and the Friends of the Scheme.
The opening ceremony on Wednesday was performed by Mr. J. A. liansome, J.P. Mr. J. G. Withinshaw presided over a fair attendance and was supported by circuit ministers and members of the committee.
The Rev. 11. Williamson presented the financial state- ment which showed that £285 Os. sd. had been raised on the first day. That sum included donations of £258 each from MrF. Parker and Mr. Bennett.

Mr. WITHINSHAW, speaking of the commencement of the scheme, said they owed as much to the late Mr. Edwin Guest as to any man in Warrington, for he was one of the first to work for the scheme. "He worked hard along with Mr. Harris, to obtain a site and it was owing to his foresight that they had secured the land on which they were going to build. What they were aiming at first was to get a good Sunday School, because if they got that the church was bound to follow. At the present time there was no Noncon- formist Sunday School- within easy reach of Norris-street. With such good trade, the present time was most opportuns to hold that bozaar—in fact he did not think they could have chosen a better time, Speak- ing of Mr. Rausome, the chairman remarked that it was an act of grace for a member of another religious body to come forward and give his help. Mr. Ransom° represented the Society of Friends, which was noted from the beginning for its good works on behalf of freedom and in succouring those who were oppressed and down trodden. They were pioneers in recent years in aiding those who were oppressed by the Turks in time of war and they looked after the wounded. The Society wan the prime mover in freeing thus° who were enslaved. Mr. Ransome was a worthy member of a worthy body and it was with great pleasure that he asked him to declare the sale open, (App'ause), UNITY OF PURPOSE.

Mr. RANSOME said they were all there with a purpose. but divided into two bodies, either buyers or sellers, Their one purpose was to raise sufficient funds to build the school and chapel and he asked both buy( rs and sellers to do their best for that worthy object. He hoped the result anticipated would be reached and even passed. There was another feature about a sale of that description. Besides the financial result, there was the greater and better purpose of the promotion of unity. Working as they had done, they had become drawn together in their own particular aphe-ee for the one
enuto by Burral.

thankful to think that the place was infinitely better th..n it would have been if the school had not been opened. She was glad t 3 hear that many people, at at present to!ally unprovided for, were disposed to welcome the Norris-street scheme as something which would help them in the scholastic direction. The Vicar of Huddersfield recently said that many of the children ho came into their schools did not even know the Name of Jesus. They hoped that, through the agency of Sunday schools, thousands would be gathered in to know that Name and find salvation. They were glad to think that the period of Sunday school life in the North of England was longer then in the South. With regard to the day schools, the Warring- ton Education Committee provided very good religious instruction of an undenominational character in the Council schools. They did not, however,want to think that the day school system represented the whole of the religious teaching that the children received. In some cases the instruction given tn the day schools was apt to he more a thing of the head than of the heart. There was more of the personal element in the Sunday school than in the day school, and therefore they must maintain their Sunday schools above every- thing. (Applause.) basking Mrs. Dodds to open the bazaar, Miss Dutton said they owed to her many practical gifts and much gracious and helpful influence. (Applause). THE COMMON PLACE PEOPLE. Mrs. DODDS emphasised a saying which had made a great impression upon her : "Not by its heroes the world lives and thrives, But by its sweet, common-place mothers and wives." The words applied eqaally to the Church which owed everything to the efforts of those sweet, common place people who gave their love and service week by week. In all lives there were days which stood out from the usual routine. So in Church life there were days which lived in their memories, and w hich they called red letter days. The Wesleyan Methodists in the Warrington circuit had many such days and she would like that day to be added to the list, so that in years to come people would refer to it as the occasion when the women had their innings on behalf of the bazaar that was held in connection with the Norris- street church. She would like the effort to be a success, not only flnoncially, but in a far wider and deeper sense, and she prayed that that day would be one of uplift and inspiration. She also trusted that, when the Norris-street Church was opened and the call came for workers young and old, there would be many ready to say " here am I, send me." (Applause). Bouquets were then presented to Mrs. Dodds and Miss Dutton by Miss Gwennie Bennett and Miss Jessie Ferguson respeAively. Mrs. WITDINSIIAW, in proposing a vote of thanks, said Mrs. Dodds was ever willing to work not only for the churches but for the town generally. . _ _

Mrs. WHEATLEY seconded. She said the workers for Warrington Methodism ought to be proud that they had two such grand women es Mrs. Dodds and Miss Dutton among them. (Applause). The vote was heartily passed.
Miss DUTTON announced that the proceeds for the previous cl:q (including a donation of £5O from Mr. Withinshaw) amounted to .£197 13s„ making a total for the two dais of 182 13s, sd, (Applause).

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 3, 1913.

indulging the hope that we shall secure him as a member of our Warrington Shakespearean Society and that during our next session it may be arranged to have a thorough sifting of cpinions on this very interesting subject. As to Dr. Mellor's disagreement with my criticism of Mr. Law's Shylock, I conclude it must be due to a fundamental difference in our mental attitude to the art of acting. He says Mr. Law's acting "on the whole struck me as being on a decidedly high level very seldom attained by amateurs." I subscribe to this wholly. Mr. Law has the preficiency of a prac- tised actor. There is nothing whatever in his manner or appearance to indicate that he is an amateur, and the pity of it, to me, is that this undoubted ability should be applied to the cultivation sif a style cf acting which, while eminently suited to the romantic melo- drama, appears artificial And strained in the repre- sentation of the tragic creations of Shakespeare's genius. Dr. Mellor cannot agree that Shylcck's exit did not evoke sympathy. I did not intend my com- ment to convey the impression Dr. Mellor has derived from it. It was the degree of sympathy—not the total absence of it—that I alluded to; and in my own case
it was only felt at the last moment of exit, instead of, as I have on many occasions known it to affect me, immediately upon the first jubilant and reviling speech of Gratiano's. _ .

But here I am confronted by the difficulty of being unable to explain my lack of this feeling without going into a clo,er analysis of the acting and, as I am conscious of having already given occasion for much heart searching, I refrain. I sincerely hope that my good friends will accept my disclaimer '• from a purposed evil." I have had no wish but for the advancement of true art. Yours truly, ALFRED PERRIS,
