From the cradle to the grave the workers are constantly .being crucified ; in fact, volumes might be written, showing (despite his faults) that the men who preduce the wealth of tile world are ever and anon battling against the great hydra-headed foe of poverty. And, so to influence this Goverament at this time to deal with this question I sincerely hope our local Co-operative Society will do its part, by arranging conferences and meetings to arouse public opinion and shew to our statesmen, that with the rest of our mem- bers throughout England, we are determined that this subject shall be tackled earnestly and that the lot of the poverty stricken worker shall be raised.—Yours BARRY WARDMAN, 4a, Amelia-street.

div.head: LAND VALUES A DOMINANT ISSUE,
div.p: LAND VALUES A DOMINANT ISSUE,

ir,—From the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer on Monday last, three important and significant facts emerge. (1.) The valuation is to be ready by March 19L5. (2.) By a Revenue Bill the valuation of agricul- cultural land is to be rectified so as to get a value with all improvements eliminated. (3.) The new valuation is to be made the basis of rating reform. The third intenticli follows upon the second for obviously as the rectification of the valuation of rural land is not required in relation to any present tax it must be for future use. Mr. Pretyman and his Land Union have made much play with the fact that a valuation of rural land is not being obtained that would afford a basis for a laud values tax. It will be interesting to know what line they will take when their criticism is met by the Revenue Bill and they are hoist with their own petard. The Budget of 1909 did not solve the problem of Liberal Finance but laid the foundations of its solution in the land valuation. The Budget of 1913 shows that a new and fruitful source of revenue will have to be found. A balance was struck between estimated revenue and expenditure but only by the non-satisfac- tion of two demands that will have to be met. The tea and sugar duties must go and are only retained by the constrained votes of members pledged to their abolition. There is the demand of the local authorities that a substantial part of the burden of £42,000,000 a year for national services cast upon them shall be resumed by the Imperial Government. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is only able to avoid a deficit by maintaining a system which is reducing local exchequers to a condition of bankruptcy. So it is evident that to meet these demands the Chancellor will have before long to find at least £20,000,000 a year from a new source. With this necessity at band the statement of the Chancellor gains in significance and it is manifest that the taxation of land values is destined to be the dominant issue in the near future.— Your &c.
R. L. OUTFIWAITE. House of Commons, S.W., 30th April 1913.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND POVERTY. Attitude of Socialists.
div.p: THE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY AND POVERTY. Attitude of Socialists.

Sir,—With reference to the question raised by your correspondent "Labor Omnia Vincit," your readers whether or not belonging to the two orthodox parties which cannot touch the question but with a six-foot stick) will, I venture to assert, all welcome any genuine effort to secure the abolition of poverty so long as they have the assurance that practical results are likely to follow. We are asked to believe that the question of the abolition of poverty is not a party question and therefore one which may be legitimately considered by a Co-operative Society, particularly so when we remember the object the founder of this co-operative movement had in view. Now it is not the slightest use ignoring the fact that it ;s a party question from its very nature. There is probably no other political question upon which there is so great a divergence of opinion and so long as political action is attempted to deal with the matter these various opinions must find expression in political parties. It is, of course, quite possible for a co-operative scciety to consider any proposal dealing with poverty on str:ctly- non-party lines but not when such pro- posal is believed to emanate from one political party for party purposes and I think this is a point that would want making perfectly clear. If I understand your correspondents rightly, their object is, .not to bring forward a definite proposal for the abolition of poverty, but to bring the society into line with other societies that are promoting confer- ences &c., for the discussion of this problem with a view to bringing pressure on this Government to deal with the problem next session, that is to say to compel the Government by force of public opinion, to do something that the public do not know how to d. I hope the Co-operative movement will lend no countenance to this.

What has impressed me moat deeply in connection with the local socialist activities is the remarkably small amount of individual initiation displayed. In this last move, for instance, the desire is to do what others are doing in other parts of the country—some one leads the way and they follow, right or wrong. Some eight or nine years ago, before the 1906 election and before the present "Labour party" in Parliament assumed its present form, I did my best both publicly and privately to convince my Socialist friends that, from the very nature of the political questions with which they had to deal, as well as from the attitude Mr. Ramsay Macdonald laid down for the prospective party, they could be nothing more than Liberals, and the Labour party merely a wing of the Liberal party. They could not, however, see it until the force of circumstances proved the truth to certain of their leaders when there was a great split in the Socialist camp and one part did not scruple to denounce the other as "Liberals." In the same way and at the same time, I also endeavoured to show our local Socialists that the way they were looking for the advent of Socialism was really leading to a state of greater servility, giving the economic arguments to substantiate my opinion. Although apparently they could see nothing in it at the time, there is a great discussion going on in their own Press on the "Servile State," which indicates that at last this truth has begun to force itself upon them. Now, if your correspondents are in real earnest, I caa ould suggest that they should do, as the Rochdale Pioneers did, bring forward in their society something of a definite nature that is likely to deal radically with the problem and not merely draw ths society into a formal sympathy with the movement to abolish poverty by the [interminable discussion of views and remedies that have already been thrashed out. We are often told that there is no cure for poverty, but "Socialism " and Mr. Blatchford has repeatedly admitted that he does not know how Socialism is to be brought e.bout ; there is, therefore, quite an open field for your correspondents to bring forward a non-party proposal.—Yours truly, JOHN A. J. MORTON. 25th April, 1913.

Sir,— Like "Hopeful" and the other correspondents who have written on this subject, I am sincerely hoping that some tangible result will accrue as a result of the discussion. For surely as Co-operators, whatever our position in life may be, or our politics or creed before the public, this is a common object upon which we can all join together—this great crusade of the war against poverty. Personally I hold and claim that Co-operation stands for something more than mere shop keeping, however successful that may be. To me it is one of the phases of the eternal struggle for the emancipation of the worker from the wage slavery of to-day to economic freedom. That poverty abounds on every hand, there is abundant evidence. At every turn of life it is so evident that we cannot get away from it, try as we will. If we glance at the conditions of the people under our present-day civilisation, we find that the majority of human beings are denied the opportunity to realise the fulness of life. One-third of the children born into the world, from the day of their birth do not enjoy sufficient food, sunshine, or fresh air. One-third of these children die before

div.head: BUILDING TRADE AND THE TAXATION OF LAND VALUES.
div.p: THE BUILDING TRADE AND THE TAXATION OF LAND VALUES.

Sir,—ln view of the many attempts made in Parlia- ment and elsewhere to create a land tax scare amongst those connected with the various building trades, it is worth while—on the principle that an ounce of practice is worth a ton of theory—to turn for evidence to those places where the taxation of land values is in actual operation. An illustrated booklet recently issued by the Lethbridge (Alberta) Board of Trade, setting forth the advantages of that town, contains the following statement : "Lethbridge haG adopted the Single Tax system. All revenue is obtained frcm the taxation of land values only. This means that the workingman's house is not taxed, neither are business blocks nor the residences of wealthier people. The buildings and machinery of industry are also exempted from taxation under this system. In fact business of all kinds is exempted, land values forming the sole basis of assessment.

The "Single tax system" referred to above must he understood to mean that all local revenue is obtained by the rating of land values. The official call for the seventh general Inter- national Dry Farming Congresslheld at Lethbridge in' October, says of the new rating system that "it encourages the erection of good buildings and sets a premium on the holding of real estate out of use." In Vancouver, British Columbia, where also rates are levied on site values and buildings are unrated, the building trades have been stimulated in an astonishing manner. So many men and so much money left Victoria (the capital of British Columbia) for Vancouver in 1910 that Victoria was forced, in self-defence, to adopt the rating of laud values, which she did in January 1911 by a vote of five to one. The effect was magical. In April 1911, Victoria's build- ing permits were £58,022 as against £38,488 in April 1910. In August, 1911, they had grown to £85,922 as against £42,563 in August, 1910; and in November, 1911, they had reached £123,325 as against £20,859 in November, 1910. it is interesting to compare the above figures with those of Seattle, U.S.A., where the old system of rating " improvements " is still in force. Seattle has a population seven times as great as that of Victoria,yet the value of building permits in Seattle fell from £204,047 in November 1910 to £89,821 in November 1911. There is a growing agitation in Seattle for the rating of land values and the unrating of improve- ments.

At the twelfth annual convention of the Union of Canadian Municipalitiee,held last summer in Windsor, Ontario, papers on [municipal taxation were read by Alderman J. Clark, of Edmonton, Alberta, and Alder- man W. Hepburn, of Vancouver. In both cities the system of exemption of improvements from taxation has been adopted. "The triumph of our land tax in Edmonton," said Alderman Clark, "is shown by the fact that in 1906 we had building permits to the value of 1,563,000 dollars, while in 1912—the first year all taxes other than land taxes were taken off— they were 15,000,000 dollars. If the previous ratio had been continued it would have required a popula- tion of 80,000 to justify this expenditure, while our population is approximately 53,000." [ Such facts should convince people connected with Ithe building trades that the taxation and rating of [ land values and the untaxing of buildings and other [ improvements will bring them great prosperity when [it is uniformly adopted in this country. When the land valuation has been completed it will be possible to replace the Increment Duty and the other small land taxes in the 1909 Budget by rates and taxes on all land values, on the lines of the proposals contained in the Land and Taxation Reform Memorial of May 1911. That would be a great advance to the untaxing and unhampering of the building trades, and to a period of general and lasting prosperity,—Yours, Sc., SINGLE TAXER.

div.head: IN THE COURTS
div.p: IN THE COURTS
Borough Police Court.
MONDAY. Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst Bolton and James Evane, Messrs. T. Locker, S.

Wright and W. Furness. ALLEGED I'HEFT FROM A WORKS.—A youth named Thomas Giblin, 22, Litford-street, was charged with stealing trom the Whitecross Company's works a hammer, value 3s. 6d.—The Chief Constable stated that Detective Holland went to prisoner's borne to make inquiries about some pigeons which had been stolen. On going into the yard they found a small shed in the course of erection, and a hammer and a piece of wire netting were being used in the work. Asked to account for the possession of the hammer, prisoner said it had been lent to him for the purpose of building a pigeon cote.—lnquiries showed that prisoner ban stolen it from the works. Prisoner further stated that a man at the works had told him to take the netting. It appeared that wire could be obtained from the works, on a note being received from the office, but it was alleged that in this case the netting had been stolen.— Prisoner was remanded until Wednesday in order tat further inquiries might be made. The youtn appeared before the presiding magistrates, on Wednesday, Messrs. J. W. Hayward (in the chaii), Alderman Smethurst. Messrs. C. Jackson Homes and W. 'l'. Williams.—ln fining the prisoner 40s. or 14 days, the Chairman said Giblin had started his career of crime very young.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), Colonel Edelsten, Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and T. Locker. "A WRETCHED PIECE OF BUSINESS."—Robert Hinctilifie was charged OD wairant with using threats to his wife on April 26th.—Complainant said her husband threatened to turn hei out. She was afraid of him.— Inspector Wainwright said it was a wretched piece of business on the man's part. The woman had to clear out of the house every week-end.—Hinchliffe was bound over in two sureties of 10 to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay the costs of the case, or one month's imprisonment. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.—TIIOIIIBB H. Williams, seaman, 21, Ellesmere-street, was charged with being a convicted thief end with having loitered in Bridge- street with intent to commit a felony early that morn- ing.—The Chief Constable said that P.C. Macdonald saw the prisoner acting in a suspicious manner about 12.5 that morning. He was going from shop to shop apparently examining the doors. He continued these actions in Mersey-street and, stopped by the officer, outside the Moulder's Arms, made some rambling statement. He afterwards said he had intended break- ing in and also that he had friends in Napier-street. The prisoner appeared to have been drinking and, in his own interests, it was lesirable that the case should be adjourned for a week. Prisoner had admitted the offences and also that he had come out of a reformatory school in July after serving three years.—The case was adjourned for seven days. "WAS SIIE TO BLAME ?"—Thomas Lynskey, 6, Eldon-street, was summoned by his wife Sarah, 13, Warburton-street for persistent cruelty, causing her to leave him on the 22nd April.—Complainant said that because she did not get her husband cigarettes, he created a disturbance and there was also trouble about his insurance card. He struck her on the jaw and burst her mouth, her teeth coming through her lips. After he had hit her three times in the face, his sister and he began to molest her.—lnspector Wainwright said defendant had frequently assaulted his wife, her mother and father. The wife was quite illiterate and defendant took advantage of that fact.—Prisoner'a complaint was that his wife went out with her mother to pick cinders and neglected their 14 months' old child.—A separation order was granted the wife, with an allowance of Bs. per week.

NE EDITOR of the " Examiner " invites correspond- ence on all subjects of public. interest. LtrrEns should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information, not abuse. COMMUNICATIONS received early in the week—except urgent matters—cau always be given the best attention.

div.head: WALKING DAY AND THE KING'S VISIT.
div.p: WALKING DAY AND THE KING'S VISIT.

Sir,—Will you allow me a small space in your valuable paper in answer to a correspt,ndent in last week's issue? I take it that Walking Day is always on the Friday nearest to the Ist July. That would be July 4th. I don't see why the question of the June .27th should be raised at all. Why, trade is so good. I think it is absurd to question the date at all. I think the employers and employees in general should have the first consideration. I notice in "The Passing Week" that in some influential quarters it is suggested to make two holidays. I would like to ask them: Would employers close down for Walking Day, restart, and stop again for their Majesties' visit? I think not. They would close down for the whole time, so you see how it would affect the workpeople in general. I think it would be the most sorrowful holiday Warrington had ever seen. I hope the Sunday school authorities may take this into consideration and bear in mind the man who has to keep the door open all the year for the children, not for one day only. This does not permit a fortnight's play after all the strikes and labour unrest we have had.—Yours sincerely,

div.head: CONSTANT READER. DR. MANSON AND A TRUE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE.
div.p: A CONSTANT READER. DR. MANSON AND A TRUE CHRISTIAN SCIENCE.

Sir,—lt is very difficult for an ordinary individual like myself to answer Mr. Doorly's letter in your last issue. Mr. Doorly seems to be rather annoyed that anyone should suggest a rational substitute for the foggy and fantastic creation of Mrs. Eddy. Let me tell him that the idea is by no means new or original, and was mooted many years ago by Sir Francis Galton whEn he stated that it was only by the power of religion that the practical application of eugenic principles could be attained. Mr. Dooby asks what truths have been garnered by modern science, and proceeds further to tell us that "Christian Scientists thoroughly, agree with and use all wholesome sanitary methods. ' I should say that these wholesome sanitary methods have been garnered by modern science, and have in no manner resulted from the teaching of Mrs. Eddy. If that teaching were to gain wide sway, I am afraid we should soon have a repetition of the devastating plagues of the middle ages. I think it is time that the followers of Mrs. Eddy dropped the title of Christian Science—which is, as far as I can make out, neither Christianity nor science—and called them- selves Eddyites ' and their system Eddyism.'— Yours, etc.,
J. MANSON.

div.p: 8, Virinmarleigh-atreet, Warrington, April 28th, 1913.

TORY CALUMNIES. Sir,—Someone has favoured me with a marked copy of the " Warrington Examiner" of the 19th April, containing a report of a speech by Mr. P. M. Oliver, prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division. The report is headed," Tory Calumnies," and contains the following passage : "The Conservatives looked upon the Liberals with views that were altogether distorted by party passion. They invented all sorts of calumnies against them, some of which were amusing, while some were very serious. An example of the amusing kind was given a bbort time ago when Mr. Touche, a Conservative Member of Parliament who was also Chairman of a Company which provided penny-in-the-slot machines for the railway stations. solemnly told a meeting of shareh)lders that the bad coin place in automatic machine had more than doubled since the Liberal Government came in power. (Laughter.) This was one form of abuse."

The best commentary on Mr. Oliver's statement is to quote the passage in my speech to which he refers. I take it from the "Financial Times " report of the proceedings "The amount of base coin has increased, and I may say that the increase in this connection has been con- tinuous since 1905,when the lowest point was touched. It is an interesting coincidence that tl-...;* item has more than doubled since the present Government came into office. (Laughter.) Ido not, however, suggest that they are responsible for the increase in the predatory habits of a section of the public. I merely mention it as a coincidence, and as indicating that there is some increase in the number of practical disciples of the gospel of free food. (Loud laughter)." I had some difficulty in tracing the quotation. as the speech was delivered as far back as 28th November, 1911. Mr. Oliver is evidently an industrious collector and preserver of things which may be used to brighten his speeches, and I feel truly sensible of the honour be has done me in treasuring this extract for 1.7 months, as an extreme example of solemn Tory abuse. —Yours faithfully, GEORGE A. TOUCHE.

House of Commons, 25th April, 1913. SHAKESPEAREAN ACTING AND NEWSPAPER CRITICISM. Mr. Alfred Perris's Reply to Counter-Critics Sir,--I suppose it will be expected that I should "bide my diminished head" after such a torrent of censure has been poured upon it for expressing my candid opinion regarding the acting in 'The Merchant of Venice." I certainly regret very much that anything I said should have occasioned Mr. W. Ashton such acute distress ; evidently the cause of his so far losing control of his feelings as to go to the length of imput- ing sinister motives to me. His letter leaves me quite unrepentant, however, in regard to the main body of my criticism, believing RS I do that good will come and not the ill effect it seems to be supposed must result from any strictures passed on the performances, in lessening the interest taken by the public in the work of the Society. No-one realises inure fully than I do the value of Mr. Law's service to the cause of amateur dramatic representation, and I have repeatedly testified to my belief in his possession of a positive genius for organising and controlling the spectacular effects .which are made such a feature in these productions. It is with his interpretation of the text of Shakes- peare and the comparatively slight regard he exhibits for the beauty of the poetry, in his effort to give melodramatic effect, that I am at variance, and I am persuaded that the diffusion of opinion on this aspect of the matter will tend to increased interest on the part of the public and improved methods on the part of the performers. The implicatioa that mine is other than "honest criticism," I pass by. I may be mistaken in my judgment, but I cannot think anyone will, on calmly reflecting, accuse me of deliberate dishonesty of purpose. The Chairman's playful allusion to newspaper criticism, (in his address at the dinner) appeAred to be effective as a bon mot, but it suggested a criterion it would clearly be inadvisable for aspirants to histrionic honours to observe. Much more frequently does the actual truth lie in the unpalatable portion of a criticism and, though it may be resented and decried, at the onset, as unfair and all the rest of it, still it acts as a stimulant—and does good. But if the notion is seriously entertained that my criti- cism of methods in acting and speaking on the stage, whether by amateurs or professionals, Is grounded in the belief that I, myself, "could act the parts much better"—and that "for some reason or other" I "work diametrically opposite, by attempting to stultify the aims and ambitions of the Society," I must enter a disclaimer. It is an absolutely false notion, and time will, I believe, establish the fact that my advocacy of simplicity in details of scenery, dresses &c., with a corresponding lessening of the cost of production and a much more thorough devotion to the study and faithful rendering of the sublime poetry—so that the blank verse shall be spoken in all cases not only as if it meant something,but with a clear indication that the speaker is thinking of what it means —and net merely measuring off so manv lengths of figured verbiage, my plea and contention will be justified I feel sure : Ist. By the realisation of the professed desire to do honour to Shakespeare's writings. 2. By the greatly increased satisfaction to the performers themselves, and, 3. By securing the full fruition of the Society's laboure in the attainment of the laudable object of benefitting substantially the local hospital. This, hitherto, has not been accomplished—at least not to the extent hoped for—owing to the great expense incurred in staging the plays. do not propose to enter into a newspaper discussion I with my friend Dr. Mellor on the intricacies and com- plexities in the character of Shylock, but I am

div.head: Peril of Prosperity.
div.p: The Peril of Prosperity.

Preaching at St. John's Presbyterian Church on Sun- day morning,the Rev. W.ffeid spoke of the unwarrantable envy and prejudice which finds its occasion in familiarity to close their eyes to the meaning and significance of life, paralysing all effort,and limiting the Divine. In the evening Mr. Reid referred to praise and popularity as of the fiercest tests of character, and to accept them in nature or measure to which we are not entitled is to injure and finally lose character. On the other hand to refuse them, almost invariably means persecution of some kind, for they who despise honours incur hatred. Prosperity may be the most terrible of trials, and an enemy who offers a kingdom is truly to be feared. Better, however, the injury worked by persecution than that produced by flattery. The former but develops character while the latter drains the soul.

div.head: MOMENTOUS BY-ELECTION.
div.p: A MOMENTOUS BY-ELECTION.

In a very few days the electors of the Altrincham Division, of which the Lymm district forms an important part, will have an opportunity of rectifying an error of judgment which in 1910 resulted in the replacement of the late Sir WILLIAM CROSSLEY by Mr. KEBTY-FLETCHER who, coming from Liverpool, suddenly raised the banner of the Unionist party and succeeded in snatching a narrow victory at the poll. It was a remarkable feat that surprised the country as well as Mr. KEBTY-FLETCHER himself, but now the constituency has the chance of making amends, there can be no doubt that the division will revert to its Free Trade allegiance. For there can be no doubt that the Altrincham Division is frankly and sincerely on the side of Free Trade. It was only the specious promises on the part of the Unionist leaders during the last contest, when like drowning men they grabbed at any passing straw, that caused the forces that had previously prevailed to slacken. In the heart of the constitu- ency 'reside the men whose lives are wrapped up with, and whose interests are the interests of Manchester, the very centre of the business life of Lancashire and the North of England. In 1906, when Tariff "Reform "was placed before them in all its native ugliness, they would have none of it and we witnessed the sight of a constituency with an unbroken Tory record of triumph rejecting the sitting member by the tremendous majority of 2,649. Then came the period of whittling down the meaning of this wonderful " reform,"Ahe nonsense about a referendum and the other mystifying agencies that were set to work. The restilt of this and of slackness, arising from the sense of security, was that Mr. KEBTY- FLETCHER found himself member for Altrincham by virtue of a majority of 119. We are glad to note that the present contingency has found the cause of progress ready for the fray. Liberals, we are fold, are anxious for the fight, the workers are quite ready, and the organization was never in better form. The trimming that has recently gone on regarding food taxes should be of special importance in the Altrincham division, where the farming interests are quite as important as the urban interests. Farmers must realise that they are not being honestly treated by the Tariff "Reformers," A large section of the party say there are to be no food taxes, some that there are, and some that the Colonies must decide whether there should be or not. If there are to be no food taxes where will the farmer benefit under a system that will increase the cost of goodsand implements he buys,while free trade in food gives him no advantaie in what he has to sell? Even [if the Colonies decide that we ought to have Protection, the home farmer would have to compete against his preferentially treated colonial brethren. At Edinburgh last January Mr. BONAR LAW said the new examples to be followed were Denmark with "practically no duties on agricultural produce," and Belgium, where "there is no duty on wheat and very few and very small duties on any other agricultural produce." Is it safe to trust these questions of life and death to a party whose members, for the lack of some fixed policy, are prepared to plunge so recklessly that no man can under- stand the drift of their movements? Free Trade has brought us prosperity; under Free Trade we are now enjoying the greatest trade boom in the history of the nation. The Altrincham electors, we fancy, will say, now they have the opportunity, that Protection is not a pressing need in this country.

div.head: MR. KEBTY FLETCHER RESIGNS.
div.p: MR. KEBTY FLETCHER RESIGNS.
BY-ELECTION IN ALTRINCHAM DIVISION.

On Thursday Mr. Kebty Fletcher, M.P., applied for the Chiltern Hundreds and so resigned his seat in Parlia- ment as member for the Altrincham Division. He announced the taking of this step to Mr. Kilvert, Chairman of the Altrincham Conservative Association, in a brief letter giving ill-health as the cause for his action.

div.head: ON OVERTON HILLS.
div.p: ON OVERTON HILLS.

One of the most popular of holiday resorts is the Mersey View pleasure ground on Overton Hills. On Whit Monday the Warrington Pioneer Band will play for dancing and there will be skating and other amuse- ments. Shelter is provided for 3,000 people.

THE MERRY MONTH OF MAY. 0! blessed month, thou time of joy, Thou'rt ever welcome here-- Thou'rt welcomed by the romping boy, To laughing maid thou'rt dear. On May-day morn, with faces bright The children call on thee, While round the Maypole, in thy light They sing and dance with glee. 0! joyful sight, so full of peace, On such a happy day: But hark! the merry voices cease— Here comes the Queen of May. The sun is smiling from the skies; The Heavens are blue and clear • The Queen looks Tound with sparkling eyes— Her subjects wildly cheer. She moves with state and dignity Towards her Royal throne, Which, decked with blossom from the tree, A real Queen may be.

Green trees o'erhang the Royal place, The children on the sward ; Look up into their May-QuPen's face And all, with one accord Declare she is the finest queen They've had for many, a year • Her power's supreme, and o'er the green In ringing accents clear. She bids them all enjoy their play An all her princely court, Joined with the subjects on this day; Prepare to share the sport. At length the sun behind the trees Sinks doWn into the West. The revellers, tired, like a breeze Melt homeward for their rest. The empty throne, on the deserted ground, And the trees—in my mind—give birth To the thou*ht that here at least can be found, Peace —with our God—on Barth. B. F.

div.head: KING'S VISIT.
div.p: THE KING'S VISIT.

The coming of King Edward in 1906 gave a great impetus to the Beautiful. Warrington movement in its early days. Is it too much to hope that the coming of King George this summer may do as much to revive a languishing but commendable institution? Yesterday the Royal train came to Arpley for a rehearsal of the July visit, showing decisively that Arpley is to have the honour of receiving their Majesties into Lancashire. May we suggest that tradesmen and others, whose premises are on the line of route along Bridge-street and Sankey-street to the Town Hall, and then towards Sankey Bridges, via Crosfield's works, should use flowers as largely as possible for their decorations? Seven years ago the device was adopted largely through- out the town with charming results.

CHILDREN AND BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON. It is with much regret that we notice that Canon Morley Stevenson, the president, and Mr. Longland, the hon. treasurer of the Beautiful Warrington Society, have found it necessary to issue a circular stating that the committee have been compelled, during the last two years, to restrict their work to assisting the school children's branch and to abandon such work as tree-planting,the care of open spaces and the encouragment of cottage and window gardening. Even the aid to the children stands in danger of being withdrawn unless the society receives more liberal support. Surely support for a movement that for a time provided the town with most substantial counter attractions to its smoke and its grime by making many of our streets into elongated gardens will be forthcoming when the need is !known.

div.head: PUBLIC BOWLING GREENS.
div.p: PUBLIC BOWLING GREENS.

Municipal bowling greens were opened in several quarters of the town on May Day, but without any official show that the importance of the occasion would seem to warrant. We are gradually building up a record in curious ways of procedure. First we have baths' foundation stones laid within the privacy of stout hoardings, then the opening of a play ground by the rough but simple method of pulling up a hurdle to allow the children to swarm in. Now we have bowling greens merely thrown open to the public by the unlocking of the gate. True, Alderman Bennett stepped forward at the St. Elphin's green and robbed the affair of its sombreness by playing the first game, but a little more might be made of our public virtues and our public spiritedness.

WARRINGTON AND RELIGIOUS FREEDOM. In another column Dr. Mellor records, in a simple but telling manner, how Oxford still clings to the system of religious tests, and, incidentally,mentions that the Warring- ton Academy, at the end of the Eighteenth Century, held out the beacon that is destined some day to show the way to complete toleration. At the Academy, in those far off times, a university was established in a small way at which Nonconformists were placed on an equality with their Church brethren. The university out-grew its original home and was transferred to Manchester, York,London and other places ; and at the present time its descendant, the Manchester College, Oxford, stands as a monument to the work of those famous Warrington workers in the cause of liberty and equality, whose figures are perpetuated in stained glass windows for all visitors to Oxford to see and to reverence.

div.head: LOST CUP.
div.p: THE LOST CUP.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield wired on Saturday to Mr. H. Ashton, at the Headingley ground : Good luck to the Wireputlers in the great event - to-day. May their skill, dash, pluck and com- bination be rewarded with victory, and the cup once more return to Warrington. The skill, dash, pluck and combination were all there, but the cup returned not. By a narrow margin, Warrington succumbed to Huddersfield, but no one felt more relieved when the game was over than the Hudders- field players. Before the match all Yorkshire seemed to be smiling and the Warrington excursionists, as they passed, thousands strong, through the stations on the way to Leeds were much impressed by the look on the faces of the populace which too plainly betokened satisfaction at the prospects of the day, mingled with sorrow for the delu- sive hopes that had tempted so many good people so far from home on a wet day. But as the game progressed the home spectators became alarmed. Why were not Hudders- field scoring? Why were they behind? Why were they not running away with the Cup? The answer came, brief but . all- sufficient, in the words of a Yorkshire spectator, standing near the writer: "Warrington's playing—it's no use talk- ing," he ,explained to his brother Tyke. Warrington played to the last minute and with a little luck might easily have brought the Cup again to Lancashire. Perhaps they will have that luck next time. In the meanwhile the players earned the respect of the rival county, and especially of that previously self-satisfied portion that has Huddersfield football ground for its centre.

div.head: CURIOUS POINT.
div.p: A CURIOUS POINT.

It is stated, though in a quarter that is, not usually regarded as serious, that Warrington failed to beat Huddersfield because the reporters were not given better facilities for travelling into Yorkshire This is a matter that should be properly considered. It might be worth a whole special train the next time Warrington reach the final if a satisfactory result could he attained by a little considera- tion in the matter of dining—and perhaps sleeping—cars.

THE NEW MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH. It will be recommended to the members of the Town Council, at their monthly meeting on Tuesday, that the Assistant Medical Officer of Health, Dr. G. W. N. Joseph, be appointed to succeed Dr. Hibbert as Medical Officer for the borough. The salary has not been fixed so that the recommendation will come before the Council in an incomplete state. Dr. Hibbert's present salary is £550 to cover the various appointments he holds under the Cprporation. It has been decided to advertise for a successor to Dr. Joseph at a salary of £250.

div.head: RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION
div.p: RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION
IN THE
SECONDARY SCHOOL. The Rector's "Deliberately Rejected"
Efforts.
NO ALTERATION IN THE TIME TABLE.

We have received from the Rector of Warring- ton (the Rev. Canon Willis) the following copy of correspondence which has taken place between him and the Education Committee on the question of religious instruction in the Secondary School : Education Office, Sankey-street, Warrington, April 22nd, 1913. Dear Sir,—l beg to inform you. that your letter of the 10th March last addressed to the Chair- man and members of the Education Committee, asking for an alteration to be made in the time- table for religious instruction in the Secondary School, has now been carefully considered by the School Management Committee, and that, on their recommendation, the Education Committee, at their meeting yesterday, decided that in 'view of their recent decision in this matter they could not see their way to accede to your request.—l am, yours truly, J. MOORE MURRAY. Rev. Canon Willis,

The Rectory, Warrington. April 24th, 1913. Dear Sir,—l beg to thank you for your r6ply of the 22nd inst., to my letter of the 10th ult. lam indeed sorry to find that the School Management Committee adheres to its resolution, and that the Education Committee endorses its recommenda- tion. _

I have striven in the highest interests ,of the future generation of the inhabitants of this town to secure a worthy treatment of the Bible in the Council Secondary School. My efforts have been deliberately rejected. The reason given for refusal is that the time allotted to secular subjects is already overloaded and that an hour and a half per week, that is 15 minutes a day, is all that can be granted for Religious Exercises. How then, I ask, is it that the other Secondary Schools, which provide a much wider range of subjects for their pupils than the Council School does for its scholars, an give more than two lours a week for real Religious Instruction without suffering harm or loss? - Let us plainly state and face the facts. Two hundred scholars of both sexes and various ages are gathered together every morning in a 'build- ing without any seating accommodation to listen, after a hymn and prayer,' for five minutes to a passage read from the Bible without exposition or comment. This is the only provision made by the Warrington Education. 'Committee for 200 of their best scholars. Will any u educationist who knows a child's threefold nature body, mind and soul say this is sufficient? Will-any really religious parent say it is satisfactory? If not let them protest and let them demand for these children that which is their right.—l am, dear sir, yours very truly, FREDERICK W. WILLIS.

HISTORY OF THE CONTROVERSY. At the February meeting of the Education Com- mittee it was reported that the Rector had re- quested that the syllabus for religious instruction in use in the Public Elementary Council Schools in the borough should be introduced into the Sec- ondary School. A. sub-committee appointed to consider this re- quest reported that they had interviewed the hesid- master of the Secondary School, who reported that the time-table already provided for an hour and a half per week to be devoted to a religious service at the opening of each morning session, and that it would be difficult to allot more time with- out overloading the time for secular instruction. Upon this report and the recommendation of the School Management Cominittee, it was resolved that Bible reading be included in the religious services held on the opening of the school, that • such literal explanations as may be necessary to irender a passage intelligible to the scholars be given by the headmaster, and that the headmaster as occasion arose should introduce brief moral lessons in lieu of Bible reading, conditionally upon the aggregate time of one hour and a half a week allowed for religious opening services being not exceeded. _ _ .

At the next meeting of the Education Commit- tee, the Rector wrote saying that he felt so strongly and deeply on the subject of religious instruction in, the Secondary School that he could not let the matter rest where it was, and asked the committee if they would allow the headmaster to give two lessons a week on the Bible instead of using the allotted time of fifteen minutes each morning for a hymn, prayer and Bible reading. He suggested that the 90 minutes allowed for each week should be so divided as to. give 50 minutes to two ,good lessons, and the other 40 minutes to a hymn and prayer each day. "If you will agree to this, I am quite sure," concluded the Rector, "you will relieve the minds of, many religious parents who do not like to complain, but are greatly distressed at the result of your delibera- tions." .

Councillor Hy. Roberts, as chairman of the Education Committee, moved that the letter be referred to the School Management Committee. and in doing so made some scathing remarks, say- ing that the school was in the keeping of the Education Committee and protesting against The style or manner of .attempted dictation conveyed in the letter, which was “not generous after the way in Which the committee had tried to meet the wishes of the Rector and those he alleged he represented." Councillor Roberts further stated that no intimation of dissatisfaction had been re- ceived from any parent, and altogether he thought the time had come when the committee 'should assert their position. Last week the Education Committee received the report from the School Management Commit- tee, saying that they could not accede to the re- quest of the Rector, and it is in respect .of the communication'of that fact 'and the Rector's re- joiner that forms the subject of the correspondence above produced.

who came out on strike last week were in receipt of 21s. a week. The carters who struck a month ago had 22/- a week. The latter dispute ;emus to have been settled by compromise half-way because of the contracts which the masters had for dealing with blocks of traffic at given prices. This illustrates that it is not a matter of prime importance to the contractors what they pay the men as it simply gets handed (in to the employer of tho contractors and becomes a charge on industry generally. Now, inas- much as industry has reaped a very rich reward during the recent years, the price of cartage ought to be fixed so as enable the owners of carts to pay their men a sufficient living wage. This principle applies generally to most trades in which low wages are paid. A great deal is made of the additional charges put upon industry by recent legislation and by a rise in wages, but this is in no way commensurate with the increased earnings which capital has reaped during late years. Both socially and economically it would be better for the country if there was a general rise in wages. These wages would, apart from drink, be spent in more useful ways than at present. The large incomes now coming to a limited number of individuals are creating an expenditure upon the production of those things which yield a poor return, or no return whatever, upon luxuries and upon unnecessary services. A general rise in the remunera- tion of labour would be a good thing for the country even if it meant a slight reduction on the earnings of capital. The earnings of capital, pure capital, have during the last six years increased 25 per cent. That is £lOO that earned £4 per aanurn as interest a few years ago can now earn as readily .15 per annum. The remuneration of labour has all round not increased more than 10 per cent., so that even if we take it that the relation of the earnings, six or eight years ago of the two factors were equitable, which is doubtful, recent developments have shown that the capital has had the, advantage by an excess rise of 15 per cent. But this is not all because against the 10 or 12 per cent. increase that labour has got in nominal remunera- tion one has to make a substantial reduction (which varies according to what the money is spent in) for the appre3iatiorl in prices. Morally, socially, physically and economically there is an unanswerable case for the payment of a living wage; true patriotism and our National well-being call for the reform with an emphasis which may not be withstood.

div.head: Alexandra Day.
div.p: Alexandra Day.

A meeting of ladies was held at the Infirmary yesterday afternoon ,under the auspices of the Ladies Infirmary Committee, and decided to hold on Satur- day, June 28, a local celebration of Alixandra Day. The principal feature of the day's proceedings will be the sale of artificial wild roses for the henefit of the Infirmary. Mr. J. H. Smethurst was appointed chairman, Mrs. F. W. Monks hon. treasurer, and Mrs. Henry Greenall hon. secretary of the committee. The Royal Train at Warrington.

Thelloyal train in which the King and Queen will travel to Warrington in July, visited Arpley station yesterday. Details were arranged as to the part of the platform at which t!..e train will be drawn up, and the exit by which their Majesties will leave the station. It is intended that all the school children of the borongh shall be accommodated on tands outside Arpley station E 0 that they may have a good view of their Majesties as they enter the open carriage in which they will drive through the town. Liberal Club Extension.

The foundation stone of the new Memorial Hall at the Liberal Club will be laid by Mrs. John Crosfield on Thursday next at 2.30 p.m. Mrs. Crosfield will also present the photographs and silver spoons given by Mr. A. H. Crosfield to the parents of children born on the day when the maternity benefit of the Insur- ance Act come into operation.—A meeting of the Ladies' Committee, Liberal Club Committee, and the Liberal Association was held last night to arrange the programme for the day.

Cheshire Lines Platelayers' and Workmen's • Provident Society. The thirty-eighth annual meeting of this society, which consists of the workmen employed in the Engineer's Department of the Cheshire Lines Railway was held at the Works, Batteraby-lane, Warrington, on Tuesday. The chair was taken by Mr. Harry Blundell, M. Inst. C. E. the Chief Engineer of the Company, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and delegates from Lancashire and Cheshire. The secrPtary submitted the annual rennrt, which stated that the number of members was 1078. A large sum had been expended in aid of 288 sick members, who had received assistance from the funds of the society, and 15 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed Mr. Thomas Pratt was re-elected secretary for the ensuing year, and Messrs. Robert Jones and William Knowles were elected auditors.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER OF. HEALTH.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER OF. HEALTH.
A 25/- MINIMUM.

Mr. Tom Mann addressed a large and enthusi- astic meeting in the Co-operative Hall, Warring- ton, on Tuesday evening. He is a born organiser and leader of .men, and possesses a remarkable power of swaying tbem by his earnest, direct and outspoken style-Of speaking. On Tuesday he thun- dered at the non-unionists, whom he called "silly fat-,heads," drew a dramatic and moving picture of the trials which ',beset, the early pioneers of trade unionism, and suggested possibilities of great extensions with regard to the brewery strike.

LIVING UPON THEIR OWN FAT. Mr. Mann made a strong plea for a minimum wage of 255. per week. He declared that no man, no matter how •good a wife he might have, could provide -the bare necessaries of life for the main- tenance of a family of six, on less than 255. per week. -He did not believe it could be done on that; in fact, a sensible interpretation of what was requisite for an ordinary civilised life, worthy of men and women, could not be obtained with a purchasing power of less than 355. Under present conditions, a very large percentage of the popula- tion of this country were compelled to live upon their own fat. By. that he meant that there were adult males -and female's who never received' in the form of nourishment the equal to that which they gave .off in physical energy- each day, The result was that they died, on the average, fifteen years earlier than they would .if they were de- cently fed, clothed, and housed. SOCIAL MURDER.

"A social crime," continued Mr. Mann, "is being continually perpetrated in this country. It may be described as social murder—the murder of men and women by scores of thousands, not by taking their lives suddenly, but because their economic surroundings are of such a vicious character that they are not able to obtain a sufficiency of life's re- quisites. They live a life of lingering illness or enfeebled health until they can no longer effec-

tively resist, and they are taken to the grave fifteen years before their proper, natural time. I believe it to be not only permi.sible, but a sacred' duty to be a rebel against such a condition of society. (Applause.) As thinking men, we know for a • certainty that there is not the slightest necessity why any man, woman or child should be in such poverty in this country. C"llear, hear.") -We know, further, that the poverty that does exist • is preventable, and that it is our duty to prevent it. It is not wise or sensible to turn to another class, outside the working class, who pre- tend to have an interest in us, and beseech them -of their charity to do something. The workers 'themselves must take such conserted action as would. enable them so to adjust the economic con- ditions that they .would be able to put in an effec- tive claim for a reasonable share of the results of their own labours." (Applause.) •

A LOW MINIMUM. The only justification for asking for such a low minimum wage as 255., continued Mr. Mann, was the fact that such an enormous percentage of workers received less than that amount. He was

told that the local brewery labourers who had struck for a wage of 235. had hitherto been receiving one guinea per week. He had.-computed that for the average family, such a *age would not allow of the expenditure of more than one penny' per meal per person for the whole year round. That was a standard of life for Englishinen, in the country of the great and glorious Shakespeare and Milton ! Even the donkey would jib effectively if he (lid not get a bit of chaff or an occasional carrot. (Laugh- ter.) Yet here in industrial and agricultural Eng- land there were men and women by the hundred , thousand not getting, sufficient to keep themselves' up to the standard of normal health, and absol- utely barring all intellectual development. They were cribbed, cabined and confined in narrow, common ruts, not permitted to share in the advan- tages .of civilization, unless it be to smell the stinks of somebody else's motor-car: (Laughter.) _ _

Rather, than call the present conditions a sin arid „a shame, he would say that workingmen ,were -dunderheaded fools for being so slow to organise, and for hesitating so long before taking definite action with a view to destroy the economic re- lationships which prevented them acting the part of capable, dignified men, and claiming a rightful share of the product of their labours. • A STATE OF SLAVERY. Non-unionists Mr. Mann described as a "silly, fat-headed lot," and "confounded nuisances," who
Were a drag On the wheel and a stumbling block .to progress. The man who, with his eyes open, deliberately refused to be identified with a union, systematically avoided his fellow-workers Who

.• -were taking concerted action to raise the standard of life, and then held out his hand to participate in the fruits of victory, must be possessed of some of the meanest qualities that could occupy men's Minds. Mr. Mann pointed out bow those Who first asserted the right of workingmen to combine were punished by transportation to convict settlements. The law, he declared, was a funny institution— something made by capitalists to enable them to remain top dogs. To the extent that workingmen had organised, would they minimise poverty. The movement did not come from the Church, Parlia- ment; or politicians, but as the direct outcome of organised effort on trade union lines. (Applause.) The slave had no chance of developing the higher qualities, and. therefore to get out of the accursed slavery which bound them was the noblest work of men. "T don't believe in carrying people to heaven," declared Mr. Mann. "Let them fight r their own way, and if they prefer to go to hell, let them go there and get out of the road." A TRANSPORT STRIKE.

• Referring to the dispute at Messrs. Walker's _brewery, Mr. Mann hinted at the possibility of calling out transport workers in support of the strikers, ..but said he did not believe in using a steam hammer to craCk a nut, unless it became absolutely necessary. He remembered how Messrs. Walkers' representatives came to see him many times during the transport .workers' strike in Liv- erpool. If the dispute was not worth a fight, he advised them to close it up. If it was worth a fight, then there was nothing for it but extension, unless a settlement could be reached. The object of those who were fighting the workers' battle, concluded Mr. Mann, was that every child born should have an adequate opportunity of physical aild mental nourishment and development, and grow up worthy of a high citizenship. They wished to wipe out poverty in order that they might abolish much human Misery. (Applause.) ' CLASS DISTINCTIONS.

Mr. Charles Dukes presided over the meeting, and commended the efforts that were being put forth to abolish class distinctions and bring about• a more equitable distribution of the/wealth which the workers produced. AN AGE OF HYPOCRISY. Mr— W. F. Rean also addressed the meeting, and declared that there never was a time when there was more hypocrisy in our land than to-day. if 'those sycophants and courtiers who surrounded the King would have the decency to suggest to him that it would be far better if he ruled over a cleaner, more wholesome and more decent Eng- land, it would be more truly patriotic than trying to gloss over such hells upon earth as existed in the north and centre of England, and, by bring- ing the King and Queen round, trying to keep the working classes from understanding their economic and social position.
PREMIER CYCLES. Excelsior Cycles, Lea Francis Cycles, £4 10/-to £l6 16/-.—Sole Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: LABOUR LEAGUE. A PERTINENT QUESTION FOR MR. HAROLD SMITH.
div.p: LABOUR LEAGUE. A PERTINENT QUESTION FOR MR. HAROLD SMITH.
The Fight Against Conscription.

The Progressive Labour League is one of the most useful and hardworking sections of the progressive forces in Warrington.the successful open-air campaigns which it has promoted having done much for the political education of the workers. The enthusiasm displayed at the annual meeting of the League, which was held at the Liberal Club, on Thursday evening, augured well for the period of activity which is to be entered upon next week. The President (Mr. E. Wynne Jones), presided over a large attendance.

div.head: SOCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL REFORM.
div.p: SOCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL REFORM.

The Secretary (Mr. J. Morton) presented his annual report as follows: —During the past year, which has been one of continued labour unrest, the League has confined its propaganda to outside work and has brought to the workingman capable exponents of the measures of progressive reform that have attained practical importance and have come within the range of definite Government action. _ _

While not overlooking the fact that the' "Tariff Reform" agitation is not yet extinct, our main effort has been to educate he labouring classes in those social and industrial reforms through which we believe the emancipation of the workers is to be attained, believing that much more satisfactory results are to be expected from the positive advocacy of alternative social reforms than from the negative process of trying to kill an already expiring agitation. The Home Rule question has had a prominent place in our campaign, Mr. J. McVeagh, M. V., addressing a large mass meeting at Bridge Foot in May and Mr. Fallon in place of Mr. Clancy, M.P., in the Co-operative Hall in September. On July 15th we joined with the Young Liberal Association in a united demonstration at Bridge Foot to celebrate the coming into operation of the Insurance Act at which Mr. J. B. Martindale was the principal- speaker. Other prominent questions including Welsh Disestablishment and the Land question have also had due attention from Messrs. Robert Lewis, Middle- ton, Kendal, G-arside, Gleave, members of the League and local friends. A series of joint meetings with the Young Liberal Association in the various wards of the town have also been conducted with good results. With regard to the present position of the league, it is felt that if possible the Executive Committee should be considerably sttengthened with a view to meeting the demands that may be made on the League within the next two or three years. The report was adopted, with a cordial expression of thanks to the sub-committee which attended to the van during the summer months. THE OFFICERS.

The officers of th-e—L—eaiu-e-v;;reelected as follavvs : President, Mr. E. Wynne Jones; vice-presidents, Messrs. E. W. James, P. Osborne, J. Elwell, M. Llewellyn, T. Barnes, H. F. ar,G. Colley and G. Walker; hon. treasurer, Mr. S. Wright; hon. secretary, Mr. J. Morton ; committee, Messrs. NV. J. Hancook, S. B. Healey, W. Miles, W. Prinsep, F. Hanametsley, A, Edwards, J. Riley,Thomas Johnson,E.Lloyd,C.J.Sheath. W. Vose, W. Unsworth, R. Pomfret, V. Dunbobbin, T. R. Ashworth, W. Scrage, G. Cliffs, R. Brown, A. Buchanan, H. Thomas, B. Jennings, J. Johnson, NV. Muskett, S. Dutton, T. Spittle, Joseph Sheath, M. Hughes, W. Scragg, jun., J. Derbyshire, and A. Thomas.

div.head: PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS.
div.p: THE PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS.

Mr. E. WYNNE JONES, in returning thanks for his re-election to the presidency, said the League ought to be in the forefront of the btttle for progress. An organization with a membership of 600 or 700 ought to be an important factor in ousting Mr. Harold Smith from the representation of Warrington. (Applause.) It was not fit and proper that an industrial town like Warrington should be represented by a gentleman who belonged to the Con- servative party. In the interests of reform, they should see to it that Warrington had 'a progressive member. The League started some years ago with a great pro- gramme, the first item being the defence of Free Trade. it was absolutely essential that they should keep that subject to the fore, because our Free Trade policy was more vitally necessary than ever, for the well-being of the great mass of the workers. TARIFF " REFORMERS " IN RETREAT

_ A great Bretton of the tariff reformers were in full retreat on the question of food taxes, and one wished that could be said of the whole of the Tory party. While there was a large section of the party who would throw over tariff reform entirely to-morrow, there was also a large section who would tax the people's food if they could get the chance. Speaking of the plight of the Tory party with regard to tariff reform, he saw that the London " Observer " had recently been pointing out that Radical cartoonists would be picturing the Tory party carrying that first constructive plank in their programme to the back of the builder's yard. The position, added that paper, was sufficient to render Disraeli dumb, had it been witnessed in his day. In the coming campaign the League would have to main- tain that Free Trade was not only the best for us, but for every other country in the world. They would be justified in claiming that, in view of recent events in America. There they were going to smash their present Protectionist system—in fact they had taken the first step and, under President Wilson, he thought they would succeed. (Applause). When they did so, it would be of great and lasting benefit to the worker,/ in America..

div.head: CARTERS' VICTORY.
div.p: THE CARTERS' VICTORY.

Another item which the League included in its pro- gramme was the defence of trade unions. They must retain that policy, for unless they insisted upon justice to the worker and his organisations, they had no right to the title of a Progressive Labour League. They congratulated the carters of Warrington on the splendid vic.,ory they won during the last few weeks. (Applause.) He noticed that Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. offered his services as a kind of intermediary in that dispute, but he was glad the offer was rejected because Mr. Smith belonged to a party which had been guilty of a con- spiracy to overthrow trade unions or, if not to overthrow, at kaat, to damage the opportunity for use- fulness of those great organisations. WHAT IS THE MEMBER DOING? Up to the present, continued Mr. Jones, be had not seen any intimation that Mr. llarold Smith had offered his services to settle the dispute at Messrs. Walker's brewery. (A Voice : "He dare not.") Perhaps Messrs. Walker were quite pre- pared to support Mr. Smith, to a great extent, in his political propaganda' but if he had the interests of the workers at heArt, as he alleged from time to time, it was a very opportune moment for him to demonstrate the fact by going to Messrs. Walker and saying It is in the interests of the workers that you should recognize their Union, for the men have as much right to organize in this way, as the employers have." (Applause.) He fancied the workers in Warrington would appreciate such an act on the part of Mr. Smith and the League might ask him when he proposed to offer his services in the dispute. They might also ask him if he did not think that Messrs Walker's labourers were entitled to a larger share of the 000,000 profit than 21s. per week ? He (the speaker) did not think that even a bonus of 10.?. was quite the w,rker's share of those large pats. The workers did not want either Christmas beef or bonuses, but a living wage. (Applause). UTOPIAN SCHEMES.

He sometimes felt that the workers of this country did not realise what a power they had, if they only acted together. They had the solution of their own difficulties in their own hands, if they would only face them. He was sorry that the progressive forces were so split up. Some people were always advocating Utopian schemes or talking about Socialism in a vague, fragmentary sort of way. Nobody knew what they meant by Socialism and he questioned whether they themselves did. The people did not want Utopian schemes that would not benefit them for a 100 years, they wanted something that would benefit them now. (Hear, hear). A better plan than talking about Socialism, Syndicalism, or any of those schemes was to point out to the worker the absolute necessity of oreanisation. By that means the worker would be able to secure a wider diffusion of everything that made for the common good and a larger share of the great profits which were the results of his own labour. (Applause). Having referred to the approaching consummation of Ireland's long-cherished aspirations, the President said the League stood for better housing, the prevention of sweating, for drastic dealing with unemployment, and a national system of education. He pointed out that part 2of the Insurance Act was the first step to tackle the unemployment problem in a eystematio way and he believed the time would come when the unemployment section of the Act would be applied to all trades. THE BLOOD TAX.

By their work throughout the country, Liberals and Free Traders had done very much to kill rood taxes, but as progressives there was another work which they were called upon to do. They had not to be satisfied with killing the food taxes ; they had got to kill the blood tax too. The attempt to revive con- scription in this country was a matter that all the workers had to face and be prepared to fight to the last ditch, because whoever stood to gain by a conscrip- tionist system, the worker stood to lose every time. He had many friends in the National Service League and they repeatedly told him that the organization they proposed was intended solely for home defence against invasion. They could all see the fallacy of that sugges- tion. There was no need for a national army for home defence if our navy was defeated, because a foreign power would not need to land a single soldier . here. All they would have to do was to block ur (Continued in nc::t column)

div.head: THEOLOGICAL DEGREES AT OXFORD.
div.p: THEOLOGICAL DEGREES AT OXFORD.
WHERE RELIGIOUS FREEDOM DOES NOT PREVAIL.
Warrington Pointed the Better Way.

On Tuesday, April 29th, the cause of religious freedom in this country received a severe blow at the hands of Convocation in the .University of Ox- forcl. As the rules of the University stand at present, examiners for theological degrees 'in Ox- ford must be memliers of the University `,! in priests' orders," and, furthermore, the degiees of B.D. and D.D. can be given to those only holding priests' orders." This means, of course, that no Nonconformist minister, no matter how eminent a theological scholar he may be, can ever be an examiner in the Theological School, and no .Non- conformist can ever hold the degree of RD. or D.D. from Oxford University: As far, as the theolof,Tical faculty is concerned, the University is a close and exclusive corporation, confined to:mem- hers of the Church of England; proficiency in theo- logical' training depends on tests, and, conse- quently, religious freedom is at a discount. Attempts have been made to alter this state of affairs, and, a short time back 'certain- proposals, Making the theological school quite free, were adopted by congregation. To make the matter clear, we ought to explain that "congregation" consists of all those 'in residence at Oxford bolding the degree of M.A. on any higher degree; that is to say, it consists' of "the men on the spot," and the men who know. Decisions made by "congre- gation" have to be referred to "convocation," which consists_of all those holding. the M.A., or higher degree, whether in residence or not. When theological matters are concerned, Oxford is in- vaded by country clergymen, prepared to defend the faith. What, then, happened was this: Con- gregation decided to get rid of theological tests, and make religious teaching and learning quite free, as, of course, they should be. Cenvocation, however, cOmpoaed largely of men who, however worthy, are somewhat. behind the times, rejected the proposals for reform by a huge majority. In consequence, religious tests remain in Oxford, and the University. lags. behinds the general feeling of all intelligent men. Such a thing is deeply regret- table, but of course it cannot last long. Sooner or later the Oxford Theological Faculty will be nde free and open. Already, almost' within the Uni- versity itself, there is free theological teaching and learning to a considerable 'extent .at Mansfield College, and wholly at Manchester College, which, Warrington people may note, owed its origin to the old Warrington Academy. The presence of these free theological colleges, . And especially of Manchester College, in Oxford, has had a pro- found effect on inside Oxford opinion; and when, in the future, the Oxford Theological School is made free and open, the influence of Manchester College will have played no small part in bringing the result about; and, indirectly, through .the con- nection with the Academy, the glory of freeing Oxford from ati religious tests will not be without

its connection with Warrington. Why the study of theology in a great university like Oxford should be liniited, and largely monopolised by membeis of one single Church to the exclusion of all others, why this should be the case, surely must pass the comprehension of every intelligent man. The position is obviously absurd. STANLEY A. MiLLOR.

div.head: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR.
div.p: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR.
PROCEEDS OVER £9OO.

Continued from Pagc 4. Mr. J. Upson performed the opening ceremony at the Old English Bazaar, at the Parr Ilell, yesterday. Mr. M. F; Hickman presided over a good attendance. At the outsat, Mr. HARRIS presented the financial statement. Mr. William Bennett had sent a further sum of £25 making his total donation one of £5O. The profit on the handbook, irreipective of sales, was £l7. Mrs. Dodds, who opened the silo on Thurs lay, gave a handsome donation of £5O, making a total for the previous day of £2OO 18s. 11d, and for the three days of £OB3 12s. 4c.

The CHAIRMAN expressed the hope that the result that day would be worthy of the Wesleyan Circuit and would surpass all expectations. He extended a hearty welcome to the Rev. Iheodore Bishop, formerly of Warrington, but now of Crewe. Having referred to the self-sacrificing work of Mr. Upson in the cause of Methodism, Mr. Hickman said the Warrington circuit was full of life and was bound to progress. (Applause.) Mr. UesoN said that some Wesleyans had not liked the idea of erecting a new building, as they feared it might effect the congregation at Bewsey-road. It was perfectly true that a considerable portion of the con- gregation now worshipping at Bewsey-road came from the district where the new chapel would be erected.. If it were found that one chapel did not supply the spiritual needs of n rapidly growing district, then they had to erect new buildines. If they were to be true to their traditions and justify their existence as a Church and prove that they were worthy sons of worthy sires, they must go forward. Methodism was never stronger, wealthier or more influentiLl than to-day. They w.nted to extend further in the Lovely-lane district and they must go forward, working hard until all their ambitions were rcaliser). In the Norris-street district people were being spiritually starved because some of theta could not pet to Bewsey-road which was never built to provide for tie needs of that distant suburb. (Applanse.) On the proposii ion of Mr. G. V. WHEATLEY seconded by Mr. J. C. HOLLAND and supported by the Rev. Theodore Bishop a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman and opener.
THE TOTAL PROCEEDS. The total proceeds of the bazaar amounted to £929 9s. Od.

div.head: ATTRACTIONS.
div.p: THE ATTRACTIONS.

Visitors to the bazaar have been provided with a multitude of attractions, in the way of concerts an side-shows. Fach evcning a choice musical programme has been submitted by Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra under the c3nductorship of Mr. Arthur D Wl3. The prize choirs of Bold-street (conducted by Mr. Frank H ickman B.wsey- road (Mr. Wm. H i pit iss) and Stock tot, Heath (Mr. F. E. Penketla) gave high class concerts which were much appreciated. The Bewsey-road Prize Baud, consisting of "some of the most renowned instru- mentalists in the country," was a decided novelty. There was an exhibition of tableaux vivants, arranged.. by Mr. H. S. Brown, of Lymm, and the Smart Set, Pierrots, from Penketh, (under the direction of Mrs Stevenson) gave a bright entertainment. Other attrac- tions were the Royal Court Marrionettes, the perform dog, a conjuring show and a _series of shooting com- petitions.

div.head: MARKET PRICES.
div.p: MARKET PRICES.
WHEAT.-49 to 4s id per 701bs. OATS.-29 3d to 2s 8d per 451bs. WHEAT STRAw.—£2 2s. Gd. per ton. OAT STRAW.—£2 26. Gd. to £2 ss. per ton. XX FLOUR.-23s 6d per 2401b5. BRAN.-11!,d. per 201bs.

ports and remain outside until they had starved us into surrender. The programme of the National Service League was not simply for home defence. Behind the agitation was the desire to foist a compulsory military system upon the country,and it was that attempt which had to be fought. Lie was very much concerned about one point, and that was that so many people who were taking an active part as officers and in other ways in the Territorial movement were believers in compulsory military training. The success of the Territorial scheme meant the death of conscription, and how those people could do all they could to improve the Territorinls and at the same time believe in conscription, he failed to understand. They told us that the training of the Territorials was not sufficient, but the scheme of training they proposed was exactly the same The Progressive Labour League stood for army reform and, until it had been found that the voluntary system was an absolute failure, they must beware of the conscriptionist system and light it by every means in their power. (Applause). WHAT THE LEAGUE STANDS FOR.

The meeting approved the following summary of the objects of the League : Industrial, Reform, by such readjustment of economic relationships as will ensure a competent wage for all. Abolition of poverty. Prevention of unemployment. A more equitable distribution of wealth. Social Reform : To secure for the masses efficient education,better housing, improved sanitary coed itions. Equality of electoral power. Improved liquor laws. Army reform. Improved provision for old age. To defend Free Trade. , Improved land laws. Defence of tracfe unions and protection of their , funds.

TRADES COUNCIL TO BE APPROACHED. It was decided to seek affiliation with the Trades and Labour Council, the Chairman remarking that such orrinisations ought not to be captured by the purely Socialistic element.
