div.head: Mimi
div.p: Mimi
CHURCH TOMS,
RELIGION IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
The Local Controversy.

A variety of interesting subjects came up for dis- cusrion at a conference ,of the clergy and lay repre- sentatives of the Rural Deanery of ‘‘ inwick, held at the tNiurch House, Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon. Abe Rural Dean (Rev. Canon Willis,) presided

div.head: NEW FINANCE SCHEME,
div.p: A NEW FINANCE SCHEME,

. _ Mr. ALDERSON SMITH (organising secretary of the Liverpool Diocesan Finance Asscciation) detailed the steps which are being taken in the Liverpool diocese to carry out the Archbishops' recommendations as to finance. He pointed out that the Liverpool diocese had not yet got a scheme into line, but steps were being taken to formulate one which it was hoped would be successful. The basis of the Archbishops' scheme was that each Rural deanery should be assessed to provide a certain sum annually for diocesan purposes and each rural deanery should assess its various parishes, according to the financial condition of each and the number of persons associated with the church. THE DEAR CH OF CLERGY. Perhaps the most pressing need of the day was that ot the provision for the training, maintenance and pensions of the clergy. All would agree that the dearth of clergy was pressing on all sides. He under- stood that in the diocese of Liverpool alone, they were ,calling out, for at least twenty-tour assistant clergy, and they were not to be found. Numbers of men 'willing and capable, were ready to come forward but the question of £ s. d. prevented them. The cost of education and the preparation for the work of the ministry was so heavy that many a desirable man was kept back through lack of means. Last year they administered bursaries to suitable candidates in the Liverpool diocese, to the amount of nearly £5OO, but they might, with advantage, multiply that many times over. With regard to the augmentation of benefices he did not think they, as a Church, ought to rest satisfied until every benefice was brought up to at least £3OO a year and a house. He believed one cause of the shortage of clergy was that educated men were called upon to maintain themselves and their families •on such beggarly stipends. £l,OOO FROM WINWICE DEANERY. It was estimated that in the diocese of Liverpool their needs, for the purposes above-mentioned an,l for church building,education, preventive and rescue work, would be not less than £lO.OOO this year. In the rural deanery of Winwick, they bad twenty-tour parishes— a tenth of the pirishes of the diocese. That meant that the deanery would he responsible for £l,OOO. That sounded staggering, but he was sure the deanery could do better than it bad done. During the last five years the average contribution to diocesan funds for all purposes had been £l6 10s. per parish. It must be left to each parish to raise its quota in the way it thought best. In many districts me free-will offering scheme had been adopted, with great success. The days were past when the rich could provide the necessary funds and the Church must rely upon the efforts and gifts of the rank and file. If they were to make the scheme a success, they must give the laity a strong and influential voice in parochial life. The Rev. G. B. Tat cusToN (Rural Dean of Bowdon) said the scheme was so tar advanced in the diocese of Chester that they expected to have the money collected by November Ist. The Hon. Rev. C. F.Crtoss (Rural Dean of Frodsharn) atid the schune was a sound one and there was every t.aburaLce that it would meet with favour. GREAT WEALTH REQUIRING DISTRIBUTION Mr. G. MATHER asked whether the Ecclesiastical Commissioners had been invited to subscribe, out of their great wealth, to the schemes? Mr. SMITH amid it was too early to approach the Commissioners with definite suggestions. 'they would rather proceed with the matter step by step. Mr. MATHER : I think this should be national, or almost imperial, and that the Commissioners should be the first to begin to distribute their wealth. I feel very strongly on that point. An Act of Parliament was passed enabling .the Commissioners to deal with the living of Winwick,but 1 don't think the bargain has yet been carripd our, whereby certain poor livings were to be increased to .£3OO a Tear.

div.head: MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.
div.p: THE MISSIONARY EXHIBITION.

The Hon. Rev CROSS gave an address on the great Missionary Exhibition which is to be held in the Empire Skating Rink in November next. He pointed out that "the man in the street" knew little and cared less about foreign missions. Even among regular Church workers sufficient thought was not given to the subject. Even if they went into the country house of the rich man and turned over the books, in what propor- tion of such homes would they find space given to periodicals dealing with missionary history and affairs? Among all classes there was an unrest and a race—a readiness not to read or to listen hut actually to see things, as was evidenced by tbe craze fur animated pictures. The missionary societies had done wisely in facing this need, this want of nature, and promoting exhibitions to supply it. THE CATHEDRAL.
The Rev. C. NARars (organizing secretary) spoke of the progress of the Liverpool Cathedral scneme.
RELIGION IN SECONDARY SCHOOLS.

The Rev. Canon GRENSTF:D, diocesan inspector, gave an address on " Religious instruction in Secondary schools." He declared that such instruction was, on the whole, in a very bad condition, and that fact, which was no new one, lay at the root of many of their troublea. He contended that headmasters of some secondary schools, in order to avoid giving offence to. people of various denominations, resorted to the negative solution of leaving out what displeased any- body and took a pride in giving undenominational reiigious instruction, or found refuge in teaching the historical facts of the Bible without explanation— and often utterly falsely by reason of the fact that explanations were not given. MAJORITIES RULE.

"My own belief, said Canon Grensted " is that we are going wrong because we do not get absolutely to the root of the matter, which is that we have to lest upon public opinion. We have ultimately to appeal not to the school, but to the parent, to use every power he possesses to get what he %ant. If he wants it sufficiently, he will get it. It is simply a question in this country of majorities and votes, and ot nothing -else." They were face to face, he continued, with two rival conceptions of human life. One was that Al I education started from above- that they,as Christians, believed in the existence of God, as a source from Whom every good and perfect gift came down. The other conception was the modern and materialistic one —that the State had nothing to do with religion, that they could make a severance between religious and secular teaching, that they could have a complete education and yet leave out religion or add it as an extra subject. The Christian conception was that religious education was an all-embracing atmosphere. It was not one of the books on the shelf, but the book case which included the books. If the State declared that it would have schools with religion left out, it was by that very act interfering, in the grossest way, with toe training of the children, for it was teaching them the dogma that morals and religion were not con- nected.

div.head: POSITION IN WARMNGTON.
div.p: THE POSITION IN WARMNGTON.

Emphasising his point that an appeal must be made to the determination of the parent, the Canon said they were in this mess because the parents did not care sufficiently about the matter. They might produce the most beautiful schemes, but they would never alter the present position of things until they did it in response to a popular appeal. They in Warrington had a dispute as to what ought to be done in their secondary school: lie had not th• slightest doubt tbat five years hence the secondary school would accurately represent what the people of Warrington wanted. If they wanted to have a godless secondary school, it would be exactly like a weather cock—it would point the way the wind blew. The godless wind would produce a godless weather cock. If they had a religiously taught school which did not represent the
real wish of the Telple, it did harm because it was, in its essence, an untruth. NO SUCH THING AS UNDENONIINATIONAL ISM

The officials of to-day were endeavoraing to stamp out definite religious teaching in the schools ; they were adopting the policy of the last Pagan Roman Emperor. Undenominationalism was an evil for exactly the same reason that witchcraft was an evil—it was an evil because it did not exist. The fact that people thought it existed was producing untold evil. There was no such thing as undenomi- national religious teaching—they might call it a heterogeneous, ill-regulated poly-denominationalism every teacher teaching in his own way and producing something, and local education authorities issuing syllabuses which they were afraid to inspect, with the result that the stit,j,ct was unorganized and neglected. People talked abut Cowper-lemple religion; it was absolute nonsense. Anyone who had read the Cowper- Temple clause would see that it was simply negative from beginning to end. Hov, could such a clause &the a thing ? A school which taught nu religion was obey- ing that clause. Finally, Canon Grensted declared that their failures were due to the tact that they were not putting principles in the forefront, but were weaving schemes instead.

div.head: 10,551 MILES OF ADVERTISING. The Opening of a New House.
div.p: 10,551 MILES OF ADVERTISING. The Opening of a New House.

The remarkable development of advertising during the past dozen years is recalled by the announcement that Messrs. C. E. Fulford, Ltd., the proprietors of the famous Zem-buk healing balm, and other well-known specialities, have found it necessary to open spacious business offices in a newly-erected and up-to-date four- storey building facing the firm's extensive Laboratories at Carlton Hill, Leeds. This new building is all required for the accommodation of the staffs daily engaged in making the firm's excellent product more widely known. Here will now he prepared and despatched not only the newspaper and magazine aivertising for the British Isles and the Colonies, hut also a succession of p4mphlets, music and novelties with a circulation of many millions annually. Of the popular Zaru-buk Alnrtnack, "The Green Book of Prophecies" alone over 80,000,000 copies have been distributed up to this yeir, which means if the books were placed in a row end-to-end they would extend over 10,551 miles.

Au important feature of Messrs. FoHord's New Premises is the specially constructed flre-proof strong room wherein are preserved the originals of the thousands of testimonia s received from grateful people all over the world who have proved for themselves the wonderful healing power of Zam-buk.

div.head: YOUNG WIFE'S SUICIDE.
div.p: YOUNG WIFE'S SUICIDE.
Distressed by Brother's Departure
for Canada.

At the Warrington Coroner's Court yesterday, Mr. F. A. Jones conducted an inquest on the body of Jane Elizabeth Mather, aged 30, wife of John Mired Mather, 5, Goulden-street, who committed suicide by cutting her throat early on Wednesday morning. The husband stated that he was a gas fitter employed by the Corporation and had )(en married for five years. Prior to her marriage, deceased was subject to fainting bouts, but had had none since her marriage. They had lived happily together and deceased appeared to enjoy good health. She was of a jolly disposition but very sensitive. On the previous 'I hursday,a brother of hers, of whom she was very fond, went to Canada, and this seemed to trouble her. On Tuesday night she appeared to be all light and sang to him for a long time. They retired to bed shortly after ten o'clock. At 5 a m. he woke up, and on discovering that his wife was not in the bedroom he called out to her. Receiv- ing no reply, he went downstairs and found her on the rug in the kitchen with her nightdress covered with blood. The open razor, with which he had shaved himself the previous evening, was by her side. He found a note on the table which had been written by her. The note was not read by the coroner who, however aid that the contents accounted somewhat for tie swoman's action.
Witness called in a St. John Ambulance man named Thomas Cawley, but his wife bad passed away. Or. Gandhi was sent for and said the deceased had been dead for half an hour.
A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind " was returned.

FIRE BELL COMEDY. ALARM TO BE FIXED TO THE POLICE BUILDINGS.
THE COMMITTEES.

The Fire Bell at Stockton Heath is to be fixed on the Police Statior. This was made known when the question came before the Cheshire Police Committee at Chester on Saturday. Mr. J. C Parr presided over a meeting of the sub- committee at Stockton Heath this month, at which tha following letter was read from the Runcorn Rural District Council.

Runoorn, 13th March, 1913. Dear Sir,—Fire Alarm Bell, Litockton Heath.— Adverting to our previous correspondence herein, I have to inform you that owing to the Chief Constable and the District Council not being able to fully agree as to the height and position of the proposed fire bell standard on the prem,ses of the new Police Station. Stockton Heath, the bell has not been erected' Unfortunately the necessity for the erection of the bell in a well-known pesition has been brought strongly to the notice of the District Council through a recent fire which occurred in Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath, in the very early hours of the morning, and the inability ot the occupier of the premises to give the necessary alarm. The District Council feel strongly that the bell should be placed against the Pelice Station building and that it should he under the control of the police. They therefore passed a resolution at their last meet- ing of which the following is a copy : "That the County Council be urged to reconsider their refusal to allow the fire bell to be placed against the Police Station building, and their objection to the police having any oversight thereof."

I shall be glad to hear at your earliest convenience whether the County Council can see their way to reconsider this question.—Yours truly, GEO. F. ASHTON. Messrs. H. J. Westbrook and NV. Mclntyre were received by the hub-committee as representatives of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee woo spoke as to the need of a fire bell.

Mr. Westbrook said that a meeting of ratepayers of the parish was held, and a very strong feeling was expressed, that inasmuch as the fire alarm bell was attached to the structure of the old police station prior to its demolition to make way for the existing new police station, and as no inconvenience had ever been occasioned to the police or any objection raised on the part of the police, the ratepayers of the parish respect- fully requested that the Standing Joint Committee should permit the bell to be again attached to the station, as to do so would give very general satisfaction to not only the residents of Stockton Heath but to the district immediately surrounding. They were quite prepared to leave the exact position in which the bell should be placed to the discretion of the Chief Constable, and would enter into such an agreement as the Clerk of the Peace for the county considered to be necessary to make it clear that by granting the permission asked for no responsibility should be attached to the police in any way with refer- ence to the user or maintenance of the bell, consequent on its attachment to the structure of the station ; and further, that the cost of attaching end maintaining the bell will be borne by the Parochial Committee. The representatives info-med the chairman that on such permission being granted the Parochial Committee would forthwith remove the present fire call station from its position in front of the Police Station, and so leave unobst noted Victoria-square in front of the station.

The Chief Constable expressed to the Chairman the views held by him, and which were that although he preferred that the decision arrived at by the sub- committee at its meeting on the 23rd October last should be adhered to, still, if the Chairman was of the opinion that the request of the deputation should on public grounds he granted, he would waive his objection subject to it being made clearly understood that

div.head: NO_RESPOSSIBILITH ATTACHED TO THE POLICE
div.p: NO_RESPOSSIBILITH ATTACHED TO THE POLICE
either for ringing the bell or the maintenance— thereof in a condition sufficient to raise an alarm on the out- break of fire,.

The County Architect stated that on architectural and structural grounds he saw no objection to the bell being attached to the portion of the building which he indicated to the deputation from the Parochial Committee, who expressed their satisfaction with such position.

The Chairman of the sub-committee recommended that the Runcorn Rural District Council be permitted, on the following conditions, to attach the fire alarm bill to the structure of the Police Station, viz. : 1. The position to be determined by the Chief Constable in consultation with the County Architect, and the work to be carried out under the supervision of and to the satisfaction of the latter official. 2. The cost of hanging the bell and the niainten- enee thereof to be borne by the Runcorn Rural District Council. 3. No responsibility to attach tr) the police with respect to the maintenance of the bell or the ringing thereof, and the rope for ringing the bell to be so arranged that the belt can be snug without entry into the Police Station premise . 4. The existing fire call but to be removed from Victoria-square. 5. The arrangement to be determinable on six months' notice, and that the foregoing conditions and such others as the Clerk of the Peace may consider necessary be embodied in an agreement to be prepared and entered into by him with the Runcorn ttural District Council.

Mr. Charlton Parr moved that this recommendation be adopted, and said that the matter bad been so fully dealt with on the minutes that it was not necessary for him to say anything more. Col. Cornwall Legh seconded. The Chairman asked Mr. Parr the reason for the change of front, and of the alteration of a previous resolution of the committee. The architect had been in favour of the bell being placed as now suggested, but he had apparently changed his mind or the committee must have done so.

Mr. Parr : I think in the minutes it explains particular point. There was very strong feeling oa the part of Stockton Heath that that minute should be altered or rescinded, and it was very fully discussed, and the Chief Constable I think waived the objection which ke formerly held, and it was resolved that it be recommended to the committee to rescind that resolution.
The recommendation 'MRS adopted. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. MR. BOTrOMLEY AND COUNTY COUNCIL TERMS.

At a meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Cora- mittee on Tuesday evening. The matter was brought up for consideration. Mr. C. Pilling presided and after the decision of the Standing Joint Committee had been read,

Mr. Westbrook said the deputation were met most courteously by the sub-committee of the Standing Joint Committee, and their case as most attentively listened to. they also urged upon the sub-committee the desirability of having a policeman on duty in tbe Police Station. He proposed a resolution "That the Com- mittee respectfully urges upon the Standing Joint Com- mittee the desirability, if not the necessity, of there always being one officer on duty in the Stockton Heath Police Station, and that they accept the conditions of the County Council, subject to the Clerk reserving in the agreements the right to replace the fire alarm box in its present position, in case the County Council determined the contract."

Mr. Bottomley said it was poor treatment by the County Council for the amount of money Stockton Heath paid in the shape of rates. It wa3 the most central position for the bell to be fixed. He would not accept the conditions under any circumstances, and would give the County Council to understand they expected better treatment from them. Mr. J. Hallows received an answer in the negative to his question as to whether it would result in an extra policeman, seconded the resolution. Mr. Bottomley thought if the matter was prosecuted further they would get better terms. He dia not think the terms should be accepted.
Mr. Westbrook said they had got everything they asked for.
On the motion being put Mr. Bottomley was the only member who voted against it.

div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.

Mr. Whitley announced that the next rate would be 2s. 11d, in the £ made up of Poor and County rate 2. 2d. and Special Sanitary rate ninepence. This is twopence in the £ less than the rate for October last year, being a total of £ll6 less than the precepts of October 10th, 1912. The rateable value of the village is £17,161 10s., and is the highest of all the 40 parishes under the District Council of Runcorn. The last rate on October 10th, 1912, was : Poor and County rate, 2F. 4d.; special sanitary rate, 93., being 3s. Id. in the £. The total precepts for this half- year were :—£2,256 as against £2,372 for the preceding half-year. The £2,256 is required by August 9th, £1,128 of the amount being due on May 9t.h. The precepts were made up as follows :—County Council, £967, as against £975 ; poor rate, £283, as against £3l (the two rates being £66 less than the preceding half-year) ; District Council Sanitary, £174 ; and Highway, £282 (which is the same as that for the last. half-year) ; special sanitary, £550, as against £6OO.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

LAW'S TENNIS IN LYMM.—In consequence of many difficulties, not the least of which has been the failure to secure suitable and permanent grounds, this popular pastime has not made the progress in Lymm which it has in other parts of the country. A strong committee was formed a short time ago to consider the desira- bility of organising a small private club, with the result that arrangements have been made for the exclusive use of the tennis courts owned by Mr. Brookes, of Vine House, Statham. The courts will be opened for tbe season on Saturday, the 3rd inst.. at 3 p.m. Applications for membership may be made to Mr. H. S. Hudson, Booth's-hill, or Mr. H. Barker, Oak Lea, Statham.

TRADESMEN' EXPERIMENT.—As no doubt our readers will remember, we mentioned in our report of the last annual meeting of the Lymm Tradesmen's Association, that the members had passed a resolution in favour of closing their shops at 7 o'clock each Monday and Tuesday evening, commencing with the first week in May. This resolution will therefore come into opera- tion on Monday and Tuesday nsxt, and the result of the experiment is eagerly awaited as opinions differ as to the desirability of the arrangement. INDEPENDENT METBODIST ANNIVERAARY.—The first of the Lymm Sunday Schools to celebrate its anniver- sary this year was that of the Cherry-lane Independent Methodists on Sunday. The preacher was Mr. George Hunter, ex-Mayor of Leigh, whose efforts were highly appreciated, especially by the large congregation at the evening service when he preached from the story of Obadiah's fsithfulness in obeying God's commands despite the anger of the wicked Queen :Jezebel (T. Kings, xviii.) His subject in the morning was " Virture," whilst at the children's service in the afternoon he gave an interesting and helpful address on " Grumbling." At each sf the services the scholars sang special hymns Miss Greenman being the organist. The total amount of the collections was slightly above that of last year. DIE MAY QUEEN.—Despite the adverse i alance occasioned by the unpropitious weather that assailed last year's festival, the Lymm May Queen Committee have been hard at work during the past few months preparing for another festival to be held on Whit- Thursdes‘, May 15th, when they hope to be favoured with a cloudless day. The success which greeted some of last year's innovations such as grand stands, etc., has encouraged the Committee to follow upon similar lines this time, with the result that seating accommo- dation for over 1,200 persons has been arranged. Our readers are advised to procure their tickets before May 15th, as up to that date sixpence will purchase tickets for both the afternoon and evening performances, whilst on the day the charge will be sixpence for each performauce.

CHOIR FESTIVAL.—The annual festival of the Lymm Wesleyan Choir was held on Sunday, when the preacher was the Rev. W. A. Beckett, superintendent minister of the Warrington Circuit. At the morning service he &livered a most appropriate sermon from the text of Colossians iii., 16, dwelling chiefly on'the many blessings to be gained from good Chnstitin music and singing. At this service the choir rendered the anthem" Like as a Father" (J. L. Hatton), while in the evening they sang " 0 Gladsome Light" (" The Golden Legend" by Sullivan). In the afternoon an augmented choir under the leadership of Mr. H. S. Brown (choirmaster and organist) gave a good interpretation of Valentine Hemery's Welsh Cantata " Rhyfelwry y Grnes " (Soldiers of the Cross), the principal vocalists being Madame Wilson. solo, " Arm me ; and a duet by Miss F. Rogerson," Beautiful Heaven"; Mr. E. Waterworth, solo," Strengthen my arm 0 Lord " ; Mr. F. Champ, solo, "Soldiers of Christ a•vake " ; a trio, "Herein is love," by Mrs. F. P. !Brown, Miss Pearson, and Miss Winstanley ; quartetta by the Misses Egerton, Jones, Mairs, and Messrs. H. Burrell, J. B. Egerton and J. Ellis.

LYAIM AS A " WATKRING PLACE."—Lymm, in common with many other parts of the country,has been cavalierly treated by the Weather Board this spring. We have been accustomed to, and expect, a little more Ccnsideration from his Solar Majesty at this time of the year. However, it is not so much the negative quantity of sunshine as the positive quantity of rain teat we have to complain of more particularly. It is rarely that the river Bollin overflows its banks in the Lvmm district, but we have now had sufficient rain to effect this phenomenon, as veritable lagoons have dis- placed the ordinary meadows,especially on the Heatley side of the township.Lymm has ambilions,many of them but to become a watering place, popular or otherwise, is not one of its aime. A number of our summer visitors— we refer of course to our feathered visitors, not to the hobble-skirt and concertina brigade—have already arrived, and can be seen most days sitting in the dripping trees and hedges, with the melancholy air of a man who has tumbled out of bed half an hour before the the proper time and does not know whether to get back again or to make the best of it; but they don't sing ! 'Fake the case of the cuckoo for instance : no sound is mere eagerly listened for, more heartily welcomed when it is heard, than the song of this arch- marauder, yet though we see him frying about, even amongst the houses, as was the case last Sunday, co far we have not heard him utter a single note ! Rain is a grand thing in a dry summer, but this is not summer, neither is it dry, and we want a change.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

DEATR or MR. JAMES MCCLAREN.—We regret to record the death of Mr. James McClaren, which took place after a very short illness, on Monday morning. Deceased had lived in Winwick for a considerable time and was well-known and respected. He had been employed at the water works for many years. He was a staunch Liberal in the days when very few aoherents of the cause were to be found in the village. The funeral took place at Winwick Church on Wednesday. A number of wreaths were sent from relatives and friends.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Prairie Outlaw:'

Mrs. F. G. Kimberley's dramatic creations can always count on a good reception in Warrington and the latest play from her pen—" The prairie outlaw " has proved one of the most popular of the series. It is a fine, breezy romance of Western life, and presents sufficient variety of incident to keep the audience on tenter hooks throughout. The story is of Rob Middleton, a settler, whose jealous temperament is pinyed upon to such purpose by an enemy that he believes his wife to be unfaithful. He becomes the head of an outlaw band which terrorises the country and there are encounters with Indians and all manner of exciting happenings. Mr. John C. Carlyle gives a whole-hearted impersonation of Rob Middleton, infusing just the necessary impulsiveness and spirit into his acting. Miss Madge Douglas, as Morita, the outlaw's wife, is a great favourite with the audience, her indomitable pluck and cheerful- ness being quite in keeping with the part. Mr. Ernest Vaughan is convincing as Josh Hawkins, the unscru- pulous sheriff who is responsible for the wrecking of Middleton's home. Other capital portrayals are those of Mr. Edward Bikker, as Rube Thompson, Mr. John Croudage as the Indian Chief, and Mr. Jay Kay, as Black Pete, the merry nigger. The scenic effects are on an elaborate scale.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Next week Mrs. Frank Bateman's Company will present an interesting repertoire. On Monday and Tuesday, the play " Which did she love?" will be the attraction; on Wednesday and Thursday" Sapho ; " and on Friday and Saturday " The King and the Orange Girl." The last-named play deals with the story of Charles 11. and Nell Gwynne. There will be two performances nightly. MR. WARBURTON'S BENEFIT.

A complimentary benefit will be given to Mr. H. L Warburton, acting manager, on Thursday, the 22nd inst. The programme will be an exceptionally attractive one,a large number of local artistes, in addition to performers from the Palace and Ilippodrorne,traving promised to take part. div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME

" Trust to Work, Honesty and Advice in preference to Luck, Pleasure and Shirk "is the moral derived from the very original sketch "Everybody," which has been presented by Mr. Ernest Edelsten's capable company at the Hippodrome this week. There are four phases to the sketch, during the enactment of which, we witness the downfall of " Everybody, ' a character powerfully undertaken by Mr. G. H. Mulcaster, who gives up his best friends, Work, Advico and Honesty and trusts to Luck. That fickle jade stands by everybody for a abort time, but eventu- ally leaves him ruined. Fortunately be turns back to his first friends, and has a successful career. The purpose of the production is achieved in a pleasing manner, the various characters being very realistic- ally presented. In addition to this great attraction, there are several smart vaudeville turns. Robb Wilton, the confidential comedian, sends the " house " into uncontrollable fits of laughter with his dry humour. He possesses a wealth of good humorous stories which be relates, together with many side- splitting gag=, in an extremely funny manner. As a policeman, Wilton's make-up and general actions are irresistibly ludicrous. Katie Hughes is a clever entertbiner, assisted by her sister Dorothy at the piano. Katie is a smart, immaculate male impetson- ator, who sings and dances well. The couple achieve a success in the song "Jessie Dear," which they render in a pleasing manner. Norton and Doon score a success in a laughable comedy act "Tim Wrong Wright." Burlesque comedy prevails and the couple are well received. Harry Halsey is indeed a clever laughter manufacturer and entertainer. He is a comedian of much abiiility, and in his latest study, "Curtains," in which he impersonates various well- known artistes as they " take the curtain," he is decidedly popular. A smart and clever acrobatic turn is provided by the original Smarte Bros. In an eccentric manner the couple perform intricate and daring feats of tumbling and balancing and are loudly applauded for their efforts. Three of the best simul- taneous dancers we have seen for some time are the Aza Trio, a combination of males who are also splen- did harmonising vocalists. '' The Hospital Hoax" is the title of a laughable picture shown on the bio scope.

CHINA'S CHANGE OF FRONT. At Wednesday evening's service at kg_i-olborne-street Baptist Church, the Rev. H. °gden spoke on "The Chinese Government and Christianity." The topic was, of course, suggested by the unparalleled appeal from the responsible heads of the new Republic for united intercession in behalf of their great Country. For this, as all interested readers are aware, Sunday last was specially reserved; and Warrington shared freely in the common response. The change which the request denotes seems very strange to those of us at home who have been accustomed to Mark the trend of things in China during the last twenty years or so. We had learned to ,think :of the ruling and eduCated classes as noPelessly proud and exclusive, and of the Chinese on the whole as bitterly hostile to the "foreign devils," and never missing an oPPortunity for active demonstration against Christian teachers. The Boxer rising in Which so many of this faith suffered persecu- . ton, even to the death, seems but an event of Yesterday': yet here already we have the leading men of the empire agreeing together to Petition the once so bitterly hated aliens to strengthen their hands in righteousness by Means of prayer. When last the local J 5 ~aPtists met in the interests of their 'missionary Society, they had specially under Consideration the claims of China, and they heard with intense satisfaction how Christianity is now advancing there by leaps and bounds; how particularly by means of Medical missions, the eyes of the people are being opened to the disinterested and self- sacrificing character of the work; and how oPposition is disappearing and adverse criticism is being disarmed. The Golborne- street pastor reviewed the situation in characteristic fashion on Wednesday night. The lesson is that home churches cannot afford to ignore the missionary movement' • ,it is to their own highest interest to regard 11, not as a mere appendage, but as an integral part of the church's life. THE MERRY MONTH. , On Thursday Knutsford observed its May- day festival, and that of the Warrington Band of -hope Union is fixed for next week. This is the month which in ancient Rome was sacred to Apollo. The old Romans sacrificed specially and exclusively to Maia, the mother of Mercury, on the first day. We iare told that the month received its name Trig before the time of Romulus, and that he continued it in honour of the Senate— the Majores or Greater Council. The Saxons Called it Tri-Milchi because at this season theY were enabled, thanks to the effect of the Young grass in favourable situations, to milk their cows to advantage three times a day. Now is the time when the spring po3t comes forth as a giant refreshed, and adds to the embarrassment of harassed editors with lines to the daisy and the cowslip —lines that scan and words that literally burn—for the less meritorious his verses, and the more audacious and persistent the poet, so that the worried newspaper man finds it difficult to keep him at bay while he calls for a waste paper basket of enlarged Capacity. Ali, well; after all, it is well to be reminded that the old painters personify this month as a lovely-countenanced youth clad in green and white robes embroidered With flowers, a garland of white and damask roses on his head, a lute in one hand, and on the fore finger of the other a full- throated song bird. What wonder that such a period should stir the imagination of even the feeblest of minor poets! HOME LIFE. I see that at St. John's Presbyterian Church, the Rev. W. Reid has been insisting O n the value of home life. here are among US those who point to disquieting signs of decadence in home life. True, these are for the moment discovered chiefly among " the idle and irresponsible plutocrats of our time and their parasites" ; but the argument is that, their example being contagious, the whole moral temperature is thus distinctly lowered. remember one of the magazines obtaining representative opinions as to this supposed le,lldency. It was generally agreed that flat "e is a foe to home life. The writer suggested as the root-fact"the awful exhaustion of the BPieed and pressure of modern life, with its telephones,d typewriters, and motors, which demands something more exciting and ~aseinating in the evening hour than to fleuPY the same room as the rest of the t'LlnilY." Dear me ! Why, that is just what :re, average married journalist ever longs for 4.11 u enjoys most of all. Dr. Barry wrote of f" .e rising generation as wholly given up to PVT.9IitY and self-indulgence. Even the Rev. v B. Meyer took for granted and suggested valloUs causes for the "slackening of home eB." It was indeed refreshing to turn from tile Pessimists to Madame Sarah Grand, who nithesitatingly gave it as her conviction that a's3uld a house-to-house visitation be made, hild the amount of happiness in the quiet i;,4ries all about us be weighed and measured would be found that, far from tring diminished, it has greatly increased ; f, at in no other country in the world is to be :11nd such a high average of domestic pros- tritY as is here vouched for everywhere by srows and rows of decent, comfortable ,e ii":a1„1 houses, bearing evidence in the neat- -41',88 and order which characterises them, in Fe Polished window panes, the tidy blinds, sPotless icurtains, and in the loving care ibestowed upon the tiny gardens, of the rf anquil home-life of a self-respecting people. "ile likes to think that this is largely true uretiiW-arrington, at all events. There is giOn, too, in these myriad small homes. div.p: LITERARY GLEAN I NGS. N ew Books and Extracts from the Magazines.
SIR RUFUS ISA ACS, THE MAN HIMSELF.

In the "Pall Mall Magazine" Mr. T. P. O'Connor writes a very delightful article on the Attorney General and brings in, by way of making a comparison,the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Of Sir Rufus Isaacs and Mr. Lloyd George he says : "If either of them could be induced to write the story of his early years, it would bear a strong resem- blance to the immortal American work known as the "The Bad Boy's Diary." The boy wasn't bad at all; he was simply a wild untamable spirit full of the joy of life, of virile and audacious courage and of a thirst for adventure and independence; just the kind of boy that grows up into a strong man."

Mr. O'Connor tells how young Rufus ran , away to sea and, coming back untamed,tried to settle down in front of ledgers in his father's office. At the age of 24 and feelins himself a dismal failure he started for , America. His luggage was in the railway ' compartment, when a message from his mother found a tender spot in his heart and called him back. At her advice he took to the study of law and for three years toiled hard at it. Three barren years at the bar followed and it was only the encouragement that came from his wife (for he had married in the period) that held him in the profession for which he had qualified. Then came the turn in the tiee and the young lawyer had to rise at four in the morning to cope with the briefs that poured in upoil. him, but according to his friend, T. P. O'Connor, prosperity has not quenched the boyish love of fun, and he is still,when among friends, tl-,e same untamable lad who ran away to s( a and could not be chained down at his father's desk. "Dismiss him for a day from the Law Courts and from the House of Commons, and he is again a rollicking boy, singing his old sailor songs, golfing ardently, tumbling down on the grass, chaffing man and woman, walk- ing with a step of fevei ish rapidity ; the lithe frame as taut as a piece of steel wire, and the temper seeming infectious, cheerful, audaciously eloquent of that joy of life which only belongs to those in whose mind and body are in the faultkss accord of perfect health."
THE MARVEL OF POSTAGE STAMP
-6OLLECTING-'.

When Rowland fill hit upon the idea of the postage stamp in 1837 he called into being a new institution, and one which had followed civilization round the globe. Everys where and in bewildering varieties we have the postage stamp. As might have been anticipated this variety appeals to those who have the instinct for collecting, but few people could have foreseen the strong hold which stamp collecting, or philately as it is called, would gain in this present age. A popular guide to stamp collecting has been issued which quite startles the ordinary person by the facts its presents. London,we are told, is the capital of the philatelic world and the Mecca of every true collector. Every desirable specimen at some period or other travels to London, and the city itself is said to have a larger philatelic community than any other city of the world. Ten philatelic societies hold their monthly or fortnightly meetings in the Metropolis,and it has been estimated that there is a popula- tion of thirty thousand who indulgein the collection of stamps. In the Strand alone, which is recognised as the principal philatelic thoroughfare of the world, there- are over a dozen stamp dealers' establishments, and vast sums are expended annually in this business. There are eighty-four stamp dealers carrying on business in the London area, and seven firms of philatelic auctioneers. Rowland Hill doubtless realized that he had done a bright thing in inventing the adhesive stamp, but who could have dreamed of a big business, not to say profession,grow - mg up around the used-up article.

div.head: NEWEST ENCYCLOPEDIA.
div.p: THE NEWEST ENCYCLOPEDIA.

Messrs. J. M. Dent and Sons,whose Every- man Library of Shilling Books has met with such a remarkable success, are now adding to the series an "Everyman Encyclopedia." Like the "Library," this consists of shilling volumes. It will be completed in twelve parts each one of which has 640 pages and more than 500 thousand swords. The parts are neatly bound in harmony with the volumes of the Everyman Library and the twelve will stand in about twelve inches of shelf room. To compress in so small a space six millions of words,all of them in clear type and very readable, is a remarkable achieve- ment. Volume 4,which is just to hand,covers the subjects under part of C and D. It has useful articles under the headings Church, Colonies, Constitution, Coal and Coal getting, Cotton and Darwinism. Some interesting men are also described, including Cromwell, Cowper and Dante. Many diagrams and pictures illustrate the text. We are impressed by the terseness and completeness of this latest Encyclopedia and advise our readers to make its acquaintance.

div.head: MACMILLAN'S SEVENPENI'TY LIBRARY.
div.p: MACMILLAN'S SEVENPENI'TY LIBRARY.

Macmillan's New Sevenpenny Series con- tains some choice novels, the latest issued being such books as "Richard Carvel," by Winston Churchill "The Philanderers," by A. E. W. Mason; "The Virginian" by Owen Wister ; and "A Village Tragedy" by Aargaret L. Woods. No one need be short of reading with such a supply ready to hand.

difficulty—and, in fact, that it is much easier to obtain than it ought to be. ANOTHER LLOYD GEORGE STORY. In the same column of the last issue of the' " Examiner " was a capital story which recalled another told against himself by the Chancellor—l mean the story of a man who, having saved someone from drowning, was presented with a public testimonial. When, after the eulogies of the Mayor, he was called upon to reply, he said "Really, I have done nothing to deserve this reward. I saw the man struggling in the water and, as no one else was by, I saw he would be drowned if I didn't save him. So I jumped in, swam to him, turned him over to see that he wasn't Lloyd George, and then pulled him out." PROVERBS.

Uncle Caleb's " interesting compilation of negro proverbs for the youngsters set me wishing that I had space for a more compre- hensive review of the subject, as I have for years been collecting proverbs from all sources, and have accumulated rather a good and fairly representative stock, and these learners of wisdom—as they are for the most part, though some are foolish and some are contradictory. Anyhow, I have hundreds of gems of crystalised wisdom from the brains and all sorts and conditions of men—men of every colour and of every tongue; but, alas, I may not enter upon the subject here. I trust, however, that examples may be further multiplied in the " Children's Corner,"
The Examiner, Saturday, May 3, 1913.

div.head: BUTTERMARKET-STREET SIXTY YEARS AGO.
div.p: BUTTERMARKET-STREET SIXTY YEARS AGO.
SOME SHOPS AND SHOP-KEEPERS, AS REMEMBERED BY THE LATE MR. F. MONKS.

As the south side of Buttermarlot-street is under the doom of speedy demolition it may be useful to set down some notes upon the occupants of the condemned and dis- appearing shops which the memory of Mr. Frederick Monks was able to furnish. Most of the buildings we shall mention are standing or only recently removed. This may perhaps add to the interest of these notes, but considerable imaginative power will be needed to picture the street as it was in its palmy days before the tide of business had been deflected elsewhere;when its shops were hives of industry, and the narrow courts and passages teemed with traffic. A RELIC OF TWO CENTURIES AGO. Going back a century Buttermarket-street is discovered as a marketing centre. It was literally the Butter Market, just as Horse- market-street was the Horse Market within the memory even of middle aged folks. In

but six licensed houses within a circle of ten yards radius is surely a record. The two large piles which stood at the entrance of Bank-street have long been associated with grocery,the name of Percival being attached to one of them in the mind of every old inhabitant. The large building now occupied by Mr. Allen was for several generations a grocers warehouse. Sixty years ago it was the business place of Messrs, Gorst and Owen, grocers,and Mr.Gorst lived upon the premises. Two shops adjoined in one of which Mr. Wheeler, the forerunner of Mr. Skelton, sold smallwares.

div.head: SMILING FIGURE HEAD.
div.p: THE SMILING FIGURE HEAD.

BUTTERMARKET-STREET.

As sketched in 1887 by Mr. Percy Davies, then a practising solicitor in town, who gave the picture to the police force. The picture, which is on a large scale, at present adorns the walls of the parade room at the new police station, just as it occupied a place of honour in the old station in Irlam-street now Buttermarket street. Mr. Hunt, who appears on the right of the picture was Chief Constable of the Borough.He retired on superannuation November, 1895, after a service of 32 years and eleven months in the borough. The lines written, in the left hand bottom corner of the picture by the artist, describe a Saturday night scene but the chief interest lies in the really fine drawing of the street buildings, which on the left, are now to dis- appear to make way for the widening of Butter market-street and the formation of the south- eastern portion of the Circus now in course of

The next was adorned by a curious orna- ment which had done duty as the figure- head of a ship, the quaint and heavy figure of a man cut in wood. The image, curious enough in itself, was made entirely in con- gruous by the addition of a large wooden hat.
those days the vendors of butter, eggs and fowls flocked in from the country and spread their wares upon the ground. This gives meaning to the inscription carved upon post of the Fox Inn.
POTA TOES AND AP PLES DOWN WARDS 1704.

An inscription recalling the puzzle of" Bill Stumps his mark" until we read it as a market instruction that potatoes and apples were not to be displayed upon the ground set apart for butter and eggs. But we are not back in those rather cramped days. We are in the Buttermarket- street that is within living memory. ,

div.head: ONE OF WARRINGTON'S RECORDS.
div.p: ONE OF WARRINGTON'S RECORDS.

The shop at Market Gate with the house adjoining were occupied by Peter Smith, grocer. The "Old Fox" needs no mention as it is with us still, but it is necessary to tell our fellow townsmen that.half a century ago it was one of four public-houses that stood side by side. First came the " Wheat Sheaf," then the "Old Fox" and next to it the "Crown and Sceptre" and the "Courier's Arms." Four licensed houses- adjoining each other and all compassed within a space of twenty yards is perhaps unique. But this was not all. Taking the other side of the street into account we find that Buttermarket-street had six public - houses within the small length just mentioned, for immediately opposite stool, the "Bear's Paw" and the" Fleece Inn. We don't pretend to be proud of these things,

This embellishment to the figure was made by George Edwards, the hatter,who kept the shop underneath and who took this method of informing the public that he could supply a hat to any head even though it should be of unusual matelial and of unusual size. Those who wish to study the result of the hatter's effort may still do so, for the figure now does duty over Mr. Unsworths's shop in Lyme-street and lavishes upon this genera- tion the smiling witchery and poise of hat that entertained our great grandfathers. " Woodfall the butcher" and William Wheeler had shops a little lower, and the and" Rope Anchor 'lnn was in the same block. Next stood the tallow chandlery of Richard Borrows, and at the corner of Croppers Brow the pawnbrokers shop of Mr. Craik. Williams paint shop was on the other corner.

"Bob " Thornley, musician. came next and then "Gandy the clogger " whose name remains yet, one of the few that can show a continuity of name and business stretching over the long half century covered by the memory of Mr. Frederick Monks.

div.head: FORTUNES FROM FEATHERS.
div.p: FORTUNES FROM FEATHERS.

OFFICIAL CONFIRMATION. In. our last issue we published some very interesting particulars regarding the profits derivable from invest- ment or participation in ostrich-farming in the Cape Midlands, South Africa. Notable official confirmation of our statements is forthcoming in the facts vouched to the Royal Colonial Institute on the 21st of April by Dr. Macdonald, one of the heads of the Department of Agriculture of the Union Government of South Africa, who said in the course of his lecture: "Ostrich farm- ing is probably the most profitable farming in the world, and it is commonly understood that some of the principal men engaged in it are making profits of some- thing like £lO,OOO a year each." There is in course of issue by the Anglo-African Bureau Ltd., 'of 5,6, 7, Southampton-street, Strand, London, W.C. the prospectus of Graaf Reinet Ostrich and Lucerne Farms, Ltd. The Bureau, which is not in any sense of the word a share-vending or stock-broking lagency, acts as the secretariat of the Graaf! Reinet Company above mentioned. It is instructed to notify the public in the Mother Country of the present issue over here of 50,000 £1 sharea. The business of the Graaff Reinet Co. has to do with the ciiltivation ef large tracts of Lucerne (alfafa grass) for fodder and the rearing of ostriches on irrigated lands in the Sundays River Valley; It is not in any way a Stock Exchange "counter.' It is intended, however, that the shares later on shall be introduced on the Stook Exchange for the purpose of an open market but not for underwriting or" gambling." The property is the key to a great irrigable territory of which much more will be heard later.

div.head: CLOTH HALLS.
div.p: THE CLOTH HALLS.

Behind the shops which have been mentioned were two Cloth Halls both of which were in use at the period of which we write. These are still in existence though some little effort is needed to picture them as they were. "Watts Cloth Hall " faces unon Bank-street and is easily distinguished by its imposing doorway and entrance steps. It is now used as a store and rather broken up,we think. The other is approached from Cloth Hall yard or from thq passage adjoining Mr. Isaac's shop. div.head: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE TO ACIDITY.
div.p: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE TO ACIDITY.

THE ORIGIN OF THE HUNGER STRIKE.
CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.

During Easter week I was in Oxford, and spent an hour in the famous Bodleian Library. This fine old- University Library is a wonderful place, and has manuscripts, books and records of all sorts. I want to tell you about one of them which I thought very interesting. It is a letter written by a boy to his father about 1700 years ago. In those days they wrote on papyrus. This was a kind of paper made from the pulp of the papyrus plant which grew in the marshes of the river Nile. The soft pulp was rolled out flat, and then the strips were crossed over each other, aud after they had been pressed the surface was varnished. This papyrus paper lasts wonderfully well, and when explorers dig it from Cie dry sand of Egypt they find it as fresh and strong as it was when buried thousands of years ago. It occurs to me while I am writing that I might make up a little article for you about the papyrus plant and papyrus letters, and I will do so in a week or two.

I started out to tell you about the letter I saw at Oxford. It is written by a boy to his father who was away at Alexandria. The funny thing about it is that the boy threatens a hunger strike if he cannot have what he wants. This is the letter :
Th. on to hi., fa hr. Them greetil g. It Ava a very witvk thing of you licit to take me wi.h you to Al.no.dria. ,tnd me a Lyre-, I implore. For if you d n't I w.,n't eat, I won' drik. S.) there now

This little note is an illustration of how letters were written in those days., They did not say "Dear father" and fiat' up "Yours truly." The name of the writer always came first and they always began with a greeting and often a prayer. You will see this in Paul's letters: " Paul an apostle of Jesus Christ to the Church at Corinth grace be to you and peace." They always put at the head of a letter the ,person who was writing and the person to whom it was addressed.

I don't know anything about Theon except what is in the letter, but I have come to the conclusion that he was a spoiled boy. If he can't have his musical instrument he will make everybody miserable. Although lam quoting his letter I have not a bit of patience with him. He may have been the person who invented the hunger strike, but I don't think fly more of him for that. "So there, now!"
I

div.head: GLEANED FROM MANY QUARTERS,
div.p: GLEANED FROM MANY QUARTERS,

To-day we begin our series of "I remember" stories, a column which will be conducted by Mr. Arthur Mounfield, our well-known contributor on Antiquarian and similar subjects relating to his native town.

Mr. Mounfield will be pleased to receive hints or I matter for these articles which will make a most, interesting record. Headers must remember on Oleic part that the stories are independent of each other and are the recollections of distinct personages. Mr. Mounfield here does but chronicle the recollections of other people, a fact which will account for the changit g character of each succeeding par.tgi aph. A Market Gate Episode. It will amuse your readers if I give you a bit of information about old Warrington that was given to me by my parents, which' they often used to chuckle over. At Market-gate, on the spot where the Maypole shop now stands, a shopkeeper named Whitby did business about 80 to 90 years ago. The roads were not very well kept in those days and as the stage coaches turned the corner they often came into contact with his window. To keep the traffic at a safe distance he placed some heavy posts about four feet from his door and window. The gossiping public who used to gather at Market-gate to collect and spread the news showed great appreciation of Mr. Whitby's posts. They were splendid supports for the Weary Willies of the day, and on Sunday all through the day the donor of the posts had the annoyance of the loud gossip and tobacco smoke that rose to his sitting-room window. He took a drastic step. A large sign board was prepared and he painted on it in large letters : DONT REST YOUR LAZY RUMPS UP AGEN OLD WHITBY'S STUMPS ON A SUNDAY.
The protest is understood to have been fairly successful and the sign board adorned Market Gate for many years. I hope your readers wont be unduly shocked at this bit of ancient history.

Bridge-Street Public Houses. I remember Bridge-street of sixty years ago- and if the subject has any interest I could tell tell the names of the Public Houses on each side of the street. Bridge-street had then nineteen public houses if I am correct in my reckoning. Why our ancestors stopped off at nineteen without making an even twenty, I don't know; but possibly I have forgotten one, and there may have been twenty after all. Starting from the bottom on the right there was the Packet House Inn standing where the present one does. Then there was the Bull's Head and a little further on the Lower Seven Stars. The next was the Royal Oak an old fashioned Inn called after the Charles 111 oak at Boscabell I suppose. The Higher Seven Stars was the next which, like most of the othLrs, had a large yard and stables. Very busy places the yards were onl market days when farmers and visitors left their vehicles there. The Rose and Crown Inn had its entrance in Rose and Crown-street and the old stone horse-mount which was near to the door can still be seen there. The Ship Inn was in Ship Yard and close to it was the Red Lion. Before the Lion was rebuilt part of the building was set back from the street and in this open space Peter Phillips used to put out a display of his chairs as specimens of his handiwork on market days. I can see the rush-bottomed chairs yet in my mind's eye. The next Inn past the Lion (which also had a good yard and stables) was the Star and Garter. Then there were three old- fashioned public-houses which all hid them- selves modestly away from the street. The first was the Swan, which was reached from the Swan Entry. Next was the Cock which stood in Cock Yard and nearest to Market- gate The Crow. These were comfortable inns, very unlike the modern pubs in every way. A network of passages ran behind the top of Bridge- street and joined together the yards of these inns and also those of the Crown and Sceptre and Wheat Sheaf in Buttermarket-street.

Coming back upon the other side of the street there was the Royal George at Market Gate, a fine old Inn in those days. The Green Dragon was next and the Eagle and Child; these you have already described. I can remember the Black Boy Yard which stood where Rylands-street now is with its stables and brew house. There was behind it a large bowling green at one time. I think the Public Hall (now the Royal Court Theatre) was built on the site of the green when Rylands—street was opened fifty years ago. There were three other Inns south of the Black Boy. First came the Feathers and then the White Bear. The third was the Roe Buck. The yard known as Roe Buck Yard had a dwelling house in it. In my time it was occupied by Ben Borrows, and was quite a good house with an approach of stone steps. There were large old buildings on both sides and these would be the places, I suppose, in which you say the Roman Catholics and early Dissenters used to worship. Your readers may form the idea that I have got my special knowledge of " pubs " by my frequent visits to them. I had better tell my younger readers that things were different then. The Inns were clean and homely places, and we went to buy a 46 pennorth of barm " for baking purposes just as comfortably as we went to the grocers. And the ale was different. These old Inns all brewed their own, and there was a rivalry as to which could produce the best. Even temperance men who would not look at wine or spirits kept to their mild and tasty Warrington ale. ARTHUR MOUNFIELD.

div.head: SONG OF HOPE.
div.p: A SONG OF HOPE.

Here is a little poem worth learning as a recitation. If it should never be repeated to other people; it is worth reciting to yourself : Never you worry, Never you fret; Flowers shall blossom Everywhere yet; Blue must the sky be Under the gray; Clouds will blow over, Another sweet day. Never you worry, Never you fret; Spring hasn't flouted The old world yet, Never you worry. Never you het Sorrow endureth. Joy shall come yet; Lo, the day faileth, Night mounts the skies; Walk in the starlight Till the sun rise. Never you worry, Never you fret; God isn't done With the old world yet. Never you worry, Never you fret: Green will the grass be On the graves yet; Those your heart longs for Draw near to you; Keep yourself ready. Keep yourself true. Those you remember, Can God forget? The best hasn't happened To any one yet.

div.head: RIDDLE.
div.p: A RIDDLE.
As a story to-day, I am copying a sparklet from an American Paper, "The Chicago Tribune." The Editor asks to believe that this is what happened lately in the office.

div.head: WHY?
div.p: WHY?
"Why is a woman like an umbrella?" asked the exchange editor.
"Because she's attached to a stick," replied the information editor. "Why is-" "Wrong. Guess again." "Because she always has to be shut up when-"
" Naw 1 You fatigue me." "Because she stands in the hall, and--" " Naw 1 it's nothing about standing in the hall."

"A woman is like an umbrella because nobody ever gets the right one. Why is—" "Ring off. That isn't the answer, either." "It's a better one than you've got." "Don't you reckon I know whether it is or not? Whose conundrum is this, yours or mine ? "

"Well, she's like an umbrella because—lt isn't because she fades with age, is it?" "You ought to be ashamed of yourself." I am. Is it because you have to put up when it's cloudy and threatening—no, that can't be it. Because she's a good thing to have in the house. Why is—"

"You're not within four counties of it." "Because you can't find any pocket in either. Why is—" "No choice. Vote again." "I won't. A woman isn't like an umbrella. There is not the slightest resemblance. You go on with your work, and let me alone." "I knew you couldn't guess it. It's because she's accustomed to reign." Then the information editor rose in his wrath, and had to be forcibly prevented from doing mischief.

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS. Flowers for Personal Decoration ; Buttons as Beautiful Accessories.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS. Flowers for Personal Decoration ; Buttons as Beautiful Accessories.
RETURN OF THE POCKET.
THE MERRY MONTH OF MAY

Here and there attempts are made, with more or less success, to revive the old time games associated with May Day, but the weather which ushers an the "merry month" is too often of such an uncongenial character that it seems to give the lie to the calendar. In these circumstances the modern custom of holding Labour processions seems more in keeping with the day than braiding the Maypole and darcing on the village green. May is by no means always the May of the poets, es a very brief inquiry into its real record will indicate. In 1909 snow fell during the m.)nth, and in 1904 there were orchards and gardens in this happy land which bore stripped trees all the summer, blackened and shrivelled by the frosts of May. A June day in 1903 brought with it four degrees of frost, and in 1902 and 1894 snowstorms mocked the poetic 3ignificance of the month of May. Nor are these 2speriences peculiar to recent times, for we read that on the 81. h of May, 1853, a train was snowed up near Sheffield It would therefore appear- that the old saying " Ne'er cast a clout till May be out" has real practical wisdom behind it. GOLD LACE.

The decorating of garments with gold lace goes back to vety ancient time, and its revival lately, after so many years of neglect, recalls the important part it formetly played on the habilments of kings, princes and the aristrocacy. Perhaps no other adornment gave rise to so much legislation for numerous sumptuary laws had to be passed at various periods to restrain its extravagant use, which led to the ruin of not a few noble families. Gold lace was especially in great request in the Middle Ages, and mention is frequently made in old inventories of frieges and laces of gold and silver. Always costly, and with heavy duties paid on it Queen Elizabeth tried to supprtss its use, among her courtiets, although she was much addicted to it herself. Gloves, scarves, stockings, shoes, and even garters were adorned with it. It was also used largely on the rich vestments of the church and one of the oldest specimens in this country was taken from the tomb of St. Cuthbet t some years ago. Queen Anne also triel to put down the fashion for wearing gold lace, and forbade its use on mantles, lappits, kerchiefs and the lighter articles of wearing apparel. FLOWER SEASON.

There is no prettier mode cf pertmal decoration than flowers, and certainly no other objects enter so largely into feminine adornment. It is therefore not a matter for surprise, but rather for congratulation, that blcssoms, real and artificial, are to be worn during the coming summer to the verge of extravag- ance. The rose will naturally come in for a full share of patronage but there will be a demand for exotics of the rarer kinds, more especially for orchids, and the more gorgeous they are the better. The corsage bouquet that has met with so much favour, will be requisitioned to put the finishing touch to the majority of the season's smart toilet,es. Hats will he covered with massed blooms,the mcst chic of the new parasols are embroidered in lovely designs of floweis in sprays and single blossoms. The popular little ruffles for the neck are most appropriately finished with tiny poses. Even bags for evening or theatre use have their bunches of real or artificial flowers. Fans, too, in addition to being painted with floral designs are 3uspended on ribbons brocaded w:th the lovliest blooms and have a bunch of flowers attached to them. It is a pretty idea to choose one favourite and suitabl9 flower and wear it throughout the season. DECORATIVE BUTTONS.

Time was when buttons were simply useful and necessary attachments that fastened garments. They are now beautiful and decorative accessories in both the feminine and the masculine toilette. The vogue for Bulgarian effects has invaded this department of dress. The familiar sober-looking Lraid buttoa has blossomed out info a brilliant if crud, affair of quite elaborate patterns. Last year the fashion for glass and crystal buttons was started. These kinds are now more elaborate and many in combinations of prevail- :ng colours deserve to be regarded as works of art. Green and white Goliath buttons—the latter with

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 3, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 3, 1913.

pearl centre and brass rim—are very effective. Very beautiful are the China barrel-shaped buttons in numerous decorative designs Some of the newest buttons have no shanks but are embroidered on to the rnatetial with silk t 3 match the dress. But the button of the hour, for excellence, is that in which pearl -in some way or other—and many of them are more ingenious. is intrcduced. DRAPERIES AND POCKETS.

The return of the pocket is announced. Whether it will be hailed as enthusiastically as before women had become so dependent on the almost as useful hand- bag remains to be seen. A t any rate, there is no place for a pocket on the severely made tailored skirt, still so generally worn or on the simple afternoon frock, which is to be favoured this summer, trimmed only with lace collar and cuffs. Then a handbag holds so very much more than a pocket could accommodate except it be of such proportions as those which our great grandmothers carried suspended from the waist under their dresses. Dressmakers have discovered that it is possible to conceal the pocket successfully in the volumenous folds of the fashionably draped skirt hence its partial revival. Draperies this season are not confined to skirts. They are a feature of all smart long afternoon and evening wraps. Only the severest style of garmetit lack folds of some kind, and these generally take an upward line towards the front, and are very narrow at the hem. CHINESE EVENING COATS.

The draped line dominates the evening coat, quite as much as it does the skirt. The Eastern influence, 30 apparent in this years' modes, is strikingly and happily shown in the newest evening wraps whose wide flowing Chinese sleeves and open fronts disclose the beautiful dresses worn under them. In Canton blue and gold brocaded silks, these garment are alto- gether desirable possessions. The collars are flat and the cuffs broad, sometimes of a contrasting colour and always richly embrAdered.The design is becoming and might be copied in much less capensive materials such as figured crepe de chine or any soft satin or silk. Old gold, telluel and beize are favourite colours for this seasons' evening coat.

div.head: SURE AND SAFE RAT EXTERMINATOR.
div.p: A SURE AND SAFE RAT EXTERMINATOR.

The natural hatred of rats by mankind has existed from the earliest times, and of lste years eminent scientists have been called upon to find means for destroying these pests. This has now been success- fully achieved by Dr. Danyr z, of the Pasteur Institute, Paris. It was brought to the notice of this scientist that rats died in numbers in a certain department in France, and some of the rats were sent to the Pasteur Institute for examination, where it was found that they were all suffer,ng from the same disease. Dr. Danysz took serum from the affected rats and gave it to others, who also died, and further research following on this rtsult led to the discovery of "Danysz Virus "and its subsequent preparation in liquid form. Animals other than rats and mice were then fed on Danysz Virus, but as the latter proved perfectly harmless to them, it could be claimed that a genuine rat exterminator that could be used with perfect safety had at last been found. Full particulars can be obtained by writirg to the Sales Department of Danysz Virus Ltd, 52 Leadenhall-street, E.U., who in addition to supplying the Virus for destroying rats and mice also undertake the clearance of all kinds of beetles, dx., from infested areas, at an inclusive charge.

div.head: GARDEN SUBURBS AND EMIGRATION.
div.p: GARDEN SUBURBS AND EMIGRATION.

Great and inspiring as is the external aspect of Bournville, the inner force, the mainsring of its being and its action, is still greater, still more moving. It stands for decent living as well as decent working, for sanitary homes as well as for sanitary factories. It makes for conditions that shall elevate, not brutalise. The idea is surely, then, greater than style. Ido not myself believe—l have never believed—that it' is waning trade which is driving the y,..uth of our country abroad ; it is the want of homes* My life an unceas- ing round from village to village,from one rural district to another, I see that en expanding population is at pressure against an inexpanding land systeir. I see many swarms but few hives. More land to the spade and plough, more village building, and those plausible men who represent Colonial Governments on the British country-side would reap a smaller harvest of humanity for the great granaries of the West.—" Agricultural Economist am! ilorticulturtl Review."

div.head: COMPLETE ' EXAMINER ' STORY.
div.p: COMPLETE ' EXAMINER ' STORY.
