WHEN THEY MET AGAIN,
BY ERNEST TREETON
Author of "The Instigator," "For Love and Justice," "The Saving of Christian Sergison," " The New Jack Sheppard," &c.

Because Richard Jocelyn was an artist in all his temperament, a lover of books and pic- tures, drama and music; because he was in- tended to write with the soul that was in him, and not to study "market prices "—that was why perverse Nature stumbled him into the Stock Exchange, and left him there as a junior of his father's firm. That was why he was a disappointed man, although he was not always conscious of it. And that was why he was quickly ruffled; though, for the same reason, he did not know that either. He would not 'begin to be able to read, know, and understand these things and mysteries within himself, and in life, until he was about fifty years of age, and at present he was only twenty-eight. And he was ruffled now; though' judging from appearances, he had no right to be. It was true. Beatrice Cardew, who stood befoi-t him, was worthy of the shortened form of her Christian name. She was " Trixie " by name; and arch, roguish, and " tricksy " by nature. While Jocelyn was as fair as a sun- beam, she was dark as a luscious, slily-peep- ing, elusive dewberry, glistening with dew- drops amid its leaves. While he loved books and studies, she revelled in the open air and sunshine of life. They were complete oppo- sites, and no doubt that was why Nature in- tended them for each other.

"I tell you what it is, Trix," he said, testily; "it must stop." "Why? Well, I shan't—there ! " she re- turned, lightly. Beatrice meant no evil, but that speech showed that she was a woman, any way. And if he had much still to learn, she had even more • for she was only twenty-three, and was full of sportiveness and playful mischief. If .they were not having their first tiff, it seemed very much like it; for Jocelyn's face darkened. No man likes to be crossed when he knows he is right; and one thing at least Jocelyn knew. He knew that he knew a great deal more of the shady tricks and craft of life than Trixie did. _ _ _ _

"Do you mean that?" he asked, intently. "Yes," she replied. "Why should I try to avoid them—why shouldn't I speak to them? They are nice enough—pleasanter than you are now. You're quite horrid, Dick! Bilious —jealous! " • Jocelyn let her run on until she had finished. "Nice enough ! " he exclaimed, warming. "Of course they are nice enough. It's part of their business to be nice. Your pater and mater receive them here; but they don't know them. I do. I tell you, though he is a member of the Stock Exchange, Mark Cleaver is an adventurer. And the woman—" " Woman ! " echoed Beatrice, with a touch of disdain. "Well, • the widow—Mrs. Sybil Shuttle- worth—his half-sister--call her what you like ! " he retorted, glowing into heat. " She is as dark as he is ! ' _ _ .

It was his misfortune to be cursed with in- sight, with the peculiar gift and power of reading character where others were blind; but his pride would not let him tell her that he had seen a great deal more than his words indicated. He would not tell her that he had seen that the whole arts of Mark Cleaver '3‘Vere directed against himself, and that Sybil Shuttleworth was aiding and abetting him. He was 'fighting against his own overthrow; but again pride and respect for Beatrice would not let him tell her that the object and end of Mark Cleaver's subtleties was the cap- ture of herself. He had seen the man's eyes, as well as his manner and his acts, and he 'knew what Beatrice did not know. "I am sure he is very nice," she rebelled, piqued, womanlike, into championing the ab- sent, if only to " draw " Dick out. The cloud in Jocelyn's face deepened. "Do you know that all Cleaver's operations in the House are directed against us?" he asked, ominously, his voice becoming tenser. "Do you know that he 'buys' against us, and sells ' against us? Do you know that he 'works' and 'rigs' the market against us Whenever he can? What for, if not to cause us a smash, in the hope of breaking us up? What for, if not to— But Jocelyn paused abruptly. He was still proud, still respectful of Beatrice's sensitive- 'ness, and the words "if not to ruin us, and make my marriage with you impossible," did not pass his lips. He only added: "He hates vs, because he hates me." • In the word " House " Beatrice knew that Dick referred to the Stock Exchange. By " smash " she knew that he referred to the possibility of his father's firm being "ham- mered" as defaulters. But, although her own . father was a leading member of the "House," 'that was about all she did know. Of the busi- ness of stockbrokering, and of the ways and :complexities of the Stock Exchange, she knew about as much as the man in the moon—per- haps rather less. That was why, with Eve's imp of mischief tripping her into teasing prankishness, she was now treading on dan- gerous ground—dangerous, because she loved her ." big boy," Dick, with all her waywardness. . You're jaundiced, Dick. It's mere fancy," she resisted, beginning to resent a little the feeling that he was lecturing her. " Fancy!" Jocelyn echoed again. "Fancy —when he is up against us whenever we enter the speculative market on our own account?" "It's clear you are jealous of him—sus- picious—and dislike him! And I don't think you ought to be ! " she still opposed. "And if I am, whose fault is it but his own?" Jocelyn protested. " Trixie, be sen- sible. Drop this freakishness, and be reason- able—or you will have to choose between .him and me." Jocelyn could have bitten off his tongue the moment after the hasty words were gone from it. In the instant he realised that he had tripped irretrievably. But it was too late; the words were beyond recall. . "Reasonable!" she retorted, warming. "Oh, you make me tired, Dick. If you keep on, I will say I will do as I like." And now she was as sorry as Dick. But pride would not let her recall her words. The gulf was widening between them. She had ;even receded coldly as Jocelyn, in speaking, had tried to pass his arm round her waist. If . he. had succeeded in kissing her again they might have laughed, and all would have been well. But with her avoidance resentful rather than wilful—all the light went out of Jocelyn's. face. "Very well, Trixie,' he said, gravely; "perhaps you would like me to go away?" Beatrice remained silent, held so by her wondering of what he was intending to say. And here Nature played her perverse tricks with them both, for he took Beatrice's silence for carelessness as to whether he went or stayed. "I can go," he continued, "and perhaps you may, COM 3 to be sorry." Surely; it was the enemy of Mother Eve that tripped her then? "Oh, now you are stupid," she tossed. Of course you won't go away" And she really meant what she said. " Trixie !" called Mrs. Cardew from the next room. . .

"Yes, mother?" Beatrice answered. "I want you a moment!" Beatrice left the room to Answer 'the call. When she returned a few moments later Jocelyn was gone. And while tears started to her eves, he, hurt and wounded, went brooding on his way homeward. They, two perfect lovers, were rent by the self-made rift between them. Which of them had been the more foolish, perhaps time would show.

Between Honolulu and Vancouver, ir the vast, sun-swept Pacific . Ocean, the British steamship Empire Queen was churning hei steady way. She had on board a passengei who had not had a place in her list when she steamed out of Sydney flarboil.r.

.Nonody on the ves'sel knew me stranger'i name. He was a castaway of the sea. The 3 had picked him 'up hem a raft, lifting and dinning with the waves. seven hundred miiei 1'4.N.113. of Honolulu--the only survivor of a floating cemetery. Four other men la 3 stretched out on the frail lashing of timber, and ropes, out they were dead. A few more hours' fierce glare of the pitiless, brazen sun, •and the lone survivor would have been dead too. No drain was left in the scorched water- keg, and the small provision barrel was empty: What had been the name of the ill-fated ship that was now lying engulfed somewhere in the boundless depths of the secret-keeping sea there was no discovering. None of the melancholy timbers exposed a name, either of ship or of port of origin. When lifted from the floating graveyard, the survivor was mur- muring " Trixie "—that was all. The rescuers saw that the left side of his head had been in- jured by a falling spar. He was unconscious in his murmuring. Perhaps the very injury to his head had been his salvation. He had been insensible to most of his companions' sufferings and miseries. In that same hour, away in London, on the far side of the world, the British steamship Homeland had been " listed " and " posted ' at Lloyd's as being thirty-four days overdue. But on board the Empire Queen they did not even know yet that such a vessel as the Homeland was missing. They restored their stranger to his former strength, but they landed him at Vancouver without learning his name or his ship; without discovering whether he had been passenger or seaman, though appearances bespoke him a passenger. His memory was gone; name and dwelling- place were alike blanks to .him. He had ceased to murmur even " Trixie "—which might have been ifo name at all, but only "tricksy." As a sole survivor he was important. The Vancouver authorities took him to the care of the Sailors' Home; but before reports and descriptions cquld be made and verified he wandered away, and was lost. Whether or not it was the Homeland that went down in the Pacific remained a mystery. And while all this drama was in progress, Mark Cleaver ceased to make war against the operations and speculations of Jocelyn and Sons on the London Stock Exchange. There was a good reason. A man was making his way from Alaska into the Yukon region of North-West Canada. He had come out to in- spect and report upon gold-Mining conces- sions, which had been acquired by the re- cently promoted Territories .Gold Mining and Development Company, of which he had be- come, a director; and that man was Mark Cleaver. Having finished his inspection, and having ,time to spare, he was now making his way into Yukon, with the characteristic ob- ject of seeing whether there was anything there that he could "snap up" on his own account. Being an adventurer, he cared little about the means by which he might acquire the " snap " or what its value might be, so long as it would serve him to float a company in London, with an excellent-sounding name, and with a hundred thousand pounds' worth of capital. Cleaver knew that Richard Jocelyn had left England for Australia two and a-half years ago, ostensibly on a business expedition ecin- nected with his father's financial interests; he knew that Jocelyn had never been heard of since. He had made good use of the passing time at the town house of the Cardevvs iii Onslow Gardens; he had left Mrs. g3,bil Shuttleworth behind, never misaing an op- portunity of referring to "Dear Mark"; and after his return to England, he hoped speedily to secure his position by mar- riage with Beatrice Cardew, who was coming gradually to accept the unwilling conviction that Dick must be for ever lost. The last man he expected to encounter in the huddle of mining shanties, called Dawson City, was Richard Jocelyn himself! _ _

Yet Jocelyn was there. But he was a strange Jocelyn. Cleaver, dark *though he was himself, and quick to grasp dark things, could not understand the wanderer's eyes. There was a curious glint in them. Though the light in them seemed to have a vagueness of memory, as if it might be a half recogni- tion, he could not tell whether Jocelyn re- cognised him or not. Who is that man?" he asked a gold prospector, whose acquaintance he had form-ed. "Oh, him? We call him Strange Jock," the digger explained. " Jock ' was all we could get out of him when he first hit the camp. Got a knock on the head away back somewhere, by the seeming of it. Queer alto- gether—don't know his name—can't remem- ber where he came from—just 'Jock' all the time. Some of the boys would give him a bang on the head, if they knew which side to hit. If it fair stretched him out it would put the balance right, and bring his memory back, they say. But it would do him up alto- gether if they hit the wrong side; so there he Purty sweet fix, ain't it? Any way, he ain't no deuced tenderfoot on some things; he's all-fired, mighty spry, wherever anything in this section is concerned. I don't know whether it's nature, like a dog, or whether it's a twist of his brains; but blame me if he ain't got a scenting nose for paying ground! He has snicked -some of the best sections going about here, and is purty considerable rich, let me tell ye ! " Rich! Memory gone! A blow—the wrong side of his head--would knock him out! As he went on, dark thoughts formed them- selves in Mark Cleaver's own mind. He was the only living man in Yukon who knew Jocelyn's name and country. He was the only man in the world who knew that Richard Jocelyn was still alive. What of it? Yes, what of it?
And there he paused, for the blackness of the thought that came to him was one to vildch even he would not give a name.

What if happenings could chance to spring up, or could be brought about, to present the possibility? In this wild, pioneer corner of the earth, where a quarrel produced the deadly blow, the swift revolver-? Again, he did not give the• plssibility a name, but it was black.

The day passed on to nightfall. Presently the lights began to blink in the shanties. Work was done; soon there would be drink, cards' dice—and, perhaps, shooting—in the rough saloons. As "Strange Jock," Jocelyn was rarely in those wild, reckless scenes. The camp did not expect him; he was "queer," and they let him go his " hnrmless " way unmolested. Like himself, his way was strange. The cat's nature for nocturnal wanderings seemed to be his also. When night came no one knew where, or how remotely around, he prowled in this far, solitary Canadian back. land, where, until now, no man's foot had ever trod.

All these things Cleaver had come to know, and he had had passing eye-evidence of them as well. He had heard the gold-diggers say, "There he goes ! " and he had seen Jocelyn's dark figure wandering around the shanties and huts. And to-night he had dark impulses to watch and follow.

Presently he saw Jocelyn skirt the camp and make his way towards Ragman's Ravine, a narrow pass between •two sharp bluffs, so called by the miners because by the time new- comers reached that point they were generally in rags.. Some adventurers never reached it at all. When reached. its _foothold was nar-

• row, rugged, and treachera4.lr a 111 PIA there was a sheer fall of forty feet low rocky cataract below. -1 the But Cleaver followed. Soon he heal- ,hat clink of a hammer, sounding weirdly in :new dark, vast, unbroken loneliness; and 11. e —the that Jocelyn was near at hand, chiPlnnli,„ost face of the jutting rock. Suddenly, a the before he was aware of it, he was uPclll wanderer in the narrowest part of the Pas— " Hello ! " he exclaimed, as if surprised. go Jocelyn made no immediate answer- ,„„t• had turned at the sound of Cleaver's step, and was now facing his old-time eneT'; Even in the darkness the strange question light in his eye seemed to be visible, as it, gleaming, like an animal's does ni ;as staring and searching. Or else it his Cleaver's fancy. When Jocelyn slxe voice was as strange as his eyes and his `idy tude, like some inquiring sound out of a °— past. you
-- You again?" he said, curiously. are no Yukon. You are a trickster.

are you doing here? Eh?" hga The way of things suited Cl'eaver. lie •nst a miner's pick-handle in his hand agal- Jocelyn's short hammer. "What's that to do with you? 4hig answered, roughly. "I suppose I can 130 " wilYFlovigifvfiiintgyNur s Jocelyn liitiAtiorig: 011 strangely. "Black—all black. Have I seeil you before—have I?" The words showed that his darkelliel memory was puzzling him. They Cleaver uneasy. For the first time he twilit possible recognition. The thought broug him desperation. he "Clear out of it, and let me pass , said, violently, forcing the issue he wonteL And he lifted his club in the night. his " Ah ! " Jocelyn exclaimed, as swiftly as -

eye saw. er With the word, he dropped his hanol:,,d and sprang, even his injured head realitti,7 intended mischief. Ready though he , Cleaver was not prepared for such ono agility as this. His wrist was gripped no a vice; they closed in a fierce wrestle' • 1%; in a moment they were down on the 1014 shelving ledge of the pass. Another movie% and they were rolling down the scarp ravine! Ten 'feet down they lodged on a juttl piece of earth and rock, Jocelyn undernic's both locked in deadly toils, panting h0t199 struggling madly. Cleaver raged desperately. He had 112 thought of "right " and " wrong " sides 01 As he heaved, he seized a dislodged luml3 rock, and drove it furiously against the rig side of Jocelyn's head. Instantly Joceiri grip snapped; his arms jerked up, and CO' lapsed in limpness. ~fs Quickly Cleaver searched Jocelyn's inine:' shirt, and secured the mine claim registrat'°, papers from its inner breast pocket. Then, 0 did he push the unconscious man? Joel, rolled over, and went dropping down to t' seething waters below. big As if with the brand of Cain already on - brow, Cleaver scrambled swiftly up the se3r,P' and stole back to the camp. The next ing he set his face towards the East. And the next morning the men of DaWs°.„ll City found Jocelyn where he had fallen I)" the bushes, half in and half out of cataract. There is human nature even in rough, lawless by-places of the earth. 'l'4 carried him a hundred miles to the dont% at Fort Orikee, and left him there, not reel'. ing that they would never see him again.

Counted as time, three months Pagg,o before the doctors would allow Jocelyn leave Fort Orikee. But now, by operati°o and skill, his memory was clear. Hours wer flying; at a far distance there were unknovr able things for him; and to him the tinig seemed an age. He asked for his papers. 4 "You had none when you came in, theL told him. "The fellows who brought yoi clown said they searched- your shanty, bilit could not find any. They guessed they 1110"0 have been washed away by the cataract wi4e.o you fell. But you have enough 'dust I,s your belt-pouch to keep you going for a ye4i Jocelyn- thought not of the geld CSd "dust." He said nothing. The face of Pt' man's Ravine was not a blank to him Cleaver's face was before him; and Cleaveris hand held the rich prizes of his papers. Perhaps on their backs were endorsed forged transfers of his mine rights,, "From Richard Jocelyn to Mark Cleaver' Robbed! et When he set forth he turned his faces ° 0 towards Dawson, but towards the East. lid. travelled fast, on and on—ever eastwar, Four days of land, six of sea, and he came the Liverpool of the homeland to which " had long been lost. London was his end. Would it all 10;6t, been misdirection and futility? The nig,'l,„, was Tuesday. In the train he looked at London morning paper he had bought. It curious to to him; the first he had seen for threg years. Suddenly, as his eye wandered over the pages, he started. Before him wag half-page advertisement--the prospectus ° the Lucky Star (Yukon) Gold Mining Cour pany, Ltd., which was now being floated W--x a capital of £250,000! The vendor was Mal: Cleaver; he was to receive £lOO,OOO in caw" £50,000 in shares, and £50,000 was to Pe allotted as working capital. From the neci scription of the properties, Jocelyn recognise f his own mine sections in the far-away Land ° the Setting Sun. The end was a realitY.. What a staggering revenge would be his! A while he sat, lost in thought, until his ey again strayed over the printed pages. Thelli once more, he started. This time he read a society marriage to be solemnised in pretty village church of Mondhurst,.. 're Sussex, near the country house of the brine., father, to-morrow afternoon. The bride Beatrice Cardew, and the bridegroom—Mu Cleaver! Time! That was his one urgent thong-, now. "Mercy save her from that fate," his prayer. He felt no bitterness for Tri);lis He knew that he had been " dead "; but `1:,0 love quivered with fear of losing her in 1-I,l' eleventh hour of his return to life. At last—Euston! He hastened to 11,,i8 father's house, to startle the butler there with the apparition of a man risen from dead. His father and mother were in Para' o' his brothers were shooting in Scotland. ro had hoped to bring the delight of surprr:' and found blankness. All the Cardew fani"P he knew, would to-night be at Mondhurst. But on the morrow's morning he mak; earl.; awake. Soon he was at Bow-street, IaYAV, sworn information for a warrant for arrest of Mark Cleaver on charges of rebb% and attempted murder. Then, with ,0 stranger, having handcuffs in his pockets set out on a journey once more—to the Pre"' church of the pretty village of Mondhurst- the The wondering villagers looked at him---%th bronzed, manly, muscular stranger, !Id wide-world light in his blue eye—as he Paeff up the path between them, and seated hire on the bench in the sunlit porch el ilhe church. The bridegroom was already in ot grey old holy place, but the Law would follow him there. Alien Presently the bride came with her fa' in There was no smile, but only gravity Trixie's face. and Jocelyn rose quietly from his seat, faced the sunlight and the lych-gate. "Am I in time, Trixie?" he a,skedtwal quietly as he had risen. "I was foolish. -" you let this thing be?" Into Beatrice's face came a sudden tele: strain; speechless, she was as one stunniii; she am ayed, and would have fallen, if.,:/°ceb it had not caught her in his arms. Tn°ll„Twer. was in blankness, he had received his al;;" in- The delay brought the "best Inall ed to quiringly from the church. div.head: BRILLIANT FINAL.
div.p: A BRILLIANT FINAL.

Few people anticipated that the meeting of Warring- ton and Huddersfield for the Northern Union Cup would provide a really great game, and that was where they were wrong, for everyone was willing to admit that it was the most brilliant final seen for many years past. Warrington certainly succeeded in giving Hudders- field a very severe fright, and if they had taken advan. tage of one chance in the second half it is more than likely they would have won. However, Warrington deserve every credit for the great fight they made, and the thanks of every one who saw the match are due to them for being the main factors in such a brilliant struggle.—" Daily Dispatch." TRUE MANLY FOOVBALL.

It was not the winners who took the eye of the impartial, but Warrington, whose really wonderful— and I tiny say quite unanticipated—display against such formidable antagoni4ts contributo.d to the finest game I have ever seen in a cup final. Warrington I will grant were beaten by a superinr side, but they were a long way from being disgraced. The " wirepulleis," as they are familiarly known have by their exposition of true manly football at Fleadingley won the hearts of all Northern Unionists, and at the game time added lustre to an alroarly brilliant record.—" Daily News."

div.head: WARRINGTON TEAM'S RETURN.
div.p: WARRINGTON TEAM'S RETURN.

Rain was falling heavily and the streets were almost deserted when, after a tedious journey, the Warring- ton team arrived home at 11.30. Their reception suggested a stronu contrast with the rejoicings which were witnessed eight years ago when they brought the coveted trophy from Leeds and made a triumphal progress through densely crowded streets. This time only a few friends of belated trippers awaited the train at Arpley station. The team took their defeat in true sportsmanlike spirit, for the magnitude of the task which confronted them in meeting Huddersfield had all along been recognized. The prevailing senti- ment which found expression among their supporters was "Hard fines," for the half-time lead had buoyed everyone up with hop's of victory. The plucky fight of the Warrington men had earned general commenda- tion and, before dispersing for their homes, they were warmly cheered.

div.head: CONGRATULATING THE VICTORS.
div.p: CONGRATULATING THE VICTORS.

Councillor Osborne, who se chairman of the Com- mittee of the Warrington Football Club was foremost among 'hose who wl3hed to see Warrington triumph sent the following telegram to the captain of the Huddersfield team : You have won the Cup, and with it heartiest congratulations of your many admirers in Warring- ton. May you always "play the game. "—Edmund
Osborne: - The telegram came personally from Mr. Osborne but we feel sure it represented the sentiments of all Warringtonians towaros the victors who had played so splendidly and won so well.

div.head: CONGRATULATIONS FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: CONGRATULATIONS FOR WARRINGTON.

- - Congratulatory messages on the splendid fight the team men have been received from " Warringtonians at Ferry Hill,Durham "the Salford Football Club, George Marsden, Wigan (who said that in his opinion that Warrington team wes the test Rugby club ever seen) and E. Halford, Bradford.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCORE Fißsr.
div.p: WARRINGTON SCORE Fißsr.

The Warrington men kept up the attack and Nicholas secured. With a short dash he drew Moorhouse out of position and then threw to Bradshaw. The wing man took the ball finely and swerving past Moorhouse, he rushed over the line to some jut as Holland bundled him out of play. It was a capital effort rewarded with cheering all round the ground-- cheering which was renewed again and again as Jolley t ,ok the kick and landed a wonderful goal right from the touch line. This success came after 25 minutes' play. The Huddersfield backs made a combined effort to get on level terms, but Brooks was proving a great thorn in

div.p: 1--hutograplb by WARRINGTON KEEPING THEIR LINES INTACT IN THE

div.head: FIRST HALF.
div.p: FIRST HALF.

their aide. Warrington returned to the attack, and a penalty to Hudderofield was a welcome relit f. A moment later Warrington had to save from a big effort by Wagstaff, but the movement ended when Jolley made his mark under difficulties. The War- rington tackling was remarkably vigorous, though clean, and their spltting was rarely at fault. Warrington had Jolley again to thank for a delight- ful save. A movement started by Grey was taken part in by all the backs, but Rosenfeld was splendidly pushed into touch by Jolley. A minute later he was again unable to keep out of touch when a yard from the cosier flag and the Warrington defence showed not the slightest sign ef wavering under extreme pressure. Half-time arrived with Warrington still leading by 1 goal, 1 try, 5 points to nil.

Union. Moorhouse and Rosenfeld ran speedily on the wings, but they lacked the genius of a man like Fish, and in my opinion are not in the same class. At half-back, the Warrington pair were fully equal to Grey and Davie, though the styles were different. Daintith did great work in his first final, and Nicholas was full of resource. The best threequarters were Renwick and Bradshaw. very little opportunity coming to Tranter and Brooks. But they kept the Rosenfel&-Gleeson wing under subjection. Forward, every man shone in turn, but none were quite so prominent as the ruddy-haired Skelhorne, who has made a great reputstion in this season's cup-tie 3, and seems marked out for further honours.

div.head: SECOND HALF.
div.p: THE SECOND HALF.

After the usual interval the teams changed ends and the battle was renewed. The rain had ceased some time before, but the wind had developed into halt a gale and was obviously going to be of great assist- ance to Huddersfield. Warrington restarted and made good ground. The Lancastrian pack wheeled the first scrummage, with the result that they at once got to the Hud,let afield quarters and grassed Holland with the ball. The Fartowners relieved with passing, but Moorhouse was easily overhauled by Bradshaw. A lot of hand-to-hand passing by Huddersfield carried play to the Warrington 25, where Gronow threw a ' possible chance away by fumbling the ball. Rosenfeld next tried to break through, but was well tackled. Once again play raged in neutral territory. Grey then set the Huddersfield backs in motion, the ball going through the hands of Davies and Wagstaff to Moorhouse, who kicked over Jolley's head. A thrilling race ensued between Itoorhouse, Renwizk and Jolley, the former just pulling through and div- ing on the ball over the line —to an outburst of applause, which was changed to " booing " as the referee disallowed the paint and gave Warrington the drop-out. There seemed some doubt on the point, but it turned out that Moorhouse had pushed Jollty off the ball, and there was no hesitation about the referee's verdict. Warrington were very bard pressed at this stage, and when Renwick brought Chesters out to assist the backs, it seemed as if Huddersfield w ere bound to score are long. The Yorkshire frwards now had a big pull in the ecrutn, and the ball was continually in the hands of the clever backs behind.

div.head: REDUCING THE LEAD.
div.p: REDUCING THE LEAD.

Huddersfield, however, were not long in reducing the lead, for Gronovr threw the ball well out to Wagstaff, who passed at the right time to Moorbouse, who forced his way over at the low corner. Holland made a good, but unsuccessful effort at goal. A minute later Warrinton bad a narrow escape, but Jolley kept his line intact. Huddersfield were now pressing for all they were worth, but the Warrington tackling was sound. Some smart passing between Grey, Davies, and Wagstaff, enabled Moorhouse to make a dash hr the line, but the Huddersfield winger was brought down. The Feirtowners were persistent in their attack, bur, they could not get the better of the opposition. A penalty to Huddersfield, given for off-side tactics against George Thomas was taken by Holland, and theugh the position was an easy one the Huddersfield full-back failed to lower the goal. Aided by a free kick Huddersfield again pressed and Grey gave to Rosenfeld, who was knocked off his feet by Jolley just as he seemed certain to go over at the corner.

div.head: HUDDERSFIELD AHEAD.
div.p: HUDDERSFIELD AHEAD.

Supporters of Huddersfield were beginning to anxiously look at their watches, and only fourteen minutes were left to go when the Yorkshire men took the lead as the result of a rather lucky try. There had been a bit of a rush by the Huddersfield forwards, and Clark, who had followed up further tnan the others, was yards offside when the ball struck a War- rington man aud rebounded to him, thus placing him onside. All he had to do was to pick the ball up and throw it out to Moorhouse, for the latter to walk in. The last try, however, was worth both the others and was the result of really clever work. No team could have stopped it by hr means. Holland gathered a kick. and instead of returning it ran round and gave to Wagstaff. The latter drew his man and gave to Moorhouse, who as the wing man dashed in for the tackle returned to Wagstaff. Then there was Jolley left to beat, and that was' accomplished by another nice pass back to Moorhouse, who trotted in for his third try of the game. 'WARRINGTON'S CHANCE.

The Warrington men at once showed that they were not done with and a great rush by the forwards carried play to the Huddersfield quarters. Holland failed V) clear and Fearnley NV.S placed on side with only ten yards to go. He seized the ball, but a moment's hesitation enabled Gleason to come up like a rocket and effect a desperate tackle almost in front of the posts. A pass by Fearnley to Skelhorne would have brought a certain try and Warrington had then only to kick a goal to beat Huddersfield in the last minute. The incident was only of a few seconds'

div.head: PRESENTATION OF THE CUP.
div.p: PRESENTATION OF THE CUP.

A considerable section of the crowd massed before the principal pavilion at the close of the game, and the players of both teams were severally congratulated by enthusiastic supporters as they made their way with difficulty to where the Northern Union Committee and officials were grouped around the Cup. It was a matter of regret that the Earl of Derby, who had been announced to present the Cup and medals to the players, was unable to attend. Mr. A. Sherwell, M.P. for Huddersfield, who performed the pleasing ceremony, said he was extremely sorry that Lord Derby was not able to be present. Although he could not hope to stand in L-ird Derby's shoes in many respects, he did not yield to his Lordship, good sports- man though he be —(hear, hear)—in his admiration for such a magnificent contest as had b-en witnessed that afternoon. He had only one regret, and that wis that, where two teams had put up such a fine, and, on the day's play, so splendidly contested a game, there were not two cups. (Cheers.) He personally believed and he thought those who had witnessed the game would agree with him—that on the afternoon's play almost as much honour fell to the losers as had fallen to the winners. On the complete records of the past season, however, he thought that football supporters in the two counties would cordially congratulate the Huddersfield team on having won that cup. (Cheers.) He had the greatest pcssible pleasure in complimenting the captain of the winning team, Wagstaff, on his generalship, to which Huddersfield owed No much.

Mr. Stierwell then banded over the Cup and winners' medals to Wagstaff and the members of the Huddersfield team, and the medals for the runners-up to Renwick, the Warrington captain Wsgstaff,in response to cries of" Speech," observed that it was the first time that Hud iersfield had won the Northern Union Cup. He thought it had been their game. A lot of people thought it would be a " walk-over" for his side, but he could tell them that t had been the hardest game in the round, and, like Mr. Sherwell, he was sorry there were not two cups. The Huddersfield team gave three 6eers for their opponents, and the Warrington men, not to be out- done in cuurtesy, heartily replied.

div.head: PRAISE OF THE CRITICS. Honours for Warrington.
div.p: THE PRAISE OF THE CRITICS. Honours for Warrington.

Warrington have twice won the enp but they have never got more honour out of any game thin they did out of their fifth final on SAturday as the following extracts from comments by the critics plainly prove.

div.head: Wst RRINC. TON'S TACKLING.
div.p: Wst RRINC. TON'S TACKLING.

No losing side has ever played a more genuinely pluckly and creditable game in the Northern Union Cup finals than did Warrington on this occasion. They were faced by a side which admittedly was stronger, heavier and:cleverer than.themselves,and yet they gave that side a" fright " that will not readily be forgotten. In these days good tackling is not so much seen as it ought to be I refer to Northern Union football, of course—for attack is accounted the greater defence in many quarter, and one passing movement is sought to be c.,uotered by another. Halloo it WAS most refreshing to see the keen and courageous way in which the Warrington men went for their opponents and brought them down. Close and impartial followers of Huddersfield's passing and repassing movements have held the view that the backs are often flattered by the lack of intelligence and want of determination shown by defending sides ; hence when the same players were confronted by the deadly Warrington tackling, they hardly knew what to make of it. The criticism was passed after the match that Huddersfield's passing was no as accurate and well- timed as it usually is. Why? Simply because the Warrington tackliag was of a quality to which the Fartown men are not accustomed.--" Yorshire Post."

div.head: TRIBUTE TO JOLLEY.
div.p: A TRIBUTE TO JOLLEY.

The day was agiinst the making of individual reputations. But I well liked the play of Jolley, the Warrington fullback. This youngster, who is, I believe, a nephew of the famous James Jolley, of Runcorn, exhibited throughout the game a remarkable ability to do the right thing at the right time. His kicking was invariably marked with judgment, and his tackling saved his side a couple of tries. Warring-
ton possess a full-back with a great future. Of that I am certain.—" Sunday Chronicle."
WARRINGTON'S PALMY DAYS.

Never, even in the palmy days of Fish and Isherwood, of Hallam and Dickenson and Hockenhall, have Warrington so delighted a Yorkshire crowd— never have a losing team come out of the match with more credit aid distinction. Warrington, with their lighter forwards, with their slower and less skilful backs, were expected to prove rather ready victims for the most talented team in the Union. That at least was the view of nine-tenths of those who best know the powers of the Huddersfield men. Yet Warrington were the first to score; they were leading by 5 paints at half-time; they kept their heads in front until an hour had passed, and the Huddersfield section of the crowd were growing anxious; and when at last they were worn down they kept their courage and fought grimly and gamely to the end. There are such things as glorious defeats. This was a glorious defeat, and the lustre of Warring- ton football was enhanced rather than dimmed by this magnificent struggle against a more scientific and accomplished team.—" Daily Mail."

div.head: duration, but it was a thrilling end to a great game. Final : Huddersfield 3 tries t 9 points). Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try 15 points).
div.p: duration, but it was a thrilling end to a great game. Final : Huddersfield 3 tries t 9 points). Warrington, 1 goal, 1 try 15 points).
THE PLAY AND THE PLAYERS.

Thus Warrington lost, but they had given Hudders- field the game of their lives, and shown football which delighted not only their own supporters, but the assembled thousands from Yorkshire. There can be no questioning Huddersfield's superiority on the day's play. They were infinitely more dangerous on the attack than the Wirepullers, and it seemed only a question of time in the second half when the heroic defence of Warrington must be borne down. But the first half showed Warrington at their best. The for- wards were brilliant in every respect. They scrummaged well, and spread out to 8F131131, the backs in a way which astonished the crowd, while the tackling of the whole team was something to marvel at. It is safe to say that the Huddersfield backs have never had so many opportunities and found themselves so well checked. Wagstaff might well show signs of anxiety, for the combination of his colleagues seemed at one time likely to go to pieces under the Warrington onslaught. But the change of ends, the help of the wind, and the unwise withdrawal of Warrington's heaviest man from the pack, gave the Fartown men. just the advantage they had lacked. Warrington's defence was still great,but it could not hold out for ever. '1 he better team won, but in my opinion, and that of many of the critics, chief honours go to the losers ! Now as to individuals. The hero of the day was unque,tionably Jolley, despite Moorhouse's "hat- trick." The Warrington custodian was a great little man. His cootnr se and pluck under pressure were the source of general admiration ; his punting was always powerful and well-directed, hut his tackling of Moorhouse, Rosenfeld and Gronow when those men were certain scorers; brought down the house. Jolley is going t, be one the great full backs of the day. On the other side Wagstaff, though shaky at first, was the genius of Huddersfield. He held the team together at a critical stage, and when the attack was persistent his strength and resource brought their full reward. There has never been a finer centre threequarter in the Northern

div.head: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.

Warrington's Victory over Barrow NEW HALF-BACK'S PROMISING DEBUT. Notwithstanding their strenuous struggle in the Cup final, the Warrington men showed no sign of staleness on Monday evening when they turned out for the much-postponed match with Barrow on the Wilderspool ground. They gave a brisk, and at times really sparkling display and, although Barrow put up a keen fight in the early stages, Warrington's all-round superiority asserted itself and the Iseult was a victory for the home contingent by 19 points to 6. The fates , were distinctly unkind to the Warrington olub,wretched weather depriving them of what would undoubtedly have been a large gate for the concluding League match. Rain fell heavily during the greater part of the first half ; the ground was in a terrible condition, and the spectators would not number more than 700. The Warrington team was the same that did duty in the cup final,except that Ruddick, the latest acquisition from Coventry, appeared at half-back Brookes being the absentee. The new man created a very favour- able impression for, he is speedy and resourceful, and not only scored twice on his own account,but frequently Initiated strong attaining movements. Barr°, started well and were the first to score. Jolley. in attempting to clear, kicked into the bands of Williams, who passed to Thomas, that player getting over near the corner. The goal kick was a failure. Warrington now attacked and Ruddick, breaking through, gave 3 good pass to Bradshaw, who missed it. Later Renwick failtd to take a pass. Receiving the ball from Daintitb, Ruddick dash clean through with • grand try, Jolley adding a goal. A promising move- ment by the Barrow backs was spoiled by Harrison knocking forward. A few moments later the visitor pro. sided another floe round of passing, covering nearly the whole length of the field, and Gifford ran over but was recalled for a forward pass. Warrington wheeled the pack, and the ball was dribbled over, for Ftarnley to score. Nicholas kicked a goal. Half-time :—Warring- rod, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points); Barrow, 1 try (3 points). Soon efter the interval, Nicholas failed at a penelty kick. Passing by the Warrington backs saw Bradshaw race through to the foil back. He passed inside to the forwards, and Thomas and Cheaters dribbled over, the latter dropping on the bll over the line. Ruddick failed at goal. Tries by Bradshaw and Ruddick came in quick succession, but Thomas and Cheaters were unsuccessful with the goal kicks. Barrow had a spell of attacking, and Gifford, snapping up the ball from a mis-kick by a Warrington man, had no difficulty in scoring. Ruddick was again prominent by breaking way from a scrummage and transferring play close to the Barrow line. The final score was :—Warrington, 2 goals, 5 tries (19 points) ; Barrow, 2 tries (6 points;.

div.head: SCHOOLBOY RUGBY CHAMPIONS.
div.p: SCHOOLBOY RUGBY CHAMPIONS.
St. James' Fine Record.

A. match in which great interest centred was played at Wilderspool on Saturday morning when St. James's met Silver-street. A win for either team meant the winning of the League championship, and a keen game was anticipated. Silver-street winning the toss elected to play with a strong wind at their backs. Rigby started and St. James' immediately pressed ; Newall early on having distinctly hard lines in not dribbling over. Play now ruled at the centre. Keen footwork was seen from both sides. St. James' pressed and Lawton was conspicuous on several occasions with strong runs. Nothing, however, was scored and a strong kick by Parr took the play to the other end. Silver-street were playing hard but Smith was able to keep his line intact despite the strong efforts of Mellor, Lawton (Silver-street), Parr and Ryder. When play reached the other end Rigby made a poor drop at goal and Munn lost a try by endeavouring to double in; the slippery nature of the turf proving his downfall. Half-time was called with no score registered. On the resumption Si James' went away at a great pace, Buckley being prominent in strong forward dashes Over-eagerness and an epidemic of drop kicks lost both ground and points for St. James'. The defence of Mellor and Parr, however, was splendid ; the tackling of the latter cams as a revelation to his supporters. About three-quarter time Skelkorn, who had been giving a good show, received the ball from the pack, went round the blind side and calmly dropped at goal; the ball just lobbed over the bar. This reverse seemed to put new life into the Silver-street boys, who until the final whistle sounded gave the Latchford team a hot time but the defence prevailed and St. James' were best represented by A. Lawton, Skelhorn, Buckley, Rigby and Smith, and the losers by Mellor, Parr and the.Lawtons. It is interesting to note that St. James' have not been beaten in a league match for two seasons and have only had 3 pints scored against them, St. Benedict's crossing their line in the first match last season.

div.head: CR I CKET MISPECTS. WARRINGTON OPEN THE SEASON
div.p: CR I CKET MISPECTS. WARRINGTON OPEN THE SEASON
TO-DAY.

The prospects of the Warrington cricket season, which opens to-day, are particularly rosy. Ashton- under-Lyne will be the visitors to Arpley and, although they are an exceptionally strong bide, they will have to strain eyery effort if they are to bring about the local eleven's discomfiture. The bowling department was the weak spot last season, but this has been con- siderably strengthened by the engagement of Hannan. the new professional, who comes from the ground staff at Old Trafford, and is reputed to be a deadly bowler. The Rev. Horace Gray ‘,l, ill not take the field to-day, but is expected to turn out later on. The eleven will be led by W.Richardson, jun., with S. Pal tridge as sub- captain. T. Wright will make a welcome re-appeal- ance with the senior contingent and is expected to do great things with the bat. The young players who showed good promise last season, have bet-n retain( d. the fixture list is a particularly attractive one, and includes Bootle (home) on Whit Monday. A new club to try conclusions with Warrington is Blackpool, who will be met at the end of the season.
The team against Ashton-under-Lyne to-day is : NV. Richardson (captain), S. Partridge, B. Si!cock, J, Callon, J. W. Pearson, S. Baxter, A. Duckworth Bannan, J. Cheaters, J. Bradburn and T. Wright.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.

Owing to the withdrawal of Wilderspool, Walker's Brewery and St. Helens Cable Company, the League is reduced to seven clubs. A new club has been secured, in the Warrington Divex C. C.—a team emanating from the insurance Offices at Bridge Foot. The season opens to-day with the match Divex v Whitecross.

div.head: LOCAL 'WEDDING.
div.p: LOCAL 'WEDDING.
ROBINSON-WATSON.

A pretty wedding took place at Penketh Wes- leyan Church on Saturday, in the presence of a large congregation, when Mr. William Robinson, son of Mr. Robinson, Orford, Warrington, was married to Miss Annie Watson, daughter of Mr. James Watson, North View, Penketh. The Bev. W. A. Beckett (superintendent minister of the Warrington Circuit) officiated. The hymn "The Voice that breathed o'er Dden" was sung, and Miss Edith Jones, of Runcorn, who was at the organ, played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by her father,. was attired in grey satin cloth, with ornamental silver trimming, and hat to match. She carried a bouquet of lilies, narcissi and white heather. The bridesmaids were Miss Mary •Watson (sister of the bride), and Miss Robinson (sister of the bridegroom). They wore dresses of white cash- mere, trimmed with saxe blue silk, and their bou- quets were composed of tulips and narcissi. Mr. Boardman, of Warrington, discharged the duties of best man. The reception was held in the infant school, over fifty guests attending. The following is a

BREWERY STRIKE. Union's Peaceful Overtures. The National Union of Gasworkers' and General Labourers' Union have issued a reply to the official notice issued by Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd., Warringtoa and Burton, regarding the dispute in pro- gress at their brewery. Mr. Arthur Lees, organiser of the National Union of Gasworkers' and General Labourers', states that the number of strikers who left the brewery was 11(i and not 6.1 as stated. He also declares that the action of the firm in discharging eight men while their notice was being served, "without due cause being stated," precipitated matters. Mr. Lees adds : We, on our part, are by no means anxious to con- tinue the difficulty unnecessarily, if the firm will make it clear that the further rise of is. a week referred to in their notice of Friday is a general offer, applicible to the men who are out as well as the men who are in, we on our side would be pre- pared to at once call a meeting of the men to con- sider whether a bridge might not be constructei to secure a settlement in the interests of the firm and the men. SEAMEN'S SUPPORT FOR THE WORKERS. At a meeting of the Nitional Union of Seamen and Firemen, held on Sunday last at Spekeland Buildings, Liverpool, when delegates were present representing the Preston, Manchester, Garaton, Birkenhead, and Liverpool branches, the following resolution was passed "it is unanimously resolved that all members of the Seamen and Firemen's Union are instructed to support the brewery workers who have grievances; also that the minimum wages for labourers should be 253. per week instead of a guinea, and that the Shops Act shall be put into force so far as managers and men behind the bar are concerned. We pledge oureelves to use all legitimate means to assist the brewery employees to gain this object, and instruct the officials of the National Seamen and Firemen's Union to spread this news on ships both when signing on and paying off." Mr. R. Chidlow, who presided, said that seamen would heartly support the brewery employees and the men behind the bar in their effort to gain fair couditions. BARMEN AND MANAGERS. On Monday afternoon delegates from Warrington and representatives of the Managers' and Barmen's Union met at Spekeland-buildings to consider the resolution of the seamen and firemen. Councillor James Stephenson, secretary of the District Council of the Transport Workers' Federation, stated that he had appealed to the Liverpool Corporation time after time to prosecute the brewers who were evading the Shops Act. At first the Home Office had stated that managers were not entitled to the benfits of the Act, but, after the fall facts had been laid before the Home Secrerary, he decided that managers were fully entitled to a weekly half- holiday. The Labour Party in the Liverpool City Council had also raised the question of the right of a manager to possession of his licence, and this would be dealt with at a very early date. Mr. P. J. )Julvaney, secretary of the Managers' and Barmen's Union, said that they were making common cause with the Warrington strikers, and were drag jug up a joint programme of grievances and their remedy to be submitted to Messrs. Walker.

Dr. Joseph has been Assistant Medical Officer of Health since last June. CHIEF INSPECTOR 'WILLIAMSON. • Well-Deserved Promotion. At a meeting of the Watch Committee on Thursday, Chief Inspector B. Williamson, of the Warrington Police Force, was promoted to the rank of superintendent. A native of Thurso, Scotland, he joined the force, as a

constable, twenty years .ago, and by dint of consistent hard work and efficiency has attained his important position. He was appointed chief inspecter four years ago, and his latest promotion will give great satisfac- faction to his many friends.

Latchford Baptist Church. The Sunday school anniversary services in connection with the above church were held on Sunday, the preacher being the pastor, Rev. .1. S. Chedburn. At each of these services special items were contributed by the children's choir. In the afternoon a musical service was held at which the Superintendent of the school, Mr. S. Al hinson, presided, and a very interesting address to the children was given by Mr. A. Elliott. The children's choir who had been very ably coached by Mr. P. Harrison, the church organist, and to whom great credit is due, rendered their pieces in a very pleasing manner. The collections for the day which amounted to nearly £6 was considered very satisfactory. Headquarters of the Irish Command, which has been located at the Royal Hospital, iiilmainham, for more than a century, is to be transferred to the building at the entrance from Dublin City to the Phcenix Pakit, hitherto used as the Royal Infirmary.
